teile.einleitung: Plant protection products are meant to protect crop plants from pests, diseases and weeds. There are many groups with different effects. Because they can also burden the environment and people, strict rules apply.
wichtigste: Herbicides work against plants, fungicides against fungi, insecticides against insects, acaricides against mites.
Glyphosate inhibits in plants the shikimic acid pathway, which animals do not have.
Several neonicotinoids were banned in the open because of bees.
Paul Hermann Müller of Basel received the Nobel Prize in 1948 for discovering the effect of DDT.
The maximum residue level and the waiting period protect food.
Systemic agents are distributed in the sap stream of the plant.

abschnitte.text: Plant protection products are named after their target. **Herbicides** inhibit or kill unwanted wild plants. **Fungicides** work against fungi, **insecticides** against insects and **rodenticides** against rodents. Against **mites** there are agents of their own, the **acaricides**. Mites belong to the **arachnids** and not to the insects.

Plant protection products work in two ways. **Contact agents** work only on the surface that has been treated. **Systemic agents**, on the other hand, are **taken up** by the plant and distributed in the **sap stream**. In this way they also protect parts that grow only later. A well-known herbicide is **glyphosate**. It blocks the enzyme EPSPS in the **shikimic acid pathway**, by which plants make certain amino acids. Animals do not have this metabolic pathway.

The Swiss chemist **Paul Hermann Müller** worked at the Basel firm **Geigy**. He discovered that the substance **DDT** works very well against insects. For this he received the **Nobel Prize** in Physiology or Medicine in **1948**, because DDT also helped against insects that transmit diseases. Later it turned out that DDT lasts a very long time in the environment. That is why it was banned in many countries.

**Neonicotinoids** are insecticides that act on the nerves of insects. They also harm pollinators such as **bees**. That is why three of these active substances were **banned for use in the open** in the EU and in Switzerland. For food, a **maximum residue level** applies to every active substance, that is, a permitted maximum amount. The **waiting period** between the last application and the harvest makes sure it is kept. Food inspection checks this.

In **June 2021** Switzerland voted on two popular initiatives: the **drinking water initiative** and the **pesticide initiative**. Both wanted to restrict the use of pesticides strongly. Supporters wanted to protect waters and health better. Opponents warned of lower yields and more imports. The people and the cantons **rejected both**.

gewusst: In Switzerland, plant protection products need approval from the Confederation before they may be sold.
Even in organic farming some plant protection products are allowed, for example certain agents made from natural substances.

teile.einleitung: The rose family is a large plant family with about 3,000 species. It includes not only roses, but also many fruit trees, berry bushes and well-known meadow plants.
wichtigste: Apple, pear and quince are pome fruits from the rose family.
Cherry, plum, apricot, strawberry, raspberry and blackberry also belong to it.
The flowers usually have five petals and many stamens.
Hawthorn and blackthorn are thorny hedge shrubs of this family.
Rose hips are the fruits of wild roses such as the dog rose.
Rowan, meadowsweet and lady’s mantle are also members of the rose family.

abschnitte.text: The flowers of the rose family are mostly **radially symmetrical**, which means they can be divided like a star into several equal parts. Typical are **five petals** and many stamens in the middle. This is easy to see in the wild rose, the apple blossom or the strawberry flower. Bred garden roses, on the other hand, often have very many petals. The flowers attract bees, bumblebees and other insects.

A large part of our fruit comes from the rose family. Apple, pear and quince are **pome fruits**: inside is a core with pips. Cherry, plum, apricot and peach are **stone fruits** with a hard stone. The raspberry is an **aggregate fruit**: it is made up of many tiny drupelets. In Switzerland, apples are the most important fruit from this family.

The **hawthorn** flowers white in May and bears small red fruits in autumn. Its thorns protect nesting birds. The **blackthorn**, also called sloe, has blue-black, very tart fruits that only taste milder after frost. The **dog rose** forms red rose hips with a lot of vitamin C, from which tea and jam are made. The **rowan** tree bears orange-red berries that many birds like to eat.

Not all members of the rose family are trees or shrubs. **Lady’s mantle** grows on meadows. In the morning, drops often glitter on the edge of its leaves. The plant releases these drops itself through water pores, which is called **guttation**. **Meadowsweet** grows on stream banks and in damp meadows. Its creamy-white flower heads smell of honey and almonds.

gewusst: Meadowsweet contains salicylic compounds that were used in the past against fever.
On the strawberry, the small yellow dots on the outside are the real fruits, namely tiny nutlets.

teile.einleitung: Pharmacognosy is the study of medicinal substances from nature. It examines substances from plants, fungi, animals and micro-organisms. It is a classic subject in the study of pharmacy.
wichtigste: Pharmacognosy deals with **biogenic medicinal substances**, that is, substances of biological origin.
A dried part of a plant as a starting material is called a **drug** in pharmacy.
Latin drug names show the part of the plant, such as Radix for root.
An **infusion** is a brew, a **decoction** a boiling down.
A **tincture** is an extract with ethanol.
In Switzerland the European Pharmacopoeia and the Pharmacopoea Helvetica apply.

abschnitte.text: In pharmacy, **drug** originally means a dried raw material from nature. It has nothing to do with narcotics. The word probably comes from Dutch “droog”, meaning dry. Examples are camomile flowers, peppermint leaves or valerian root. Pharmacognosy checks whether a drug is genuine, pure and of good quality.

Drugs carry Latin names that name the part of the plant. **Radix** means root, **Folium** leaf, **Cortex** bark and **Semen** seed. Valerian root, for example, is called “Valerianae radix”. In this way experts all over the world know exactly which part of which plant is meant.

In an **infusion** you pour boiling water over the drug and let it steep. This suits delicate leaves and flowers. Hard parts such as bark or roots are boiled, which is called a **decoction**. In a **maceration** you steep the drug cold. A **tincture** is an extract with a mixture of ethanol and water that keeps for a long time.

The requirements for medicinal drugs are set out in so-called **pharmacopoeias**. Switzerland applies the **European Pharmacopoeia**, the Pharmacopoea Europaea. The **Pharmacopoea Helvetica** supplements it with national rules. The treatment of illnesses with herbal medicines is called **phytotherapy**, from the Greek “phyton” for plant.

gewusst: The active substance of aspirin is related to salicylic acid, which occurs in the bark of willows.
The heart medicine digitoxin originally comes from the red foxglove, a poisonous plant.

teile.einleitung: Lichens are a partnership between a fungus and a partner that carries out photosynthesis. This partner is called the photobiont. It is a green alga or a cyanobacterium.
wichtigste: The **photobiont** is the partner in the lichen that carries out photosynthesis.
The most common green alga in lichens is **Trebouxia**.
A common cyanobacterium in lichens is **Nostoc**.
The photobiont supplies the fungus with carbohydrates, and the fungus offers protection and water.
The Swiss scientist Simon Schwendener recognised the dual nature of lichens in 1867.

abschnitte.text: In a lichen a fungus lives together with a photobiont. The photobiont uses light to make **carbohydrates**. Green algae release mainly sugar alcohols such as ribitol, cyanobacteria more often glucose. The fungus feeds on these. In return it offers protection against drying out and strong radiation, and takes up water and minerals.

The green alga **Trebouxia** occurs in very many lichen species, but is rare living freely in nature. The cyanobacterium **Nostoc** can also fix nitrogen from the air. Some lichens with green algae contain cyanobacteria in little chambers of their own. These are called **cephalodia** and mainly serve to fix nitrogen.

In a layered lichen body there is a cortex of fungal threads on top. Below it comes the **algal layer** with the photobiont. In this way it gets light and is still protected. Many lichens produce **soredia** as fine as dust: tiny grains of algal cells wrapped in fungal threads. This way both partners reach a new place together.

**Simon Schwendener** from the St Gallen Rhine Valley interpreted the green cells in lichens as algae in 1867. His theory was fiercely disputed at first, but is now considered confirmed. In 2016 researchers also found single-celled **yeasts** from the group of basidiomycete fungi in the cortex of many lichens. So a lichen is often a partnership of more than two partners.

gewusst: Lichens react sensitively to air pollutants and are therefore used to judge air quality.
Many lichens grow only a few millimetres a year.

teile.einleitung: **Quinoa** is a plant from the Andes whose seeds are eaten like grain. It has been grown for thousands of years in the highlands of Peru and Bolivia. Because it is gluten-free and nutritious, it is now popular all over the world.
wichtigste: Quinoa comes from the **Andes**.
It is a **pseudocereal**, because it is not a grass.
It belongs to the **amaranth family**.
The seeds are coated in bitter **saponins**.
For the **Incas** it was an important staple food.
Quinoa is **gluten-free**.
In 2013 the UN declared the International Year of Quinoa.

abschnitte.text: Quinoa has been grown for **thousands of years** in the highlands of **Peru** and **Bolivia**. It even grows there at heights of around **4,000 metres**. For the **Incas** it was an important staple food alongside potatoes and maize. They regarded it as a sacred plant. Even today, almost the entire world harvest comes from Peru and Bolivia.

True cereals such as **wheat** or **rice** are grasses. Quinoa is not a grass, but it produces similar seeds that are cooked like grain. That is why it is called a **pseudocereal**. It belongs to the **amaranth family**. It is related to amaranth, spinach and beetroot.

The seeds are coated in **saponins**. These are soap-like bitter substances on the skin of the seed. They protect the plant from birds and insects. To people they taste unpleasantly bitter. That is why quinoa has to be **washed thoroughly** before cooking.

People with **coeliac disease** cannot tolerate **gluten**, the sticky protein found in wheat, rye and barley. Quinoa contains no gluten, so it is suitable for them. In **2013** the **UN** declared the International Year of Quinoa. It wanted to draw attention to the value of the plant for feeding the world. After that, demand rose sharply around the world. Quinoa is now also grown in Europe, even in Switzerland.

gewusst: At home, quinoa is often cooked as a side dish like rice, but it can also be pressed into flakes.
Depending on the variety, the plant can have red, yellow or almost black seeds.

teile.einleitung: The **Ramsar Convention** is an international agreement to protect wetlands. It was concluded in 1971 in the city of Ramsar in Iran. Its secretariat is based in Gland in the canton of Vaud.
wichtigste: The Ramsar Convention protects **wetlands** of international importance.
It was concluded on 2 February 1971 in Ramsar in Iran.
At first the focus was on protecting **waterfowl and wading birds**.
The secretariat is in **Gland VD**.
2 February is World Wetlands Day.
Threatened sites are placed on the **Montreux Record**.
Swiss Ramsar sites include the Bolle di Magadino and Les Grangettes.

abschnitte.text: Its full name is the Convention on **Wetlands** of International Importance, especially as Waterfowl Habitat, meaning a home for **waterfowl and wading birds**. Wetlands include moors, marshes, lake shores, river deltas and floodplains. Many **migratory birds** depend on a chain of such sites to rest on their journeys. That is why protecting them needs many countries to work together.

The convention was concluded on **2 February 1971** in the city of **Ramsar** on the Caspian Sea in **Iran**. It is named after that city. 2 February is now **World Wetlands Day**. Since 2021 it has also been an official UN day.

Under Article 2 of the convention, each state names **at least one wetland** of international importance when it joins. This is placed on the Ramsar List. The state also promises to make **wise use** of all its wetlands. Sites whose ecological condition is getting worse or is under threat are on the **Montreux Record**. It is named after the conference of the contracting parties held in Montreux in 1990.

The **Ramsar Secretariat** is based in **Gland VD**, in the same building as the International Union for Conservation of Nature, the **IUCN**. There are Ramsar sites in Switzerland too. The **Bolle di Magadino** are a river delta with floodplain forest and reeds on Lake Maggiore, where the Ticino and the Verzasca flow in. **Les Grangettes** near Noville VD lie on the Rhône delta in Lake Geneva. Both are important resting places for waterfowl and migratory birds.

gewusst: The Ramsar Convention is one of the oldest worldwide nature conservation agreements.
The Montreux Record is named after a town on Lake Geneva, very close to the secretariat in Gland.

teile.einleitung: The phloem is the conducting tissue that distributes sugar in plants. In German it is called “Siebteil”, the sieve part. In trees it lies directly under the bark.
wichtigste: The phloem transports mainly **sugar**, which is made in the leaves.
In German the phloem is called **“Siebteil”**.
The conducting cells are called **sieve tubes**, and they are supplied by **companion cells**.
Sieve tube cells are alive but have no nucleus.
The sap flows upwards or downwards depending on need.
Aphids pierce the sieve tubes and suck the sugar sap.

abschnitte.text: In the leaves sugar is made by **photosynthesis**. The whole plant needs this, including the roots, buds and fruits. The phloem distributes the dissolved sugar to them. It works together with the **xylem**, the wood part that carries water up from the roots. Both often lie together in **vascular bundles**.

The **sieve tubes** consist of cells lined up one after another. Their cross walls have many fine pores like a sieve, hence the German name “Siebteil”. The sieve tube cells lose their nucleus as they develop, but stay alive. Next to each lies a **companion cell** with a nucleus. It takes over metabolic tasks for the sieve tube.

In the phloem the sap flows from where sugar is made or stored to where it is needed. In summer a lot of sugar flows from the leaves to the roots. In spring stored sugar can flow upwards to the new shoots. Ripening fruits also receive a lot of sugar.

If you remove the bark of a tree all the way round down to the wood, this is called **ringing**. The phloem is lost as well. The roots no longer get any sugar and the tree slowly dies. **Aphids** pierce the sieve tubes on purpose with their mouthparts. They pass out the surplus sugar as **honeydew**. The name phloem comes from the Greek “phloios” for bark.

gewusst: Bees collect honeydew from aphids. From it forest honey is made.
Some ants look after aphids and get the sweet honeydew from them.

teile.einleitung: Fungi are neither plants nor animals, but form a kingdom of living things of their own. What we see in the forest as a mushroom is only the fruiting body; most of it lives unseen in the soil. Some fungi are delicious, others deadly poisonous.
wichtigste: Fungi form a kingdom of their own; they are more closely related to animals than to plants.
The underground web of threads of a fungus is called the mycelium.
The visible mushroom with cap and stem is only the fruiting body.
Many fungi live with tree roots in a partnership called mycorrhiza.
The death cap causes most fatal mushroom poisonings in Europe.
In Switzerland you can have collected mushrooms checked at an official mushroom inspection.
In 1928 Alexander Fleming discovered the first antibiotic from a mould.

abschnitte.text: Fungi have no chlorophyll and so cannot carry out photosynthesis. They feed on other living things or their remains. Fungi include **basidiomycetes** such as the cep, but also moulds and single-celled yeasts. Experts estimate that there are several million species of fungi in the world, of which only a small part have been described.

The actual fungus is the **mycelium**, a fine web of threads in the soil or in wood. In wet weather it forms **fruiting bodies**, which grow out of the ground. A fruiting body usually consists of the stem and the cap. Under the cap lie gills or tubes, in which millions of tiny **spores** form.

Many fungi are **decomposers** and turn dead wood and leaves into soil. Others form a **mycorrhiza** with trees: the fungus supplies water and minerals, and the tree gives sugar back. The fly agaric, for example, lives together in this way with birches and spruces. Without fungi, the forests would be smothered in leaves and wood.

The **fly agaric** with its red cap and white spots is poisonous. Much more dangerous is the inconspicuous death cap, which can destroy the liver. Popular edible fungi are the cep, the button mushroom and the **“Eierschwämmli”**, which is called chanterelle elsewhere. In case of poisoning in Switzerland you can reach Tox Info Suisse on the emergency number 145.

If you collect mushrooms, you should have them checked at an official **mushroom inspection** before eating them. In many municipalities there are trained inspectors for this. Some cantons have rules, such as a maximum amount per person or protected days on which collecting is forbidden. In the Swiss National Park, collecting mushrooms is completely forbidden.

**Yeast** is a single-celled fungus that ferments sugar and so forms carbon dioxide. The little gas bubbles make bread dough rise. Moulds give cheeses such as Camembert their flavour. In 1928 Alexander Fleming discovered **penicillin** from a mould, and it has since saved countless lives.

begriffe.erklaerung: The underground web of threads of a fungus.
The visible part of the fungus with cap and stem.
Tiny reproductive cells of fungi.
A partnership between fungi and plant roots.
A place where experts check collected mushrooms.

gewusst: In the Ofenpass area in the canton of the Grisons grows a honey fungus whose mycelium spreads over several football pitches.
The cell walls of fungi contain chitin, the same substance that insect shells are made of.
A single large fruiting body can release billions of spores.

teile.einleitung: **Pyrophytes** are plants that are adapted to fire. They survive fires or even benefit from them. The word comes from the Greek “pyr”, which means fire.
wichtigste: Pyrophytes survive fires or even need them.
The **cork oak** protects itself with thick cork bark.
Some pines have **serotinous cones** that only open through heat.
Eucalypts sprout again after a fire from buds under the bark.
A **lignotuber** is a woody swelling with many buds.
Substances from smoke, the **karrikins**, trigger germination in some plants.
In the savanna pyrophytes are especially widespread.

abschnitte.text: In some regions fires happen regularly, for example in the **savanna**, in the Mediterranean region or in Australia. Plants that live there have developed special tricks. They are called **pyrophytes**. Some survive fires almost unharmed. Others even need the fire for their seeds to germinate.

The **cork oak** of the Mediterranean region has a particularly thick bark of cork. It insulates the living tissue against heat. In this way the tree survives fires that kill other trees. The Californian **giant sequoia** also has a very thick, fibrous bark. Fire removes litter and competition, so that its seeds can germinate on open mineral soil.

Some species of pine have **serotinous cones**. Resin often seals them for years. Only the heat of a fire melts the resin, and the cones open. The seeds then fall on freshly exposed ground. There they have little competition and a lot of light.

Many **eucalypts** in Australia have dormant buds, protected under the bark. After a fire they sprout anew along the trunk and branches. Other plants have a **lignotuber**. This is a woody swelling at the base of the trunk that stores reserves and carries many buds. If the shoot burns off, the plant grows back from it.

When plants burn, substances form that are called **karrikins**. They get into the soil with the smoke. In some plants they trigger **germination**. For the seeds this is a sign that light and space are available after the fire. In the savanna, grasses with protected buds also survive the regular grass fires.

gewusst: The cork for bottle corks comes from the cork oak, whose bark grows back after being stripped.
Some seeds germinate almost only after a fire, because they wait for the substances in smoke.

teile.einleitung: Phosphate fertilisers supply plants with the nutrient phosphorus. Without phosphorus no plant can grow. The raw material for it is scarce, and Switzerland has to import it.
wichtigste: Plants need phosphorus for energy transfer with **ATP** and for genetic material.
The largest reserves of rock phosphate lie in **Morocco**.
**Superphosphate** is made when rock phosphate is treated with sulphuric acid.
Phosphate hardly moves in the soil, because it is bound firmly.
Mineral phosphate fertilisers can contain **cadmium**.
From 2026, phosphorus must be recovered from sewage sludge in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Phosphorus is in **ATP**, the energy carrier of the cells. It is also part of DNA, RNA and the membranes of cells. Without phosphorus, energy metabolism and cell division do not work. Besides nitrogen and potassium, phosphorus is therefore among the most important nutrients in fertiliser.

Phosphate fertiliser is mostly made from **rock phosphate**, which is obtained by mining. By far the largest part of the world’s reserves lies in Morocco, including Western Sahara. Rock phosphate, often the mineral **apatite**, dissolves poorly. Treated with sulphuric acid, it becomes **superphosphate**, which dissolves in water and is taken up well by plants. In the 19th century **guano**, deposited droppings of seabirds from islands off Peru, was an important fertiliser.

Depending on the pH, phosphate combines with calcium or with iron and aluminium. These compounds dissolve poorly. That is why phosphate mostly stays where it was fertilised. Many plants live together with fungi, the **mycorrhiza**. The fine fungal threads reach much more soil than the roots, supply the plant with phosphate and get sugar in return.

Many rock phosphates naturally contain **cadmium** and in some cases uranium. These pollutants can build up in the soil with long fertilising. Too much phosphate getting into streams and lakes leads to strong algal growth. Switzerland has no phosphate deposits of its own. That is why the waste ordinance **VVEA** requires that from 2026 phosphorus be recovered from sewage sludge and animal meal.

gewusst: The element phosphorus was discovered in 1669 by Hennig Brand when he boiled down urine.
Nothing else can replace phosphorus: every living thing needs it.

teile.einleitung: A regional nature park is a larger area in Switzerland with especially beautiful nature and landscape. Unlike in a national park, ordinary people live and work there in villages.
wichtigste: The label “Park of National Importance” is awarded by the Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN).
There are three categories: national park, regional nature park and nature discovery park.
A regional nature park must be at least 100 square kilometres in size.
The label is valid for 10 years at a time.
Each municipality decides for itself whether to take part.
The parks are based on the Federal Act on the Protection of Nature and Cultural Heritage.

abschnitte.text: A **regional nature park** is a rural area with valuable nature, beautiful landscape and old villages. It is meant to **protect nature and the landscape** and at the same time strengthen a **sustainable economy**. Unlike the Swiss National Park, **villages, farming and businesses** are allowed there. Farmers, craftspeople and hotels carry on working, but are expected to take nature into account.

Switzerland has three categories of **Parks of National Importance**: the **national park**, the **regional nature park** and the **nature discovery park**. A nature discovery park lies close to a city and lets visitors experience wilderness. The basis for all three is the Confederation’s **Federal Act on the Protection of Nature and Cultural Heritage**. Well-known regional nature parks include the Parc Ela in the Grisons, the Gantrisch Nature Park in the canton of Bern and the Jurapark Aargau.

The label **“Park of National Importance”** is awarded by the **Federal Office for the Environment**, FOEN for short. A regional nature park must be at least **100 square kilometres** in size. The label is awarded for **10 years** at a time. After that, it is checked whether the park has achieved its aims, and the label can be renewed. The Confederation and the cantons also support the parks with money.

A nature park does not come into being from above. **Each municipality decides for itself** whether it wants to take part, often at the municipal assembly or at the ballot box. So the local population has a say. Some park projects have also failed because municipalities said no.

Cheese, meat, honey or timber from a park can carry the label **“Produkte Schweizer Pärke”**, meaning products of Swiss parks. It shows that a product **comes from a park** and was made there. This way local businesses benefit, and customers support the region. Many parks also offer hiking trails, guided tours and activities for school classes.

gewusst: The Swiss National Park in the Engadine was founded as early as 1914, long before the regional nature parks.
A regional nature park can extend across the borders of several cantons.

teile.einleitung: Paracelsus was one of the most famous doctors of the early modern period. He was born in what is now the canton of Schwyz and worked for a time in Basel. He wanted doctors to observe for themselves instead of only believing old books.
wichtigste: Paracelsus was born around 1493 in Egg near Einsiedeln in the canton of Schwyz.
He was a doctor, natural scientist and philosopher and travelled all over Europe.
In Basel he was town physician and gave lectures in German instead of Latin.
In 1527 he threw a work by the physician Avicenna into the St John’s fire.
He made remedies from minerals and metals and is regarded as a pioneer of medicinal chemistry.
He died in 1541 in Salzburg.

abschnitte.text: His real name was **Theophrastus Bombast von Hohenheim**. He was born around 1493 in **Egg near Einsiedeln** in what is now the canton of **Schwyz**. His father was a doctor there. He later gave himself the name **Paracelsus**. “Para” means roughly “beyond”, and the name is often interpreted as meaning that he wanted to surpass the famous Roman physician **Celsus**.

Paracelsus studied medicine and then travelled through many countries of Europe. Among other things he worked as a doctor with soldiers and in various towns. On the way he also learned from miners, craftsmen and healers. He was a doctor, **natural scientist** and **philosopher** all at once. He wrote many books, some of which were printed only after his death.

In 1527 Paracelsus became **town physician in Basel** and was allowed to teach at the university. At that time scholars taught almost only in **Latin**. Paracelsus, however, gave his lectures in **German**, so that more people understood him. At the St John’s fire he publicly threw a work by the famous physician **Avicenna** into the flames. In this way he protested against a medicine that only repeated old writings. Because of many quarrels he left Basel again soon afterwards.

Paracelsus wanted to use **alchemy**, from which chemistry later grew, for medicine. He made medicines from substances such as **mercury**, **sulphur** or **antimony**. That is why he is regarded as a **pioneer of medicinal chemistry**. Famous is his idea that the amount decides whether a substance heals or is poisonous. It is often summed up like this: “The dose makes the poison”.

Paracelsus also held ideas that no longer count today. One example is the **doctrine of signatures**. According to it, the look of a plant shows what it heals. A heart-shaped plant was therefore supposed to help the heart. Science has not confirmed this idea. Paracelsus died in 1541 in **Salzburg**.

gewusst: The sentence “The dose makes the poison” is still often quoted today in the study of poisons, toxicology.
In Einsiedeln the famous doctor who was born there is still remembered today.

teile.einleitung: Seed stock means seeds that are sown to grow new plants. Whether tomatoes in the garden or wheat in the field, good seed is the basis for every harvest.
wichtigste: Open-pollinated seed grows into plants like the parent plants.
With F1 hybrids, the offspring have uneven characteristics.
Seed is best stored cool, dry and dark.
Germination rate shows how many seeds can still germinate.
Rule of thumb: sow two to three times as deep as the seed is thick.
Light germinators are hardly covered with soil.
On Spitsbergen there is a large seed vault for seeds from all over the world.

abschnitte.text: With **open-pollinated** seed, the harvested seeds grow into plants with the same characteristics again. So you can collect your own seeds every year. It is different with **F1 hybrids**. They come about by deliberately crossing two different varieties. The first generation is often very productive and uniform. Their offspring, however, have **uneven characteristics**, so it is hardly worth harvesting your own seeds from them.

Many gardeners harvest seeds from open-pollinated varieties themselves. With **tomatoes**, the seeds are often left to **ferment** with the fruit juice for a few days. This dissolves the **germination-inhibiting gel layer** around each seed. After that the seeds are washed and dried. Seed is best stored **cool, dry and dark**, for example in paper bags in a cool place.

A **rule of thumb** says: sow about **two to three times as deep** as the seed is thick. So large beans go deeper into the soil than tiny carrot seeds. **Light germinators** need light to germinate, so they are hardly covered with soil. A **seed tape** is a paper strip on which the seeds are already stuck at the right spacing. This makes it much easier to sow very small seeds.

The **germination rate** shows how many seeds can still germinate. It is usually given as a percentage. It decreases over the years, faster in some species and slower in others. You can test it yourself: for example, you place ten seeds on damp kitchen paper and count after a few days how many have germinated.

To make sure that old and rare varieties are not lost, seeds are kept in **seed banks**. The largest seed vault in the world is on **Spitsbergen**, a group of islands far in the north of Norway. It is built into a mountain, and the seeds are stored there deep-frozen. In Switzerland, the foundation **ProSpecieRara** works to preserve old varieties of vegetables, fruit and farm animals.

gewusst: The seed vault on Spitsbergen was opened in 2008 and can hold millions of seed samples.
Lettuce is also among the light germinators.

teile.einleitung: Phytochrome is a light sensor in plants. It mainly measures red light and far-red light. In this way the plant notices whether it is standing in light, in shade or in the dark.
wichtigste: Phytochrome senses **red** at about 660 and **far-red** at about 730 nanometres.
Red turns the form Pr into the active form **Pfr**, and far-red turns it back.
In lettuce seeds, the colour of the last flash of light decides whether they germinate.
In shade a lot of far-red remains, so plants stretch.
The pigment in phytochrome is an open-chain **tetrapyrrole**.
Thale cress has five phytochromes, phyA to phyE.

abschnitte.text: Phytochrome occurs in two forms. **Pr** absorbs red light and becomes **Pfr** as a result. Pfr absorbs far-red light and becomes Pr again. The form Pfr is regarded as biologically active and triggers the light responses. The light-absorbing part is **phytochromobilin**, a linear tetrapyrrole. Blue light is picked up by other receptors, such as the **cryptochromes**.

Lettuce seeds only germinate after being lit. In the 1950s researchers in the USA lit such seeds alternately with red and far-red. If the sequence ended with red, the seeds germinated. If it ended with far-red, there was no germination. This showed that phytochrome can be switched back and forth.

Leaves absorb red light but let far-red through. Under a leaf canopy the ratio of red to far-red is therefore low. Phytochrome measures this and triggers **stretching growth**. The plant grows quickly upwards to escape the shade. Seedlings in complete darkness grow long, pale and with small leaves. This growth form is called **etiolation**.

**Short-day plants** flower when the nights are long enough. They measure the length of uninterrupted darkness. A short flash of red in the middle of the night forms Pfr and interrupts the night. Then there is no flowering. A following flash of far-red cancels this effect again.

gewusst: Nurseries use artificial light at night to control the flowering time of some ornamental plants.
Phytochromes do not occur only in plants; similar light sensors also exist in bacteria.

teile.einleitung: **Pollen** is a fine dust that flowers produce. It is carried from flower to flower by the wind or by animals such as bees. For bees pollen is important food, and some people get hay fever from it.
wichtigste: Pollen is the fine dust of flowers.
Grasses and hazel release their light pollen into the wind.
Bees carry pollen as little lumps on their hind legs, the **pollen baskets**.
Pollen is protein-rich food for the bee larvae.
In Switzerland hazel often sheds its pollen as early as February.
Some people react to pollen with **hay fever**.
Rain washes pollen out of the air.

abschnitte.text: Pollen consists of many tiny **pollen grains**. Plants need it so that flowers can later turn into fruits and seeds. For this the pollen has to reach another flower. This is called **pollination**. Single pollen grains are so small that you can only see their beautiful shapes under the **microscope**.

Grasses, **hazel** and many trees have very light pollen. The **wind** blows it far through the air to other plants. So that enough arrives, these plants make huge amounts of it. In spring it sometimes lies as a **yellow layer** on cars and windowsills. Hazel flowers very early; its yellow catkins often shed pollen in Switzerland as early as February.

Other flowers are pollinated by insects. **Bees** comb the pollen out of their fur and stick it to their hind legs. These lumps are called **pollen baskets**. In the hive the pollen serves as food for the **larvae**, because it contains a lot of protein. While collecting, the bees also carry pollen from flower to flower.

In some people the body reacts too strongly to pollen. The nose runs, you have to sneeze and the eyes itch. This is called **hay fever**. After **rain** people affected often feel better, because the drops bring the pollen out of the air to the ground. Pollen forecasts help people prepare for days with a lot of pollen.

gewusst: The pollen grains of every plant species have a shape of their own, and experts can tell the species from them.
In the mud of lakes pollen often survives for a very long time and reveals which plants used to grow there.

teile.einleitung: The horse chestnut is a large tree with hand-shaped leaves and white flower spikes like candles. In autumn children collect its shiny brown fruits for crafts.
wichtigste: The horse chestnut originally comes from the Balkans.
Its leaves look like a hand with fingers.
The white flower spikes stand upright like candles and mostly bloom in May.
The fruits sit in a green, spiky case.
In autumn the ripe horse chestnuts fall from the tree.
For people, horse chestnuts are inedible, unlike sweet chestnuts.
Deer and wild boar like to eat them.

abschnitte.text: The leaves of the horse chestnut are large and **hand-shaped**: from one stalk, usually five to seven leaflets grow like the fingers of a hand. The flowers stand in **upright flower spikes** that recall white candles. The horse chestnut mostly blooms **in May**. Each individual flower has a coloured patch that is first yellow and later red. This is how bees can tell which flowers still have nectar.

After flowering, the fruits grow. They sit in a **green, spiky case**. **In autumn** they fall from the tree, the case splits open, and the shiny brown chestnuts come out. For people they are **inedible** and slightly poisonous. **Deer and wild boar**, however, like to eat them. Foresters and gamekeepers sometimes collect them as winter food.

abschnitte.titel: Not to be confused with sweet chestnuts
abschnitte.text: The hot **marroni**, or roasted sweet chestnuts, sold at stalls in winter come from the **sweet chestnut tree**. In Switzerland this grows especially in Ticino. The sweet chestnut and the horse chestnut look alike, but they are not closely related at all. The case of the sweet chestnut has many fine, sharp spines, and its leaves are long and toothed. Horse chestnuts must not be roasted and eaten like marroni.

The horse chestnut originally comes from mountain forests in the **Balkans**. It reached central Europe in the 16th century. Today it grows in parks, avenues and school playgrounds, because it gives plenty of **shade** in summer. It was often planted in beer gardens to keep the cellars cool. Children make **little animal figures** from horse chestnuts and cocktail sticks.

gewusst: A small moth, the horse chestnut leaf miner, makes the leaves of many trees turn brown as early as summer.
Substances from horse chestnuts are used in ointments and remedies for the veins.

teile.einleitung: Trade winds are the most reliable winds on Earth. All year round they blow almost always from the same direction towards the equator. Even Christopher Columbus let them carry him across the Atlantic.
wichtigste: Trade winds are steady winds that blow from high to low pressure near the equator.
They blow between about 30 degrees latitude and the equator.
In the northern hemisphere they come from the north-east, in the southern hemisphere from the south-east.
The deflection comes from the rotation of the Earth.
At the equator the trade winds meet in the Intertropical Convergence Zone.
For centuries sailing ships used the trade winds to cross the Atlantic.
The trade winds are part of a big air circulation called the Hadley cell.

abschnitte.text: **Trade winds** are winds in the tropics and subtropics that blow very steadily. They arise between the high-pressure areas at about 30 degrees latitude and the low-pressure belt at the equator. Air always flows from high to low **air pressure**. That is why the trade winds blow constantly towards the equator.

At the equator the sun heats the ground and sea especially strongly. The warm air rises, and a low-pressure area forms at the ground. At height the air flows off to the north and south and sinks again at about 30 degrees latitude. This circulation is called the **Hadley cell**, after the Englishman George Hadley, who described it in 1735.

Because the Earth rotates, the trade winds do not blow exactly south or north. The **Coriolis force** deflects them to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern hemisphere. In this way the **north-east trade wind** and the south-east trade wind arise. Their names tell you which direction they come from.

In 1492 Christopher Columbus sailed with the north-east trade wind from the Canary Islands to America. Later, merchant ships used the trade winds regularly, which is why in English they are called **trade winds**. Feared, on the other hand, were the windless zones. In the **horse latitudes** and the doldrums at the equator, ships sometimes lay stuck for weeks.

Where the trade winds meet at the equator, moist air rises and forms huge thunderclouds. That is why it rains almost daily there, and rainforests grow. In the areas where the air sinks at 30 degrees, on the other hand, it is dry, and there lie great deserts such as the Sahara. The trade winds also drive ocean currents, for example the North Equatorial Current.

On islands such as the Canaries or Hawaii, the trade winds blow especially regularly. The side of the mountains that the wind hits is often green and rainy. The far side, on the other hand, stays dry. Surfers and sailors in these areas value the steady **trade wind** very much.

begriffe.erklaerung: The weight of the air pressing on a place.
The deflection of winds by the rotation of the Earth.
A big air circulation between the equator and the subtropics.
Zones of little wind at about 30 degrees latitude.

gewusst: The name “horse latitudes” is said to come from sailors having to throw horses overboard in a calm because the drinking water ran short.
Trade winds can carry Saharan dust as far as South America, where it fertilises the Amazon rainforest.
When the trade winds weaken in the Pacific, the weather phenomenon El Niño can arise.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland it is in principle forbidden to clear forest. This ban on clearing in the Forest Act makes sure that the forest area is kept and that the forest can continue to protect people.
wichtigste: Clearing is the permanent or temporary use of forest land for another purpose.
Clearing is forbidden, and exceptions need a permit.
For permitted clearing, replacement planting in the same area is usually required.
The Forest Police Act of 1876 laid the foundation for forest conservation.
The forest distance rule says how far buildings must be from the edge of the forest.
Article 77 of the Federal Constitution tasks the Confederation with protecting the forest.

abschnitte.text: Under the **Forest Act**, **clearing** is the **permanent or temporary use of forest land for another purpose**. So it is not about felling timber: foresters may fell trees as long as forest grows back. It only counts as clearing when the land is used for something else, for example a road, a house or a gravel pit. The basic rule is clear: **clearing is forbidden**. Exceptions need a **permit**, and for this there must be important reasons.

If clearing is permitted, **replacement in kind** usually has to be provided. This means that new forest is **planted** somewhere else **in the same area**. In this way the forest area stays the same size. In some cases the law allows measures for nature and landscape instead. A **forest distance** rule also applies: buildings must keep a **minimum distance from the forest edge**.

In the 19th century, many forests in the mountains were heavily felled. The wood was needed for heating, building and factories. After that there were **severe floods**, because the ground no longer held back the rainwater. That is why the Confederation passed the **Forest Police Act** in **1876**. It laid the foundation for **forest conservation** in Switzerland. Since then the forest area has grown again.

In the Alps the forest is especially important. It **protects against avalanches, rockfall and debris flows**. A debris flow is a stream of water, mud and stones. Many villages, roads and railway lines lie below **protection forests**. If these were cleared, people there would be in danger. This too is a reason for the strict ban on clearing.

The protection of the forest is even written into the **Federal Constitution**. **Article 77** tasks the Confederation with making sure that the forest can fulfil its **protective, productive and welfare functions**. The productive function means that it supplies wood. The welfare function means that it offers recreation, cleans air and water and gives animals and plants a habitat. The present Forest Act dates from **1991**.

gewusst: About a third of the area of Switzerland is covered by forest.
If forest grows by itself on an abandoned alpine pasture, after some time that area counts legally as forest.

teile.einleitung: Every plant consists of countless tiny building blocks, the plant cells. They are so small that you can see them only under the microscope. Even so, in every single one there is a small factory that can even make food from sunlight.
wichtigste: Plants are built of many plant cells.
The cell wall of a plant cell consists mainly of cellulose.
Plant cells have chloroplasts, animal cells do not.
The large vacuole stores cell sap and keeps the cell firm.
Robert Hooke was the first to describe cells in 1665, when he looked at cork under the microscope.
If you put a plant cell in strong salt water, it loses water and shrinks.
Most plant cells are only about a tenth to a hundredth of a millimetre in size.

abschnitte.text: On the very outside the plant cell has a firm **cell wall** of cellulose. It gives the cell shape and support, a little like cardboard. Directly under it lies the thin **cell membrane**, which decides which substances get in and out. Animal cells have only a membrane and no cell wall.

**Chloroplasts** are small green bodies in the cells of leaves and stems. They contain the pigment chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis. In a single leaf cell there can be dozens of them. Because animal cells have no chloroplasts, animals have to eat their food.

The **vacuole** is a large sac that often fills most of the cell. It stores cell sap with water, sugar, salts and sometimes pigments. When it is well filled, it presses against the cell wall, and the cell is firm. This internal pressure is called **turgor** and makes plants stand upright.

The **nucleus** contains the genetic information and controls the cell. In the cytoplasm float other parts, for example the **mitochondria**, the power stations of the cell. They gain energy from sugar, as in animals too. Through tiny channels in the cell wall, neighbouring cells are linked with one another.

The Englishman **Robert Hooke** looked in 1665 through a microscope that he had built himself at thin slices of cork. He saw small chambers and called them cells, after the Latin word for a small chamber. In 1838 Matthias Schleiden recognised that all plants consist of cells. A year later Theodor Schwann showed the same for animals.

If you put cells of a red onion in strong salt water, water flows out of the vacuole. The cell contents shrink and detach from the cell wall, which is called **plasmolysis**. In pure water the vacuole fills up again. That is why lettuce leaves wilt if you salt them too early.

begriffe.erklaerung: The firm covering of the plant cell made of cellulose.
A green body in the cell in which photosynthesis takes place.
A storage sac with cell sap in the plant cell.
The internal pressure that keeps the plant cell firm.
Shrinking of the cell contents through loss of water.

gewusst: Cellulose is the most common natural substance on Earth, and paper and cotton also consist largely of it.
Chloroplasts probably descend from bacteria that moved into other cells a very long time ago.
Onion skin is so thin that you can see its cells well even with a simple school microscope.

teile.einleitung: Phytotherapy is treatment with medicinal plants. The Greek word “phyton” means plant. For thousands of years people have used plants against ailments.
wichtigste: Phytotherapy means **herbal medicine**.
A dried part of a plant used as a remedy is called a **drug** in pharmacy.
In an **infusion** you pour hot water over the herbs.
A **tincture** is a plant extract made with alcohol.
Since 2009 complementary medicine has been in the Federal Constitution.
In Switzerland **Swissmedic** authorises medicines, including herbal ones.

abschnitte.text: Well-known medicinal plants are camomile, peppermint, fennel and valerian. In pharmacy a dried part of a plant such as camomile flowers or valerian root is called a **drug**. Here this has nothing to do with intoxicants. Many plants contain **essential oils**, which evaporate easily and smell strongly. Some relieve cramps or reduce inflammation.

In an **infusion** you pour boiling water over delicate parts such as flowers and leaves and let them steep. Hard parts such as roots are often boiled. For a **tincture** you put plant parts in alcohol. It dissolves the active substances out and makes the extract keep for a long time. There are also herbal tablets, ointments and drops.

You should only collect medicinal plants if you recognise them for certain. Some look confusingly like poisonous species, and a mix-up can be dangerous. Herbal remedies can also have side effects. St John’s wort, for example, can change the effect of other medicines. So if in doubt, you ask at the pharmacy or the doctor.

On 17 May 2009 the people and the cantons accepted a constitutional article on **complementary medicine**. Phytotherapy is part of it too. Herbal medicines need authorisation from **Swissmedic**, the Swiss authority for medicinal products. This checks whether they are safe and have the promised quality.

gewusst: The Chinese researcher Tu Youyou found the malaria drug artemisinin in sweet wormwood and received the Nobel Prize for it in 2015.
Many modern medicines are based on substances that were first discovered in plants.

teile.einleitung: The Salvinia effect describes how some surfaces hold a thin layer of air permanently under water. It is named after the floating fern Salvinia, whose leaves can perform this trick.
wichtigste: The effect is named after the floating fern Salvinia.
It describes a permanent layer of air under water.
The hairs on the leaves of Salvinia molesta look like whisks.
The tips of the hairs attract water, the rest repels it.
Salvinia molesta originally comes from South America.
In shipping, the effect is meant to reduce friction on the hull.
The backswimmer also holds a layer of air.

abschnitte.text: **Floating ferns** of the genus Salvinia are small ferns that drift on the surface of the water. A well-known species is **Salvinia molesta**. It originally comes from **South America** and has spread strongly in many warm countries. Its leaves are densely covered with hairs. Even when they are pushed under water, they stay dry, because a **layer of air** stays between the hairs.

The hairs on the leaves of Salvinia molesta have a special shape. Several fine hairs grow from one stalk and are joined at the tip. This makes them look like tiny **whisks**. The hairs are **water-repellent**. Only their tips **attract water**. There the water stays stuck as if glued. This traps the layer of air underneath so that it cannot escape.

Experts in **bionics** learn from nature in order to develop new technologies. The Salvinia effect was studied more closely by researchers around the botanist Wilhelm Barthlott. One idea is to coat ship hulls with a similar surface. A layer of air between hull and water would **reduce friction**. Ships could then use less fuel.

Some animals also make use of such layers of air. The **backswimmer**, a water insect, holds a layer of air on its body in a similar way to the floating fern. A thin layer of air that water insects use under water **for breathing** is called a **plastron**. Oxygen from the water can flow into this layer of air. In this way some insects can stay under water for a long time.

gewusst: Wilhelm Barthlott is also known for his research into the lotus effect, in which water simply beads off leaves.
Salvinia molesta is regarded in many countries as a troublesome water plant because it can cover whole lakes.

teile.einleitung: A leaf looks thin but consists of several layers. Just below the surface lies the palisade mesophyll. Here the leaf does most of its work with light.
wichtigste: The palisade mesophyll lies directly under the upper epidermis.
Its elongated cells stand upright and close together like fence posts.
The cells are full of chloroplasts.
Most of the leaf’s photosynthesis takes place in the palisade mesophyll.
Palisade and spongy mesophyll together form the mesophyll.
Sun leaves have a thicker palisade mesophyll than shade leaves.

abschnitte.text: On the very outside a leaf has a thin skin, the **epidermis**. It protects the leaf above and below. In between lies the green leaf tissue, the **mesophyll**. It consists of two parts: at the top the **palisade mesophyll**, below it the loose **spongy mesophyll**. Through the leaf also run the leaf veins, which carry water and sugar.

A **palisade** is a fence of closely set posts. This is just how the cells look under the microscope. They are elongated and stand **upright** to the leaf surface. In this way very many cells fit under the area on which the light falls. Between them there are only small gaps.

abschnitte.titel: The power station of the leaf
abschnitte.text: The palisade cells are densely filled with **chloroplasts**. In these green parts is the **chlorophyll**, and there **photosynthesis** takes place. Because the palisade mesophyll lies just under the upper epidermis, it gets the most light. That is why most of the sugar is made here. The dense green layer is also the reason why the upper side of many leaves is a darker green than the underside.

Even on the same tree, leaves are built differently. **Sun leaves** on the outside of the crown often have several layers of palisade cells. As a result they are thicker and use the strong light well. **Shade leaves** inside the crown are thinner and larger. In cross-section under the microscope you can see the difference at once in the palisade mesophyll.

Under the palisade mesophyll lies the **spongy mesophyll**. Its cells are irregularly shaped and leave large air spaces. Gases flow through these spaces. On the underside of the leaf lie the **stomata**, through which carbon dioxide gets in and oxygen and water vapour get out.

gewusst: Chloroplasts can move in the cell. In very strong light they turn to the side to protect themselves.
The leaves of most grasses have no typical palisade mesophyll, because they stand more upright.

teile.einleitung: The plane tree is a large broadleaved tree with striking, mottled bark. You often see it along streets and in squares in towns. Its leaves look similar to maple leaves.
wichtigste: The bark of the plane tree flakes off in **plates**.
Its fruits are small **balls** on long stalks.
The leaf looks very like a **maple leaf**.
Plane trees often grow along **streets** and in **squares**.
The seeds have **fine hairs** and fly on the wind.
Plane trees can grow **over 30 metres** tall.

abschnitte.text: The most striking thing about the plane tree is its bark. It keeps flaking off in **plates**. Underneath, lighter, young bark appears. This creates a pattern of grey, greenish and cream-coloured patches. This is how you recognise a plane tree even in winter.

The plane leaf has several pointed lobes like a **maple leaf**. That is why the commonest plane tree here is called the **London plane**, in German “Ahornblättrige Platane”, literally the maple-leaved plane. The fruits are rough **balls** on long stalks. They often hang on the tree until winter. In spring they break up into many small seeds with a ring of **fine hairs**, which fly away on the wind.

Plane trees cope well with **exhaust fumes**, heat and hard ground. That is why they often stand in avenues and squares in towns. Their broad crown with large leaves gives a lot of **shade** in summer. Beneath it is pleasantly cool on hot days. In Swiss towns too, plane trees line many streets and lakeside promenades.

Plane trees are large, strong trees. They can grow **over 30 metres** tall, as high as a house with ten storeys. As a **broadleaved tree** the plane sheds its leaves in autumn and rests in winter. In spring it sprouts anew.

gewusst: The London plane is probably a cross between the oriental plane and the American plane.
Plane trees can live to be several hundred years old.

teile.einleitung: **Cushion plants** grow very densely and flat as a round dome on the ground. In this way they survive cold, wind and short summers in the high mountains. In the Alps, moss campion and purple saxifrage are among the best-known examples.
wichtigste: Cushion plants form many short, closely packed shoots.
Inside the cushion it is often warmer than in the surroundings.
Old leaves stay in the cushion and store water and nutrients.
The flat, round shape lets the wind glide over it.
Cushion plants grow very slowly and can live for decades.
In the mountains you should not tread on cushions.

abschnitte.text: Life in the high mountains is hard: it is cold, windy and the summer is short. Cushion plants have developed a special way of growing. They form many short shoots that lie **tightly together**. This produces a dense, **domed cushion** that rises only a little above the ground. From far away it looks like a little pillow on the rock.

abschnitte.titel: A little heater of their own
abschnitte.text: Between the dense shoots the air hardly moves. The sun warms the cushion, and the **warmth stays** stored in it for a long time. That is why it is often warmer inside than in the surroundings. The **dead leaves** stay in the cushion and rot slowly. Like a sponge they hold on to moisture and supply nutrients.

A low, domed shape offers the **wind** hardly any surface to attack. It simply glides over the cushion. The plant is neither bent over nor dried out. Snow and ice crystals can also do less harm to it. So the shape is a clever adaptation to the harsh climate.

The **moss campion** forms flat, pink-flowering cushions on rock and scree. The **purple saxifrage** also grows as a low cushion and has violet flowers. It is among the flowering plants that climb highest in the Alps. In the Valais Alps it has been found at over 4,000 metres.

In the high mountains only a little warm time is left each year for growing. Cushion plants therefore grow **very slowly**. A large cushion can be many decades old. If it is trampled, it takes a very long time to recover. If you **stay on the paths**, you protect these special plants.

gewusst: A cushion the size of a plate can be older than the people hiking past it.
The purple saxifrage often flowers shortly after the snow melts.

teile.einleitung: The giant hogweed is a huge plant with white umbrella-shaped flower heads. It looks impressive, but it is dangerous: its sap makes the skin sore in sunlight.
wichtigste: The giant hogweed grows up to about 3 metres tall.
It originally comes from the Caucasus.
Its white flower heads can grow as big as a bicycle wheel.
It flowers in summer.
Its sap causes blisters like burns in sunlight.
If sap gets on your skin: wash it off at once and avoid the sun.

abschnitte.text: The **giant hogweed** comes from the **Caucasus**, a mountain range between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea. It was brought to Europe as an ornamental plant in the 19th century. It can grow **up to about 3 metres** tall. Its stem is thick, hollow and often spotted red. The leaves are huge and deeply cut. It belongs to the **umbellifers**, like carrot and fennel.

abschnitte.titel: Flower heads as big as a bicycle wheel
abschnitte.text: The giant hogweed flowers in **summer**. Its flowers are **white** and sit in large umbrella shapes, the **umbels**. These can grow **as big as a bicycle wheel**. A single plant produces very many seeds. This is how it spreads quickly, along stream banks, woodland edges and paths. There it pushes out native plants.

The sap of the giant hogweed contains substances that make the skin **sensitive to light**. If sap gets on the skin and the **sun** then shines, **blisters like burns** appear. They heal slowly and can leave scars. That is why you should **never make pea-shooters** or toys from the hollow stems. It is best not to touch the plant at all.

If sap has got on your skin, you should wash the area thoroughly at once with **water and soap** and then **avoid the sun**, ideally for several days. If there are strong skin reactions, go to the doctor. Anyone who spots a giant hogweed can report it to the **municipality**. Experts remove the plant wearing protective clothing.

Plants that people have brought in from distant regions are called **neophytes**. If they spread strongly and harm nature, they are called **invasive**. The giant hogweed is an invasive neophyte in Switzerland. It may not be sold or planted here.

gewusst: The giant hogweed usually flowers only once in its life, and then the plant dies.
The skin damage is not caused by the sap alone, but only by its interaction with sunlight.

teile.einleitung: Some animals and plants are becoming rarer and rarer and could soon disappear. To notice this in good time, experts keep Red Lists. Like a traffic light, they show how seriously a species is threatened.
wichtigste: If a species is on the Red List, its population is under threat.
The best-known Red List is that of the International Union for Conservation of Nature, the IUCN.
The IUCN has its headquarters in Gland in the canton of Vaud.
Species are divided into categories from not threatened to extinct.
Switzerland also keeps its own Red Lists, published by the Federal Office for the Environment.
In Switzerland about a third of the species studied are threatened.
Red Lists help to plan protection measures and to preserve habitats.

abschnitte.text: A **Red List** is a register that shows how seriously species of animals, plants and fungi are threatened. The colour red stands as a warning signal. The worldwide list has been kept by the **IUCN** since the 1960s. In addition, many countries and regions have their own Red Lists.

The IUCN divides species into levels, much like a traffic light. They range from **least concern**, through near threatened, vulnerable and endangered, to critically endangered. Then come extinct in the wild and fully **extinct**. For some species there is simply not enough data.

Experts count how many animals or plants of a species are still alive and how fast the population is falling. They also check how large the **range** is and whether it is broken up. From this, the threat level is worked out according to fixed rules. The lists are revised regularly, because the situation can change.

In Switzerland the **Federal Office for the Environment**, together with specialist bodies, publishes Red Lists for birds, amphibians, plants, insects and many other groups. Species of wetlands, dry meadows and waters are especially threatened. Examples are the tree frog and many dragonflies. The main causes are the loss of habitats, intensive farming and building development.

Targeted protection can help species to recover. The **bearded vulture** was wiped out in the Alps and has been reintroduced since 1986, in Switzerland since 1991. The beaver, the ibex and the lynx have also returned to Switzerland. Worldwide, the mountain gorilla, for example, has recovered somewhat thanks to protection measures.

Natural gardens with native plants, hedges and piles of stones offer a habitat to many animals. A small **pond** without fish can help amphibians and dragonflies. Staying on the paths and not picking protected plants spares nature. Anyone who wants to know more can join nature conservation organisations or report species.

begriffe.erklaerung: A register of threatened species of animals, plants and fungi.
The International Union for Conservation of Nature, based in Gland in the canton of Vaud.
The number of living things of a species in an area.
Not a single living thing of this species is alive any more.

gewusst: On the worldwide Red List, more than 40,000 species are considered threatened.
The IUCN was founded in 1948 and today brings together states and nature conservation organisations from all over the world.
There are also Green Lists, which show where conservation efforts have been especially successful.

teile.einleitung: Plasmodesmata are fine channels through the cell walls of plant cells. They join the insides of neighbouring cells to one another. In this way substances can travel directly from cell to cell.
wichtigste: Plasmodesmata are fine **bridges of cytoplasm** through the cell walls.
Through them neighbouring cells exchange substances.
Plasmodesmata are typical of **plants**.
In animal cells, **gap junctions** have a similar job.
All the cell contents joined in this way form the **symplast**.
Many plasmodesmata lie in thin places in the wall, the **pits**.

abschnitte.text: Plant cells are surrounded by firm **cell walls**. Without connections they would be cut off from one another. Plasmodesmata are tiny channels through these walls. Through them the **cytoplasm** of neighbouring cells is joined. In the middle of many plasmodesmata runs a fine tube that belongs to the cell’s inner membrane system.

Through plasmodesmata **water**, **sugar** and messenger substances travel directly from cell to cell. Even some proteins get through. In this way cells can coordinate with one another and pass on nutrients. Animal cells have no cell walls. In them, channels made of proteins, the **gap junctions**, take on a similar job.

Through the plasmodesmata, the cell contents of a plant form one connected network. This is called the **symplast**. The space of the cell walls outside it is called the **apoplast**. So substances can travel either through the inside of the cells or through the cell walls. Particularly many plasmodesmata lie in the **pits**, places where the cell wall stays thin.

A large part of the plasmodesmata arise during **cell division**. When the new cell wall is built, fine connections stay open. These become the plasmodesmata. These routes are also used by **plant viruses**. Many have special transport proteins with which they widen the channels and travel from cell to cell.

gewusst: Plasmodesmata were described in 1879 by the botanist Eduard Tangl.
Plasmodesmata are so fine that you can only really see them with an electron microscope.

teile.einleitung: Mushroom poisoning happens when you eat poisonous or spoiled mushrooms. Some mushroom poisons are very dangerous and act only late. That is why identifying mushrooms safely is so important.
wichtigste: The most dangerous poison of the **death cap** is called **amanitin**.
In the **fly agaric**, ibotenic acid and muscimol act on the nervous system.
Spoiled edible mushrooms can cause a **false mushroom poisoning**.
If you suspect poisoning, get medical help **at once**, even without symptoms.
The silver spoon test is a dangerous mistake.
**VAPKO** is the association of official mushroom inspectors in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The **death cap** contains **amanitin**. This poison inhibits a vital process in the body’s cells. Cooking, frying or drying do not destroy it. The **fool’s webcap** contains orellanine, which damages the kidneys. The damage often shows only after several days. The **fly agaric** contains ibotenic acid and muscimol, which can cause confusion and cramps.

Some poisonous mushrooms look like edible ones. The orange **jack-o’-lantern mushroom** can be mistaken for the chanterelle. It grows in clusters on wood and has true, thin gills. It causes violent vomiting and diarrhoea. The **brown roll-rim** was once considered edible. After several meals, however, the body can form defence substances that destroy its own red blood cells. It is now considered poisonous.

Edible mushrooms can also make you ill. They contain a lot of protein and water and therefore spoil quickly. Old mushrooms, or ones stored for a long time in plastic, can cause stomach and bowel upsets. This is called **false mushroom poisoning**. That is why you collect only fresh mushrooms, carry them in a basket and use them soon.

abschnitte.titel: What to do in an emergency
abschnitte.text: With some poisonous mushrooms, symptoms appear only when organs are already damaged. That is why, if you suspect poisoning, you get medical help **at once**, even if you still feel well. The earlier treatment starts, the better the chances. Old household rules do not help: a **silver spoon** does not turn black with the death cap. Only the mushroom inspection is reliable, and its experts are often trained by **VAPKO**.

gewusst: The death cap is responsible for most fatal mushroom poisonings in Europe.
In Switzerland you can reach Tox Info Suisse round the clock on the number 145.

teile.einleitung: Photosynthesis is perhaps the most important process on Earth. In it green plants use sunlight to make their own food. As a by-product, the oxygen we need for breathing is produced.
wichtigste: In photosynthesis, plants use sunlight to make food.
The starting materials are carbon dioxide and water.
Glucose is produced, and oxygen as a by-product.
Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts.
Leaves look green because chlorophyll reflects green light.
Many plants store the sugar as starch, for example in the potato.
According to the overall equation, twelve molecules of oxygen are produced for two molecules of glucose.

abschnitte.text: The word **photosynthesis** means roughly “putting together with light”. Plants, algae and some bacteria use the energy of sunlight to make sugar from simple substances. They are therefore the basis of almost all **food chains**. People and animals also live, in the end, from this energy.

The plant takes in **carbon dioxide** from the air and water from the soil. From these it makes glucose, that is, **glucose** (grape sugar), and gives off oxygen. The overall equation reads: 6 CO2 and 6 H2O, with light, give C6H12O6 and 6 O2. So for two molecules of glucose, twelve molecules of oxygen are released.

Photosynthesis takes place in the **chloroplasts**, small green bodies in the leaf cells. They contain the pigment **chlorophyll**, which captures red and blue light. Green light is reflected, which is why leaves look green. In autumn the chlorophyll is broken down, and yellow and red pigments become visible.

With the sugar the plant gains energy and builds new cells, for example from cellulose. Surplus sugar it often stores as **starch**. The potato keeps starch in its tubers, cereals in their grains. When we eat bread, rice or chips, we are therefore using stored solar energy.

The Englishman Joseph Priestley showed in 1771 that a plant makes air breathable again in which a candle had gone out. The Dutchman **Jan Ingenhousz** found out in 1779 that plants need light for this. Much later the American Melvin Calvin worked out how the carbon is built into sugar. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1961.

Through the photosynthesis of bacteria and plants, oxygen entered the atmosphere over billions of years. A large part of today’s oxygen comes from the sea, where tiny **plankton** carry out photosynthesis. Plants also remove carbon dioxide from the air and so slow climate change. Coal, oil and natural gas were also formed from living things that once stored solar energy.

begriffe.erklaerung: The green leaf pigment that captures light.
The green cell body in which photosynthesis takes place.
Grape sugar, the main product of photosynthesis.
A storage form of sugar, for example in potatoes and cereals.

gewusst: A sprig of a water plant in a glass forms visible oxygen bubbles in the sun.
The oxygen from photosynthesis comes from the water, not from the carbon dioxide.
Without photosynthesis there would be no ozone layer, because ozone is made from oxygen.

teile.einleitung: Fish and many small animals breathe the oxygen that is dissolved in the water. How much of it there is depends on the temperature, on plants and on the movement of the water.
wichtigste: Cold water can dissolve more oxygen than warm water.
At 20 degrees, a litre of water dissolves at most about 9 milligrams of oxygen.
Deep lakes are completely mixed in spring and autumn.
In summer the thermocline separates warm and cold lake water.
In ponds rich in plants, oxygen is scarcest in the early morning.
Stonefly larvae indicate clean, oxygen-rich water.

abschnitte.text: Oxygen from the air dissolves in water. The **colder** the water is, the more gas it can take up. At 0 degrees it is about 14 milligrams per litre, at 20 degrees only about 9 milligrams. In hot summers, things therefore get tight for fish. Trout and grayling need cool, oxygen-rich water.

A fast-flowing **mountain stream** is usually very rich in oxygen. The water is cold and is strongly **churned up** over stones. A lot of air gets in as a result. Sensitive animals such as **stonefly larvae** live here. They need a lot of oxygen and hardly tolerate pollution. If you find them, the stream is usually clean.

In summer the surface of a deep lake warms up, while the water below stays cold. Between them lies the **thermocline**, where the temperature drops sharply over a few metres. It prevents the upper and lower water from mixing. In **spring and autumn** the water has about the same temperature everywhere. Then the wind can turn over the whole lake and bring oxygen down to the bottom.

abschnitte.titel: Day and night in the pond
abschnitte.text: During the day, water plants and algae give off oxygen through **photosynthesis**. At night they cannot do this, but they go on using oxygen for breathing. Animals and bacteria also breathe all night. That is why the oxygen content in a pond rich in plants is usually lowest **in the early morning**.

If too many nutrients get into a lake, many algae grow. When these die and are broken down on the bottom, a lot of oxygen is used up there. Some lakes in the canton of Lucerne, such as **Lake Baldegg**, have therefore been artificially **aerated** for decades. More important, though, is that fewer nutrients get into the water, for example thanks to sewage treatment plants.

gewusst: A litre of water contains much less oxygen than a litre of air.
Fish take up the dissolved oxygen with their gills.

teile.einleitung: Boletes, or pore fungi, have no gills on the underside of their cap but a spongy layer of fine tubes. They include popular edible mushrooms such as the cep, but also bitter and poisonous species.
wichtigste: Boletes have a spongy underside to the cap made of tubes.
The small openings of the tubes are called pores.
The spores form on the inner walls of the tubes.
The cep is a popular bolete.
The bitter bolete looks similar but is very bitter.
The larch bolete grows near larches.
Satan’s bolete, with its red stem, is poisonous.

abschnitte.text: Many mushrooms have thin blades under the cap, the **gills**. Boletes are different: the underside of their cap looks like a **sponge**. It is made up of many fine **tubes** standing close together. The small openings at the bottom are called **pores**. The **spores** are formed on the **inner walls of the tubes**. They trickle out and are spread by the wind.

Many boletes live closely with particular trees. Their fine fungal threads wrap around the tree roots. The fungus supplies the tree with water and minerals, and the tree gives the fungus sugar. This partnership is called **mycorrhiza**. The **larch bolete**, for example, grows only near the **larch**. The cep is often found near spruces, beeches or oaks.

If you press on the tubes of many boletes or cut into them, they **turn blue**. This is caused by substances in the fungus that react with the oxygen in the air. This colour change is not dangerous and says nothing about whether a mushroom is edible. It does help experts to tell different species apart.

The **cep** is one of the most popular edible mushrooms. The **bitter bolete** looks similar to it. It is not poisonous, but it is so **bitter** that a single mushroom spoils a whole dish. **Satan’s bolete** has a red stem, smells unpleasant and is **poisonous**. In Switzerland, many municipalities offer an **official mushroom inspection**. You should always have the mushrooms you have gathered checked there.

gewusst: In many boletes the tube layer can easily be peeled away from the flesh of the cap.
A large cep can weigh more than a kilogram.

teile.einleitung: Parsley is one of the best-known kitchen herbs. You sprinkle it over potatoes, soups and salads. The plant comes from the Mediterranean region and is related to the carrot.
wichtigste: There are mainly curly and flat-leaf parsley.
Parsley belongs, like the carrot, to the umbellifers.
Fresh parsley contains a lot of vitamin C.
Parsley is biennial and mostly flowers in the second year.
In root parsley, it is mainly the root that is eaten.
Flat-leaf parsley can be confused with the poisonous fool’s parsley.

abschnitte.text: In the shop you mostly find two kinds. **Curly parsley** has frilly leaves and looks pretty as a decoration. **Flat-leaf parsley** has flat leaves and usually tastes stronger. Both belong to the same species. The plant originally comes from the **Mediterranean region** and today grows in many gardens and on balconies.

Parsley belongs to the plant family of the **umbellifers**. This also includes the **carrot**, celery, dill and caraway. You can recognise the family by the flowers: many small flowers sit on stalks that spread from one point like the spokes of an umbrella. Such a flower head is called an **umbel**.

Parsley is **biennial**. In the first year it forms only leaves, which you can harvest continually. In the **second year** a tall stem grows with yellow-green umbels of flowers. Then it forms seeds and dies. The leaves then no longer taste so fine. In **root parsley** it is mainly the thick, pale root that is eaten. You cook it like a vegetable in soups.

Fresh parsley contains a lot of **vitamin C**. Eaten raw it is therefore especially healthy, because part of the vitamin is lost in cooking. Very popular are **parsley potatoes**: boiled potatoes with butter and chopped parsley. It is best to put the herb on the food only at the end.

Flat-leaf parsley looks similar to **fool’s parsley**. This grows wild and is **poisonous**. Other poisonous umbellifers also look similar. That is why you do not simply pick herbs in the wild, but take them from your own garden or buy them.

gewusst: By weight, fresh parsley contains more vitamin C than a lemon.
Parsley seeds germinate very slowly. It can take several weeks until the first little leaves appear.

teile.einleitung: The rose is regarded as the “queen of flowers”. It is one of the most popular plants in gardens and bouquets, known for its beautiful flowers and delicate scent.
wichtigste: The rose is often called the “queen of flowers”.
Many roses have a lovely scent.
A red rose is given as a sign of love.
A simple wild rose usually has 5 petals.
The apple belongs to the same plant family as the rose.
Garden roses are cut back hard in spring.
A rose needs a lot of sun to flower well.

abschnitte.text: The **rose** has been admired for a long time and is often called the **“queen of flowers”**.
