There are thousands of varieties in many colours, from white through yellow and pink to dark red. Many roses have a **lovely scent**. A **red rose** is given as a **sign of love**. Roses appear in poems, fairy tales and coats of arms.

Roses originally grew wild. A simple **wild rose**, such as the dog rose at the edge of a wood, usually has **5 petals**. In autumn its flowers turn into red **rose hips**. Garden roses have been bred over centuries and often have many more petals, which make the flower look full. The sharp parts on the stem are, by the way, **prickles**, not thorns: they can easily be broken off.

The rose belongs to the **rose family**. Many kinds of fruit also belong to this family: the **apple**, the pear, the cherry, the plum and the strawberry. If you look closely, you can see that apple blossoms and wild rose blossoms look alike. They too have five petals.

abschnitte.titel: Caring for roses in the garden
abschnitte.text: A rose needs **plenty of sun** to flower well, and good, loose soil. In **spring** garden roses are **cut back hard**, and they then sprout strongly again. In **summer** you cut off **faded flowers** so that **new flowers** come. A **climbing rose** pulls itself up walls, fences and arches. Its long shoots are tied to a support.

In Switzerland, **Rapperswil** on Lake Zurich is known as the **city of roses**. There are several rose gardens there with many different varieties. In many castle gardens and public parks, too, large rose beds bloom in summer. Jam or tea is made from the rose hips of wild roses.

gewusst: To make a single litre of rose oil you need several tonnes of rose petals.
Rose hips contain a lot of vitamin C.

teile.einleitung: Biochar is made when plant remains are heated strongly without oxygen. It looks like barbecue charcoal but is used mainly for soils and in agriculture. Because it stores carbon for a long time, it is also regarded as a help for the climate.
wichtigste: Biochar is made by pyrolysis in a lack of oxygen.
Its many pores give a very large inner surface.
In the soil its carbon is broken down only very slowly, so it is a carbon sink.
Before being worked in, it is charged with nutrients, for example with compost.
The English technical term is biochar.
In animal husbandry it serves as a feed additive.

abschnitte.text: Wood remains, green cuttings or other **biomass** are heated strongly without, or with very little, **oxygen**. The process is called **pyrolysis**. The biomass does not burn in the process but is **charred**. Combustible **pyrolysis gases** form. In modern plants they are burned in a combustion chamber. The heat keeps the pyrolysis going and can also be used for heating.

Biochar is full of tiny **pores**. This gives it a huge **inner surface**. It can hold on to **water** and **nutrients**. In addition, **micro-organisms** find a habitat in the pores. That is why biochar can make a soil looser and more fertile.

As they grow, plants take **carbon dioxide** from the air. When they rot, it goes back into the air. In biochar, on the other hand, the carbon is in very stable ring structures. It is broken down in the soil **only very slowly** and stays there for a long time. That is why biochar is regarded as a **carbon sink**. The English technical term is **biochar**, from “bio” and “char” for charred material.

abschnitte.titel: Charge first, then into the soil
abschnitte.text: Fresh, uncharged biochar soaks up nutrients like a sponge. If you put it straight into the earth, it would take nutrients away from the plants. So it is first **charged**. You mix it with **compost**, **slurry** or dung. Later it releases the nutrients slowly to the plants.

Barbecue charcoal and biochar are both made by charring. The difference lies in the **purpose of use**. Biochar for the soil has to meet strict **quality requirements**, for example low levels of pollutants. In **animal husbandry**, small amounts are mixed into the feed as **feed charcoal** to support digestion. Through the dung the charcoal later also gets into the soil.

gewusst: In the Amazon region there are very fertile, dark soils called terra preta. They contain a lot of charcoal that people added long ago.
A single gram of biochar can have an inner surface of several hundred square metres.

teile.einleitung: Rendzina is a soil type that forms on limestone or dolomite. It is dark, stony and not very deep, and in Switzerland it is especially common in the Jura.
wichtigste: A rendzina forms on limestone or dolomite.
Typical is the sequence of an Ah horizon over a C horizon.
The name comes from Polish.
Rendzinas are especially common in the Jura.
They store little water.
Their pH value is neutral to slightly alkaline.

abschnitte.text: Soils form over a very long time from rock that weathers. The **rendzina** forms on **limestone** or **dolomite**. It is **shallow**, which means that after only a few centimetres to decimetres you hit stones or solid rock. Experts describe soils in layers, called **horizons**. Typical of the rendzina is **Ah over C**: at the top is a dark, humus-rich layer (Ah), and directly below it the parent rock (C).

In Switzerland, rendzinas are especially common in the **Jura**, because there is a lot of limestone there. They are also found in the **Limestone Alps**, often on slopes. The name **rendzina** comes from **Polish**. It is said to recall the sound a plough makes when it scrapes over stony ground. The soil is usually rich in lime and has a **neutral to slightly alkaline pH value**.

Because the rendzina is so thin and stony, it **stores little water**. In dry summers, plants there soon suffer. It is therefore not very suitable for arable farming. On the other hand, **semi-dry grasslands** often grow on sunny slopes, species-rich meadows with many flowers, butterflies and sometimes orchids. Beech woods also thrive on rendzinas.

gewusst: On semi-dry grassland over rendzina, dozens of plant species can grow in just a few square metres.

teile.einleitung: The parasol mushroom is one of the largest mushrooms in our woods. Its flat, wide cap recalls a sunshade. It is a popular edible mushroom, but you must be sure to recognise it.
wichtigste: “Parasol” is the French word for sunshade.
The parasol mushroom is also called the giant umbrella mushroom (“Riesenschirmling” in German).
Its cap can grow about 25 centimetres wide.
On the stem sits a thick ring that can be slid up and down.
The stem is long and has a brown snakeskin pattern.
You eat only the cap, often breaded like a schnitzel.

abschnitte.text: The **parasol mushroom** gets its name from the French word for **sunshade**. Another name is **giant umbrella mushroom** (“Riesenschirmling” in German). The opened cap is flat and wide and can grow about **25 centimetres** across, as big as a big plate. On the pale cap sit brown scales, and in the middle it is darker. Young mushrooms look quite different: their cap is closed and round like a drumstick.

Typical is the **stem**. It is long and slender and has a brown pattern that recalls **snakeskin**. At the top of the stem sits a thick **ring**. You can slide it up and down the stem. Under the cap lie white **gills**, fine little blades in which the spores are formed.

The parasol mushroom likes bright places. You find it at **woodland edges**, in **clearings** and on meadows, mostly from summer into autumn. It feeds on dead plant remains in the soil. Often several mushrooms stand together nearby.

With the parasol mushroom you eat only the **cap**. The stem is tough and fibrous. The large, flat cap can be **breaded** like a schnitzel and fried. That is why it is also called the **mushroom schnitzel**. Mushrooms should always be cooked through well.

There are smaller umbrella mushrooms that are very poisonous and look like the parasol. So the rule is: eat only mushrooms that you know for certain. In Switzerland, many municipalities have a **mushroom inspection**. There trained experts check the collected mushrooms free of charge. Children should never collect or try mushrooms without adults.

gewusst: A large parasol mushroom can grow over 30 centimetres tall and so is among the largest gilled mushrooms in Europe.
A good identifying mark is the movable ring on the stem.

teile.einleitung: A **Plenterwald**, or selection forest, is a forest in which young, middle-aged and old trees grow mixed together on the same area. It is never cut down completely; only single trees are felled at a time. In Switzerland there are famous examples, above all in the Emmental and in the Jura.
wichtigste: In a selection forest, trees of all ages stand side by side.
The forest has a tiered structure from the ground to the crowns.
Only single trees are ever harvested, never whole areas.
Typical tree species are silver fir, spruce and beech.
The Emmental is a classic selection forest region.
The forester Henri Biolley from Neuchâtel made selection forestry known internationally.
In Switzerland clear-felling is forbidden by the Forest Act.

abschnitte.text: In a selection forest small, medium and large trees grow closely mixed. This structure is called **tiered**, because the green reaches from the ground right up into the crowns. So there are no areas where only trees of the same age stand. The forest therefore always looks similar, even after many years. The German word “plentern” means roughly to take out single trees.

The forester keeps choosing single trees that are ripe or that disturb others. Only these are felled. In this way the forest stays permanently **closed** and renews itself all the time. The opposite would be **clear-felling**, in which a large area is cut down at once. The Federal Forest Act forbids clear-felling in Switzerland in principle.

Under the dense canopy of the big trees only a little light gets through. Young trees therefore have to put up well with **shade** and often wait a long time until a gap appears. **Silver fir**, **spruce** and **beech** can do this above all. These three tree species therefore form the classic selection forests of Switzerland. When a big tree is felled, the waiting young trees grow upwards faster.

In the **Emmental** the farmers’ forests have been managed by selection for generations. There stand some of the most impressive selection forests in Europe. In the Jura of Neuchâtel, the forester **Henri Biolley** managed forests in the Val-de-Travers on this principle from the end of the 19th century. He measured the timber stock regularly in order to know exactly how much wood he was allowed to harvest. In this way he became known far beyond Switzerland.

Many forests in the mountains protect villages and roads from avalanches, rockfall and landslides. A selection forest is well suited to this, because it **never has big gaps**. The ground stays constantly covered by forest, and the protective effect never stops. The forest also keeps providing timber without disappearing. That is why selection forestry is regarded as a particularly **sustainable** way of using a forest.

gewusst: A selection forest can look almost the same over many decades, although trees are being harvested all the time.
Henri Biolley checked the timber stock of his forests with regular measurements, an idea that was new at the time.

teile.einleitung: If you collect mushrooms, you should have them checked before eating them. In many Swiss municipalities there is an official mushroom inspection for this. There experts look at every mushroom closely.
wichtigste: You take collected mushrooms to the **mushroom inspection**.
The expert is called a **mushroom inspector**.
You bring mushrooms **whole, with the stem**, to the inspection.
It is best to carry mushrooms in a **basket**.
You must never taste unknown mushrooms.
You have the mushrooms checked **every time** after collecting.

abschnitte.text: In many Swiss municipalities there is an official **mushroom inspection**. There trained **mushroom inspectors** check every collected mushroom. They recognise which mushrooms are edible and which are poisonous. Poisonous or spoiled mushrooms are sorted out. Many inspectors are trained by the association **VAPKO**.

For the inspection you need the **whole mushroom**. The stem and its bulb at the base also help with identifying. It is best to carry mushrooms in a **basket**. There they get air and are not crushed. In a plastic bag they spoil quickly.

You must **never taste** an unknown mushroom. Some mushrooms are deadly even in the tiniest amounts. Nibble marks from snails or other animals also do not show that a mushroom is edible. An **app** recognises mushrooms only from a photo and can be wrong. That is why you have mushrooms checked even when an app has recognised them.

Many cantons allow only a **maximum amount** of mushrooms per person and day. This leaves enough mushrooms in the forest. Any amount collected may contain a poisonous mushroom. So the rule is: you have edible mushrooms checked **every time** after collecting, even if you have collected often before.

gewusst: If you suspect mushroom poisoning in Switzerland, Tox Info Suisse helps on the number 145.
A single death cap can make a whole mushroom dish dangerous.

teile.einleitung: A **podzol** is an acidic, nutrient-poor soil that forms mainly under coniferous forest and heath in a cool, damp climate. Typical is a pale, ash-grey layer beneath the surface. This soil also occurs in the Swiss Alps.
wichtigste: The name comes from Russian and means roughly “ash soil”.
Podzols usually form under coniferous forest and heath.
They form mainly in a cool, damp climate, for example in Scandinavia.
Acidic seepage water washes iron and humus downwards.
What is left behind is a pale **eluvial horizon**.
In some podzols a hard layer forms, the **ortstein**.
Podzols are not very fertile for farming.

abschnitte.text: Soils consist of several layers called **horizons**. In the podzol you can see these layers especially clearly. Under a dark top layer of needles and humus comes a pale, almost white layer. Below it lies a rust-brown or dark layer. The name comes from Russian and means roughly **ash soil**, because the pale layer looks like ash.

abschnitte.titel: Coniferous forest, heath and a cool climate
abschnitte.text: Podzols form mainly under **coniferous forest** and **heath**. Needle litter and heather form many acids as they break down. In a **cool, damp climate** the litter breaks down only slowly, and a lot of rain seeps through the soil. Such conditions exist, for example, in Scandinavia. In the higher parts of the Swiss Alps, where coniferous forests and dwarf shrubs grow, you also find podzols.

The process by which a podzol forms is called **podzolisation**. Acidic seepage water dissolves iron, aluminium and humus substances in the upper soil. These are washed downwards and build up again deeper down. What stays behind at the top is mainly pale quartz sand. This is how the ash-grey **eluvial horizon** forms, and below it the darker **illuvial horizon**.

In some podzols, iron and humus cement the illuvial horizon into a hard layer. This is called **ortstein**. Roots hardly get through it, and water can back up above it. Podzols are strongly acidic and leached out, so **poor in nutrients**. For arable farming they are hardly suitable without a lot of lime and fertiliser; forests often grow there instead.

gewusst: A podzol can have such clear stripes that you can recognise the layers from far away.
Ortstein can become so hard that foresters used to have to break it up with heavy ploughs before they could plant trees.

teile.einleitung: Plant pathology is the science of plant diseases. It studies their causes, course and control. The name comes from the Greek “phyton” for plant and “pathos” for suffering.
wichtigste: Plant pathology deals with the **diseases of plants**.
The **disease triangle** consists of host, pathogen and environment.
A **chlorosis** is a yellowing, a **necrosis** is dead tissue.
**Biotrophic** pathogens need living tissue, **necrotrophic** ones kill it.
With the **hypersensitive reaction**, plants stop some pathogens.
Anton de Bary is regarded as the founder of modern plant pathology.

abschnitte.text: A plant disease only breaks out when three things come together. It needs a susceptible **host plant**, a pathogen able to cause disease and favourable **environmental conditions**. If one of the three factors is missing, the plant stays healthy. That is why many fungal diseases occur mainly in wet years.

In a **chlorosis** leaves turn yellowish because there is too little chlorophyll. The cause can be a pathogen, but also a lack of nutrients. A **necrosis** is dead tissue, which often turns brown or black. Many fungal and bacterial diseases show themselves through such spots.

**Obligate biotrophic** pathogens can only feed and multiply on living tissue. They usually cannot be grown on culture media; an example is the **rust fungi**. **Necrotrophic** pathogens release enzymes and toxins, kill the cells and live on the dead tissue. The grey mould **Botrytis cinerea** attacks, among other things, strawberries and grapes in this way.

In the **hypersensitive reaction** plants let the cells around a site of infection die off quickly. Biotrophic pathogens then find no living tissue there any more. Whether a micro-organism causes a disease is tested with **Koch’s postulates**. In the 19th century **Heinrich Anton de Bary** proved that a micro-organism causes potato blight and is not a result of the rot.

gewusst: Potato blight caused a great famine in Ireland in the 1840s.
Fire blight is a dangerous bacterial disease of apple and pear trees that is closely monitored in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The residual flow is the water that remains in a river or stream when part of it is diverted for a power station. It makes sure that fish and other living things can survive below the water intake as well.
wichtigste: Residual flow is the amount that remains in the river after water has been taken out.
The Water Protection Act of 1991 sets minimum residual flows.
The basis is the flow measure Q347.
Existing power stations usually have to follow the rules when their licence is renewed.
Electricity production and the protection of waters are in conflict.
In 1992 voters rejected the initiative “To Save Our Waters” and accepted the law.

abschnitte.text: Many hydroelectric power stations in Switzerland take water from a stream and lead it through tunnels to the turbines. Below the intake, much less water then flows in the stream bed. This stretch is called the **residual flow stretch**. The **residual flow** is the amount of water that **remains in the river** after the water has been taken. If it is too small, the stream almost dries up, the water becomes warm and fish no longer find a habitat.

The **Water Protection Act of 1991** prescribes minimum residual flows. The basis is the measure **Q347**. This is the flow that is reached or exceeded on **347 days a year**, so on almost all days. Under **Article 31**: up to a Q347 of 60 litres per second, **50 l/s** must remain. For every further 10 l/s, **8 l/s** are added.

A stream has a Q347 of **80 l/s**. That is 20 l/s more than 60, so twice 10 l/s. The minimum residual flow is 50 + 2 × 8 = **66 l/s**. A river with a Q347 of **100 l/s** is 40 l/s above 60, so four times 10 l/s. Here 50 + 4 × 8 = **82 l/s** applies. For larger waters, the law contains further steps, and the cantons can set additional requirements.

With residual flow, two interests are in **conflict**: more water for the turbines means more **electricity from hydropower**. More water in the stream means better **protection of aquatic habitats**. Many power stations have very long licences. Existing plants usually only have to comply fully with the new rules when their **licence is renewed**. Below storage power stations there is also **hydropeaking**: the flow varies greatly and quickly.

In **1992** the people voted on two proposals. The popular initiative **“To Save Our Waters”** wanted stricter protection and was **rejected**. The new **Water Protection Act** with the residual flow rules, on the other hand, was **accepted**. To this day there is discussion about how much water should stay in the streams, especially because Switzerland wants to produce more renewable electricity.

gewusst: Hydropower supplies more than half of the electricity in Switzerland.
Q347 means: only on about 18 days a year does less water flow than this value.

teile.einleitung: **Primary production** is the name for the formation of organic biomass from inorganic substances by autotrophic living things such as plants and algae. It is the basis of almost all food webs. Without it there would be no animals, no fungi and no people.
wichtigste: Autotrophic living things build biomass from carbon dioxide, water and minerals.
In the open ocean **phytoplankton** does most of the work.
In the deep sea, chemoautotrophic bacteria and archaea carry out primary production without light.
It is often given in grams of carbon per square metre per year.
On land the tropical rainforest has the highest primary production per area.
In the open sea, nutrients such as nitrogen or iron often limit growth.

abschnitte.text: **Autotrophic** living things make their own food. Plants and algae use light energy to build organic substances from **carbon dioxide**, **water** and minerals. This process is called photosynthesis. All the newly formed biomass is called **primary production**. Animals, fungi and bacteria live from it directly or indirectly.

In the open sea there are no plants fixed in one place. There, tiny, freely floating algae and cyanobacteria carry out almost all the photosynthesis. They are called **phytoplankton**. Light and carbon dioxide are mostly plentiful at the surface. **Nutrients** such as nitrate or iron, by contrast, are scarce. That is why large parts of the open sea count as nutrient-poor **ocean deserts**.

At hot springs in the deep sea, the **hydrothermal vents**, it is pitch dark. Even so, primary production takes place there. **Chemoautotrophic** bacteria and archaea gain energy from the oxidation of substances such as hydrogen sulphide. With it they build biomass. Whole communities of worms, mussels and crabs live from them.

Primary production is a **rate**: biomass formed per area and time. It is often given as **grams of carbon per square metre per year**. It is particularly high in the **tropical rainforest**, where warmth, light and water are plentiful all year round. Deserts and polar regions, by contrast, yield only a little biomass per area.

A classic method in water is the **light and dark bottle method**. In the light bottle photosynthesis and respiration take place, in the dark one only respiration. From the difference in oxygen values you work out the production. Today **satellites** also help: they measure the chlorophyll at the sea surface and so show where a lot of phytoplankton is growing.

gewusst: Phytoplankton is tiny, yet it supplies a very large part of the world’s primary production.
On satellite images you can see algal blooms in the sea as greenish swirls.

teile.einleitung: Plankton are tiny living things that float in the water and are carried by the current. There is plant plankton and animal plankton. It lives in seas, lakes and ponds.
wichtigste: The Greek word plankton means **that which drifts**.
Plant plankton is called **phytoplankton**, animal plankton **zooplankton**.
The **water flea** belongs to the zooplankton in fresh water.
Water fleas eat mainly tiny **algae**.
Active swimmers such as fish are called **nekton**.
Phytoplankton supplies about **half** of the oxygen that plants on Earth produce.

abschnitte.text: Plankton cannot swim deliberately against the current. It is carried by the water. That is where the name comes from: in Greek, plankton means **that which drifts**. Nekton is quite different. It includes strong swimmers such as fish, which decide for themselves where they swim.

**Phytoplankton** consists of tiny algae that carry out photosynthesis. “Phyton” means plant in Greek. Important members are the **diatoms**. They build themselves a shell of silica, made of two parts like a box. The phytoplankton of the seas supplies about half of the oxygen that the Earth’s plants produce.

Animal plankton, or **zooplankton**, includes, for example, the **water flea**. It is a tiny crustacean that floats in lakes and ponds. With its little legs it filters algae out of the water. In this way it helps keep the water clearer. Zooplankton in turn is food for fish.

abschnitte.titel: Up and down through the day
abschnitte.text: Much zooplankton travels up and down every day. By day it hides in the **dark depths** from fish that hunt it by sight. At night it rises to the surface, where there are many algae. In this way it can feed under cover of darkness. Plankton is at the start of many **food chains** in the water.

gewusst: Some kinds of plankton can glow. Then the sea sparkles at night; this is called bioluminescence.
Jellyfish also count as plankton, although some grow quite large: they drift with the current.

teile.einleitung: Thousands of years ago, people built their villages on the shores of lakes and in moors. Their houses stood on piles. The remains of these pile dwellings are now part of the UNESCO World Heritage, and about half of the sites lie in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Pile-dwelling settlements arose in the New Stone Age and the Bronze Age.
Since 2011 the prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps have been part of the UNESCO World Heritage.
The 111 sites lie in six countries, 56 of them in Switzerland.
In the winter of 1853/54, pile-dwelling remains were discovered in Obermeilen on Lake Zurich.
In the damp ground without oxygen, wood, seeds and fabrics are preserved.
With dendrochronology, timbers can often be dated to the exact year.

abschnitte.text: In the winter of **1853/54** the water level in **Lake Zurich** was very low. At **Obermeilen**, old piles and many finds came to light. The Zurich antiquarian **Ferdinand Keller** interpreted them as the remains of **pile dwellings**. After that, similar settlements were discovered on many Swiss lakes. This is called the **pile-dwelling fever**, because suddenly everyone was looking for them.

Ferdinand Keller imagined villages on large platforms in the middle of the water. This romantic picture shaped the idea of the lake dwellers for a long time. Research today sees it differently. Many houses stood on the **shore**, on the beach ground, which was at times **flooded** at high water. So the houses were raised on piles but did not stand in the middle of the lake. The settlements date from the **New Stone Age** and the **Bronze Age**, roughly between 5000 and 500 BC.

In pile-dwelling settlements an especially large number of things are preserved. In the water-saturated lake bed there is no **oxygen**, so **wood**, **seeds** and even **textiles** hardly rot. So we know a lot about the life of the people. They grew cereals, kept animals and gathered berries and nuts. For cords and cloth they grew **flax**, whose seeds also supply oil.

The timbers of the piles can often be dated **to the exact year**. The method is called **dendrochronology**. Every tree forms a tree ring each year, which is wider or narrower depending on the weather. You compare the pattern of a piece of wood with a long reference curve. In this way you find out in which year a tree was felled.

Since **2011** the “Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps” have been part of the **UNESCO World Heritage**. The **111 sites** lie in Switzerland, Germany, Austria, France, Italy and Slovenia. **56** of them lie in Switzerland, so about half. Most of the remains lie invisible under water or in the ground. Many finds are shown by the **Laténium** in Hauterive on Lake Neuchâtel, one of the largest archaeology museums in Switzerland.

gewusst: The lake dwellers left no writing. Almost everything we know about them comes from finds in the ground.
Because the sites lie under water, some archaeologists work as divers.

teile.einleitung: A **ranger** looks after nature in a nature reserve. Rangers explain to visitors why there are rules, watch animals and keep people safe. In Switzerland rangers work, for example, in the National Park and in nature parks.
wichtigste: Rangers protect nature in protected areas.
They explain the rules to visitors in a friendly way.
They watch animals through **binoculars** without disturbing them.
They count animals such as ibex or birds.
They close dangerous paths or report damage.
In Switzerland they work in places such as the National Park.

abschnitte.text: A ranger works outdoors in a **protected area**. They make sure that the **rules** are followed. At the same time they explain nature to visitors. In the **Swiss National Park** there are park wardens and rangers. There are also rangers in nature parks and other protected areas.

Rangers explain in a friendly way **why** there are rules. For example, you should stay on the path so that plants are not trampled and animals are not disturbed. If someone leaves **rubbish** behind, the ranger speaks to them. They point out the rules in a friendly way. For serious breaches there can also be a **fine**.

An important tool is the **pair of binoculars**. With it the ranger can see animals from a distance without disturbing them. Sometimes rangers **count** the animals in their area, for example ibex or birds. This shows how the animals are doing. These figures help to protect nature.

Rangers are out and about in all weathers. That is why they need good shoes and **weatherproof clothing**. After a storm, fallen trees or falling rocks can make a path dangerous. Then the ranger **closes** the path or reports it. This is how they make sure nobody is hurt.

gewusst: In the Swiss National Park, visitors must always stay on the marked paths.
Rangers often have special training in which they learn a lot about plants, animals and how to deal with people.

teile.einleitung: Bark is the outer covering of trees and shrubs. It protects the wood underneath, much as our skin protects the body, and many species of tree can be recognised by it.
wichtigste: Bark protects the tree.
The outer, often cracked layer is called the outer bark.
As the tree grows thicker, the bark often splits open.
The birch has white bark with black patches.
The beech has smooth, grey bark.
Cinnamon is dried tree bark.
The woodpecker taps at the bark to find insects.

abschnitte.text: **Bark** protects the tree from **drying out**, from heat and frost, from animals and from fungi. It is made up of several layers. The outer, often **cracked** layer is called the **outer bark**, and it consists of dead cells. Below it lies the **phloem**. It carries the sugar made by the leaves downwards to the trunk and roots. If the bark is damaged all the way round the trunk, the tree can die.

Between the bark and the wood lies a thin, living layer, the **cambium**. This is where the tree grows in thickness every year. Inwards it forms wood, and outwards it forms phloem. Because the trunk grows thicker but the old outer bark cannot grow with it, the **bark often splits open**. This is how the deep furrows seen on old oaks come about.

Every species of tree has its own typical bark. The **birch** has **white bark with black patches**. The **beech** has **smooth, grey bark**, even in old age. The oak has thick, deeply furrowed outer bark. On the plane tree the bark flakes off in pieces, so that the trunk looks patchy. This makes it possible to identify trees even in winter when they have no leaves.

abschnitte.titel: Life on and under the bark
abschnitte.text: Many small animals live in the crevices of the bark: spiders, beetles and insect larvae. The **woodpecker** taps at the bark with its hard beak to find **insects** underneath. Lichens and mosses also like to grow on bark. Some beetles, such as the **bark beetle**, live directly under the bark and can cause weakened spruces to die.

The spice **cinnamon** is actually **dried tree bark** from the cinnamon tree, which curls into little rolls as it dries. **Corks** for bottles are made from the thick bark of the **cork oak**. In the garden, chopped bark is spread on beds as **bark mulch**. It keeps the soil damp and lets fewer weeds grow.

gewusst: The cork oak survives having its cork bark stripped off, and then grows new bark.
The white colour of birch bark comes from a substance called betulin.

teile.einleitung: Pesticides are agents used to control pests, fungal diseases or unwanted plants. They help to secure harvests, but can burden waters, beneficial animals and people. In Switzerland there is much debate about them.
wichtigste: Fungicides work against fungi, herbicides against unwanted plants, insecticides against insects.
The waiting period is the minimum time between the last application and the harvest.
With the action plan of 2017, the Confederation wants to halve the risks of plant protection products.
In June 2021 the voters rejected the pesticide initiative and the drinking water initiative.
Long-lived substances such as DDT build up along the food chain.
With frequent use, pests can become resistant.

abschnitte.text: The word **pesticide** is a general term. **Fungicides** inhibit fungi, for example **mildew**. They are often used in viticulture and fruit growing. **Herbicides** control weeds that compete with the crop plants for light, water and nutrients. **Insecticides** are aimed at harmful insects. There are also natural agents: **pyrethrum** is obtained from the dried flowers of certain **chrysanthemums** and is permitted to a limited extent in organic farming.

For every product and every crop, a **waiting period** is laid down. After the last application you have to wait this long before harvesting. By then the residues fall below the permitted **maximum levels**. In **integrated pest management**, a **damage threshold** is also observed. Only when the infestation is so strong that the loss of yield would be greater than the cost of treatment is spraying done.

Some substances are hardly broken down in nature. A well-known example is the insecticide **DDT**. It builds up in living things, and from step to step of the **food chain** the amount rises. This is called **biomagnification**. Birds of prey at the very end of the chain had such high levels that their eggshells became thin and broke. DDT is therefore banned today in many countries.

With every treatment, a few pests survive that are naturally resistant. They multiply and pass this trait on. After many applications, a large part of the pests is finally **resistant**. That is why active substances are rotated and other methods are used, for example beneficial animals, robust varieties or crop rotation.

In 2017 the Confederation decided on the **Action Plan for Plant Protection Products**. The aim is to **halve** the **risks** for humans, waters and beneficial animals. On 13 June 2021 Switzerland voted on the initiative “For a Switzerland without synthetic pesticides” and the **drinking water initiative**. Supporters wanted to protect the environment and drinking water better, opponents feared lower harvests and higher prices. Both initiatives were **rejected**.

gewusst: By quantity, herbicides are among the largest groups of pesticides.
After the DDT ban, many populations of birds of prey recovered.

teile.einleitung: The concept of planetary boundaries describes limits to the strain the Earth system can bear. If humanity stays within these limits, the Earth is likely to stay stable. The concept was presented in 2009.
wichtigste: **Johan Rockström** presented the concept in 2009 with an international team.
It includes **nine** planetary boundaries.
According to the “Planetary Health Check”, **seven** of them were exceeded in 2025.
For ozone depletion the situation has improved thanks to the Montreal Protocol.
For climate change, **350 ppm** of CO₂ counts as the limit.
Inside all the boundaries lies humanity’s **safe operating space**.

abschnitte.text: Johan Rockström of the **Stockholm Resilience Centre** published the concept in 2009 with other researchers. They asked: how much can humans burden the Earth without it falling out of balance? In the last roughly 10,000 years, the **Holocene**, the climate was very stable. Within the boundaries, the Earth is meant to stay in a similarly stable state. Beyond them the risk of abrupt, irreversible changes rises.

The concept distinguishes **nine processes**. They include climate change, the integrity of the biosphere, land use, fresh water, ocean acidification and the depletion of the ozone layer. The **biogeochemical flows** concern nitrogen and phosphorus, which get into the environment through fertiliser. **Novel entities** include substances made by humans such as plastic and chemicals. A further boundary is air pollution by aerosols.

For climate change the researchers set **350 ppm** of CO₂ as the safe value. Today the concentration is well above 400 ppm. The boundary for novel entities was assessed as exceeded for the first time in 2022. The “Planetary Health Check” of 2025 reported ocean acidification as exceeded for the first time too. That meant **seven of nine** boundaries had been crossed.

For **ozone depletion** the situation has improved. The **Montreal Protocol** of 1987 gradually banned ozone-damaging substances such as CFCs, and the ozone layer has been slowly recovering since. The concept is being developed all the time. Since 2022, for example, **green water** has been assessed separately. This is the soil moisture that plants use. Blue water, by contrast, flows in rivers, lakes and groundwater.

gewusst: The number seventeen is not one of the planetary boundaries, but belongs to the UN sustainable development goals.
The ozone layer shows that worldwide agreements can relieve a planetary boundary again.

teile.einleitung: A **pollen allergy**, also called hay fever or **pollinosis**, is an overreaction of the immune system to harmless flower pollen. It is among the most common allergies. In Switzerland about one person in five is affected.
wichtigste: The technical term for hay fever is **pollinosis**.
Antibodies of the class **immunoglobulin E** (IgE) are responsible.
Mast cells release **histamine**, which causes sneezing and itchy eyes.
Left untreated, asthma can develop, the so-called “**Etagenwechsel**” (a change of floor).
People allergic to birch pollen often also react to raw apples.
With **hyposensitisation** you can get the immune system used to pollen.
MeteoSwiss runs the national pollen monitoring network.

abschnitte.titel: A false alarm of the immune system
abschnitte.text: The immune system protects us from pathogens. In an allergy, however, it takes harmless proteins in pollen for dangerous ones. It makes antibodies of the class **immunoglobulin E**, or **IgE** for short. These attach to certain defence cells, the **mast cells**. When the body comes into contact with the pollen again, a rapid defence reaction starts.

When pollen binds to the IgE on the mast cells, these release the messenger substance **histamine**. Histamine widens blood vessels and irritates nerves. That is why you have to sneeze, the nose runs and the eyes itch and water. Mainly the mucous membranes of the **nose** and **eyes** are affected. Medicines that slow histamine are called **antihistamines**.

If a pollen allergy stays untreated for a long time, the inflammation can move from the upper airways into the **bronchi**. Then **allergic asthma** develops. This process is called the “**Etagenwechsel**”, German for a change of floor, because the symptoms move one storey lower. That is why experts recommend having a pollen allergy treated early.

An allergen of **birch** is similar to a protein in the **apple**. The immune system mixes the two up. Many people allergic to birch pollen therefore feel an itch in the mouth when they eat raw apples. This is called a **cross-allergy**. Cooking usually destroys the protein, so many people affected cope well with apple sauce.

In **hyposensitisation**, also called specific immunotherapy, you regularly receive small amounts of allergen as an injection or tablet. The immune system becomes more tolerant as a result. The treatment usually lasts three to five years. In Switzerland **MeteoSwiss** measures the pollen in the air at numerous stations. From this come pollen forecasts for people affected.

gewusst: According to aha! Swiss Allergy Centre, about a fifth of the Swiss population suffers from a pollen allergy.
In Switzerland the pollen season often begins as early as winter with hazel.

teile.einleitung: In space there is no air to breathe, and it is alternately scorching hot and icy cold. Anyone working outside the spacecraft there needs a spacesuit. It is like a small, personal spacecraft in human shape.
wichtigste: Astronauts need a spacesuit in space because there is no air to breathe there.
The suit supplies oxygen and removes the carbon dioxide that is breathed out.
It creates an inner pressure, without which body fluids would start to boil.
It protects against extreme heat, cold, radiation and tiny particles of rock.
The first person in open space was Alexei Leonov in 1965.
The Swiss astronaut Claude Nicollier made a spacewalk at the Hubble telescope in 1999.
An outside spacesuit weighs well over a hundred kilograms on Earth.

abschnitte.text: A **spacesuit** is an airtight protective suit for people in space. A distinction is made between suits for launch and landing and **spacewalk suits** for work outside the spacecraft. The launch suits protect the wearer if the cabin loses pressure. The spacewalk suits are much bigger and heavier, because they have to withstand hours in space.

The suit is made of many layers: an airtight inner layer, layers of insulation and a tear-proof outer skin. In the backpack there is a **life support system** with oxygen, a battery, radio and cooling. Under the suit the astronaut wears underwear with thin tubes through which cooling water flows. A gold-coated visor on the helmet protects the eyes from the glaring sunlight.

Without pressure, the water in the body would turn to vapour at normal body temperature. In the sun, objects in space heat up to over 100 degrees, and in the shade they cool to far below minus 100 degrees. There is also dangerous **radiation** from the Sun. Tiny **micrometeorites** fly faster than a rifle bullet and could injure an unprotected person.

On 18 March 1965 the Soviet cosmonaut **Alexei Leonov** became the first person to go out into open space. His suit swelled up, and he had to let out air to fit back into the capsule. In 1969 Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin stepped onto the Moon in their Apollo suits. Today NASA uses the **EMU** on the International Space Station, and Russia uses the Orlan suit.

**Claude Nicollier** from Vevey is so far the only Swiss person to have been in space. Between 1992 and 1999 he flew four times on the Space Shuttle. In December 1999 he left the shuttle on a spacewalk to repair the **Hubble Space Telescope**. Since then Switzerland has had another ESA astronaut, Marco Sieber, in training.

The suit has a lower inner pressure than the air on board, so that it stays flexible. That is why astronauts breathe pure oxygen for a long time beforehand, to avoid decompression sickness. A spacewalk often lasts six to eight hours, so the suit has a drinks pouch and a **nappy**. On their chest astronauts wear a list printed in mirror writing, so that they can read it with a mirror on their wrist.

begriffe.erklaerung: An airtight protective suit for space.
Work done by an astronaut outside the spacecraft.
Technology that supplies oxygen, cooling and power.
A tiny, very fast particle of rock in space.

gewusst: In space the heavy spacewalk suit seems to weigh nothing, but it is still sluggish and hard to move.
The gloves are the hardest part, because the fingers have to work against the inner pressure.
Some of the suits for the Apollo Moon landings were made by a company that otherwise sewed bras.

teile.einleitung: Rotting, or “Rotte” in German, is the process in which microorganisms break down organic waste using oxygen, producing compost. It takes place in every garden compost heap and also in large composting plants.
wichtigste: Rotting is the aerobic breakdown of organic matter by microorganisms.
Aerobic means that the breakdown needs oxygen.
Besides humus, it produces mainly carbon dioxide, water and heat.
Composting runs through a breakdown phase, a conversion phase and a build-up phase.
A rotten smell shows a lack of oxygen, often because it is too wet.
The self-heating test determines the degree of rotting, and the cress test the compatibility with plants.
Actinomycetes give mature compost its smell of forest soil.

abschnitte.text: **Rotting** means the **aerobic breakdown** of organic matter such as leaves, grass clippings or kitchen peelings. Aerobic means that **oxygen** is needed for it. The work is done by countless **microorganisms**, mainly bacteria and fungi, and later also small animals such as worms and woodlice. Besides humus, the main products are **carbon dioxide, water and heat**. That is why a compost heap can get really hot inside.

In the **breakdown phase**, bacteria very quickly decompose easily degradable substances. The temperature often rises to 60 degrees Celsius or more, which can kill disease-causing germs and weed seeds. In the **conversion phase**, the heap cools down, and fungi break down more resistant substances such as wood. Finally comes the **build-up phase**. Now stable **humic substances** form, and compost worms mix the material.

Mature compost smells pleasantly of **forest soil**. This smell is produced by **actinomycetes**, also called ray fungi. If a compost heap, on the other hand, smells rotten, of **hydrogen sulphide**, like rotten eggs, oxygen is missing. This often happens when the material is **too wet** or too dense. Then putrefaction starts instead of rotting. Turning it over and adding dry, coarse material such as chipped wood help.

In large plants, **windrow composting** is often used. The material is piled into **long heaps**, called windrows. Machines turn the windrows regularly so that enough air gets in. In Switzerland, green waste from many municipalities is turned into compost in this way. Some of it is also fermented, producing biogas without oxygen.

The **self-heating test** is used to determine the **degree of rotting**. Compost is put into an insulated container and the test measures how much it still warms up. The less heat is produced, the riper the compost is. The **cress test** checks whether the compost is safe for plants. Cress is sown on compost and compared with how well it germinates and grows.

gewusst: The smell of fresh earth after rain comes partly from the same substance that actinomycetes produce.
In a single gram of compost live millions of microorganisms.

teile.einleitung: The marigold is a popular garden flower with bright orange or yellow blooms. It flowers from summer until autumn and has also been used as a medicinal plant for a long time.
wichtigste: The flowers of the marigold are mostly orange or yellow.
A garden marigold usually lives for only one year.
It gets its German name from its curved, ring-shaped seeds.
It belongs to the daisy family.
In rain and in the evening, many marigolds close their flowers.
Its Latin genus name is Calendula.
It often flowers until the first frost.

abschnitte.text: The **marigold** has flowers in bright **orange or yellow**. It grows to about knee height and has soft, slightly sticky leaves with a spicy smell. The garden marigold is an **annual**: it grows from a seed in spring, flowers and dies off in autumn. It often sows itself again, though, so that new plants come up the next year.

The marigold belongs to the **daisy family**, like the sunflower and the daisy. What looks like a single flower is really made up of many small flowers sitting tightly together in a “little basket”. In **rain** and **in the evening**, many marigolds close their flowers. In the morning, in fine weather, they open again.

After flowering, the **seeds** form. They are **curved** and look like little rings or hooks. The marigold’s German name, “Ringelblume”, meaning “ring flower”, comes from these **ring-shaped seeds**. The Latin genus name is **Calendula**. It recalls the Latin word for the first day of the month, perhaps because the plant flowers for so long.

In the past, marigold petals were used in the kitchen **to colour food yellow**, for example butter, cheese or soups. The petals are edible and make salads colourful. The marigold is best known as a **medicinal plant**. **Marigold ointment** has long been used for minor skin injuries.

Marigolds are easy to grow and need a **sunny spot**. From early summer they often flower **until the first frost in autumn**. If you cut off the faded flowers, new buds form. Bees, bumblebees and hoverflies like to visit the flowers. Many gardeners plant marigolds among the vegetables because they bring the garden to life.

gewusst: On a single marigold you can often find seeds of different shapes: curved, winged and hooked.
Where the garden marigold originally comes from is not known exactly, probably from the Mediterranean region.

teile.einleitung: Red clover is a common plant on meadows and pastures. It has round, pink to red flower heads and leaves in three parts, and it makes the soil more fertile.
wichtigste: A normal clover leaf has three leaflets.
For many people, a four-leaf clover means good luck.
The flower heads of red clover are round and pink to red.
Bumblebees can easily reach its nectar with their long tongues.
Cows like to eat red clover especially.
Like peas and beans, red clover is a legume.
It makes the soil more fertile.

abschnitte.text: A clover leaf normally consists of **three leaflets**. That is why the genus is called Trifolium in scientific terms, which means “three-leaf”. In red clover the leaflets often have a pale patch. Very rarely you find a clover leaf with **four leaflets**. For many people such a find is a sign of **good luck**.

The flower head of red clover looks like a **round little head**. It is made up of many small, tube-shaped individual flowers. They are **pink to red**. If you pull out a single flower and suck at the lower end, it tastes **a little sweet**. That is the nectar. Because the tubes are long, the **bumblebee**, with its long tongue, can reach it especially well.

Red clover is a **legume**, like peas and beans. **Nodule bacteria** live on its roots. They can fix nitrogen from the air. The plant uses this nitrogen to grow. When parts of the plant rot in the soil, the nitrogen reaches the earth. In this way **red clover makes the soil more fertile**, without any artificial fertiliser.

On meadows and pastures in Switzerland, red clover is widespread. **Cows** like to eat it especially, because it contains a lot of protein. Farmers often sow it together with grasses as **clover-grass**. From it they get fresh fodder and hay. Many insects such as bumblebees and butterflies also visit the flowers.

gewusst: When red clover was grown in New Zealand, at first it hardly produced any seeds. Only when bumblebees were brought there from Europe did it work.
A four-leaf clover comes about through a rare change during growth. You often have to search through thousands of leaves before you find one.

teile.einleitung: Rime is a delicate, white coating of ice that grows on branches, grasses and fences on cold winter days. It forms when fine droplets of fog freeze onto objects in frosty weather.
wichtigste: Rime can be seen in winter, often on foggy, cold days.
It does not fall from the sky like snow, but grows directly on objects.
It grows most on the side that the wind comes from.
Thick rime can become so heavy that branches break off.
If the sun shines warmly, the rime melts.

abschnitte.text: In winter there is often **fog** over the land. The tiny water droplets in the fog can stay liquid even though the air is below zero. They are said to be **supercooled**. When they hit a cold branch or a blade of grass, they **freeze on at once**. Droplet by droplet, a white layer of ice made of fine needles and scales grows in this way. So rime does not fall from the sky like snow; it **grows directly on the objects**.

The wind drives the fog droplets against trees, fences and posts. That is why rime grows most on the side **that the wind comes from**. Sometimes long plumes of ice form, all pointing in the same direction. From them you can read which way the wind has been blowing. On mountains and in the Jura, where fog and wind often come together, the coating becomes especially thick.

Rime turns a landscape into a white fairy-tale picture. But when the layer of ice becomes very thick, it is **heavy**. Branches can then **break off**, and the ice can cause damage to power lines. As soon as the **sun shines warmly** or milder air arrives, the rime **melts** and falls down in small pieces.

gewusst: Rime and ordinary hoar frost are not the same thing: hoar frost forms without fog, directly from the water vapour in the air.
Rime can keep growing for days, as long as fog and frost last.

teile.einleitung: **Producers** are living things that make their own food. They include mainly plants and algae, which make sugar with sunlight. They stand at the start of every food chain.
wichtigste: Producers build energy-rich nutrients from simple substances.
Green plants use **photosynthesis** for this.
On land **sunlight** is the source of energy.
In the sea, tiny algae in the plankton are the most important producers.
The newly formed biomass is called **primary production**.
In the deep sea there are bacteria that make food by **chemosynthesis**.

abschnitte.text: In ecology, living things are sorted by how they feed. **Producers** make their own food. They build energy-rich substances from **water** and **carbon dioxide**. **Consumers** such as animals, by contrast, eat other living things. All consumers live directly or indirectly from the producers.

Green plants make their food by **photosynthesis**. Their green pigment, **chlorophyll**, captures **sunlight**. With this energy they build **glucose** from water and carbon dioxide. Oxygen is produced too. A **beech** is therefore a producer. A cep, by contrast, has no chlorophyll and cannot make food from light.

In the sea the most important producers are tiny **algae in the plankton**. They are called **phytoplankton**. They are so small that you can only see them under the microscope. Even so, they form the basis of almost all food chains in the sea. Small crustaceans eat the algae, fish eat the crustaceans, and so on.

abschnitte.titel: Without light in the deep sea
abschnitte.text: In the dark deep sea there is no light. At hot springs, producers live there all the same. They are **bacteria** that gain energy from **sulphur compounds**. With it they make nutrients. This process is called **chemosynthesis**.

How much biomass the producers newly build in a certain time is called **primary production**. It is given per area and time. The more producers grow, the more food there is for the consumers. That is why plants and algae are indispensable for every ecosystem.

gewusst: A large part of the oxygen we breathe comes from tiny algae in the sea.
Fungi sometimes look like plants, but they are not producers.

teile.einleitung: If you leave a houseplant by the window for a long time, you soon notice that it leans towards the light. Plants cannot move from place to place, but they grow deliberately towards the sun. This movement is called phototropism.
wichtigste: Phototropism is the growth of a plant towards the light or away from the light.
Houseplants on the windowsill grow towards the light.
Shoots mostly grow towards the light, roots often away from it.
The movement is controlled by the plant hormone auxin.
Auxin collects on the shady side and makes the cells there grow more strongly.
Charles Darwin and his son Francis studied phototropism around 1880.
Plants sense mainly blue light for this movement.

abschnitte.text: **Phototropism** is made up of the Greek words for light and turning. It means a growth movement set off by light from one side. If the plant grows towards the light, this is called **positive phototropism**. If a part grows away from the light, this is called negative phototropism.

The tip of the shoot uses light sensors, the **phototropins**, to feel where the blue light comes from. The hormone **auxin** is then shifted to the shady side. There the cells stretch more than on the lit side. Because one side grows faster, the shoot bends towards the light.

Charles Darwin and his son Francis described experiments with grass seedlings in 1880. If they covered the tip with a small cap, the seedling no longer bent towards the light. They concluded that the tip sends a messenger substance downwards. The Dutchman Frits Went proved this substance in 1928; it was later called **auxin**.

Young **sunflowers** turn their buds with the sun from east to west during the day. Fully grown flowers, on the other hand, mostly stay facing east. In the forest, seedlings grow towards gaps of light in the leaf canopy. Ivy, with its clinging roots, rather climbs towards the dark wall.

A plant on the windowsill leans more and more towards the window over time. If you turn the pot a little every few days, it grows evenly and straight. Plants with too little light become long, thin and pale, which is called **etiolation**. Potatoes in a dark cellar show this with their long, pale shoots.

Light is vital for plants, because they use it for photosynthesis. Through phototropism they bring their leaves into the best position. Besides light, plants also react to **gravity**, which is called gravitropism. That is why roots grow downwards and shoots upwards, no matter how a seed lies in the soil.

begriffe.erklaerung: A growth movement of a plant in response to a stimulus.
A plant hormone that promotes the stretching of cells.
The plant’s light sensor for blue light.
Long, pale growth when there is a lack of light.

gewusst: Darwin wrote a whole book about plant movements, which appeared in 1880.
Fungi such as the pilobolus also aim their spores exactly towards the light.
On the International Space Station, researchers studied how plants grow by light alone without gravity.

teile.einleitung: Photosystem II is a large protein complex in the thylakoid membrane of chloroplasts. It uses light energy to split water. In the process the oxygen we breathe is produced.
wichtigste: The reaction centre of photosystem II is called **P680**.
The light-driven splitting of water is called **photolysis**.
A **manganese-calcium cluster** catalyses the oxidation of water.
One O2 molecule needs **four** light excitations.
The first electron acceptor is **pheophytin**.
The herbicide **diuron** blocks the QB binding site.

abschnitte.text: At the centre of photosystem II lies a special pair of chlorophylls, **P680**. The number gives the wavelength in nanometres at which it absorbs light most strongly. When P680 is excited, it gives up an electron. The first recipient is **pheophytin**, a chlorophyll without magnesium. From there the electron travels to the quinones **QA** and **QB** and on to plastoquinone.

The oxidised P680 takes the missing electron from water. This splitting is called **photolysis**. In it, water breaks down into oxygen, protons and electrons. This is made possible by the **oxygen-evolving complex** with a cluster of four manganese, one calcium and oxygen bridges, written Mn4CaO5.

To make one O2 from two water molecules, four electrons must be removed. Each excitation of P680 removes one. So **four excitations** are needed. Bessel Kok described in 1970 how the cluster passes through the states S0 to S4. This model is called the **Kok cycle**. Only in the change from S4 to S0 is oxygen released.

The **D1 protein** carries important parts of the reaction centre. Strong light and reactive forms of oxygen damage it easily. The plant therefore keeps breaking it down and building it in anew. Some weedkillers attack photosystem II. **Diuron**, also called DCMU, occupies the QB binding site and interrupts the flow of electrons.

gewusst: Almost all the oxygen in the air comes from the splitting of water by photosystem II.
Photosystem II works together with photosystem I, whose reaction centre is called P700.

teile.einleitung: Plants grow from a small seed into large growths. For this they need light, water, warmth and nutrients. In Switzerland they grow mainly in spring and summer.
wichtigste: Plants need light, water, warmth, air and nutrients from the earth.
From a seed grows a seedling, from which a plant with flowers develops.
Before flowering the plant forms a closed **bud**.
A stem grows in length mainly at its **tip**.
In spring and summer plants grow most with us.
**Bamboo** is among the fastest-growing plants in the world.

abschnitte.text: If you put seeds in the earth, you **sow**. In the seed is a tiny plant with a store of food. If the seed gets water and warmth, it germinates. First a root grows downwards, then a **seedling** upwards. The seedling becomes the plant, and this later forms buds and flowers.

With the **light** of the sun, plants make sugar in their green leaves. For this they also need air and water. The roots fetch the water from the soil, together with **nutrients**. Warmth makes sure that everything goes fast enough. If one of these is lacking, the plant grows poorly.

Plants grow in length mainly at their **tips**. There new cells are constantly forming. The roots too keep growing into the earth at their tips. Trees also become a little thicker every year. This is how the **annual rings** form in the wood.

In spring the days become longer and warmer. Then trees put out leaves and many flowers begin to bloom. In summer plants grow most strongly in Switzerland. In winter it is cold and the days are short. So many plants **rest** until it gets warmer again.

gewusst: Some species of bamboo grow more than half a metre in height in a single day.
Plants grow towards the light: a house plant at the window leans towards the pane over time.

teile.einleitung: Ruderal plants grow on rubble, wasteland, railway land and path edges, that is, in places that people have disturbed. They are often the first plants to settle on an open area.
wichtigste: The term comes from the Latin word for rubble.
Ruderal plants are first colonisers of open areas.
Typical features are many seeds and rapid growth.
Coltsfoot is a typical pioneer on rubble and clay.
Butterfly bush from China is regarded as an invasive neophyte in Switzerland.
Canadian fleabane comes from North America.
Ruderal areas offer wild bees flowers and open nesting ground.

abschnitte.text: The word **ruderal plant** comes from the Latin word for **rubble**. It refers to plants that grow on **disturbed areas**: on building sites, gravel areas, railway land, wasteland and path edges. There the ground is often open and stony and is changed again and again. Many other plants cope badly with this. Ruderal plants, however, make use of exactly such gaps.

Ruderal plants are **first colonisers** or **pioneers**. Typical of many of them are **many seeds and rapid growth**. Their seeds are often spread far by the wind or stay able to germinate in the soil for a long time. A well-known example is **coltsfoot**. It settles early on open rubble and clay areas and flowers yellow in early spring, even before its leaves appear.

Among the ruderal plants there are also many **neophytes**, that is, plants that have only come to us from other continents in recent times. **Canadian fleabane** from North America has small white daisy-like flowers and often grows on wasteland. The **butterfly bush** from China often grows on railway land. It is regarded as an **invasive neophyte** in Switzerland because it spreads strongly and can push out native plants.

Ruderal areas in the city sometimes look untidy. For nature, however, they are valuable. They offer **flowers** for insects and **open nesting ground**. Many **wild bees**, in fact, dig their nests in the ground. Plants such as chicory or viper’s bugloss also bloom there and attract many insects.

abschnitte.titel: When nothing is disturbed any more
abschnitte.text: If a ruderal area is left undisturbed for a long time, it changes. First perennial herbs and grasses grow, then **bushes and trees**. In time these **push out** the ruderal plants, because they take their light away. Experts call this development **succession**. Anyone who wants to keep ruderal areas therefore has to open them up again now and then.

gewusst: Many ruderal plants have followed humans for thousands of years and grow where there are settlements, paths and fields.
On old railway stations and goods yards you often find a surprising number of different plant species.

teile.einleitung: The black locust is a tree from North America that now also grows in many places in Switzerland. In early summer it is fragrant with white clusters of flowers, but its bark and seeds are poisonous.
wichtigste: The black locust comes from North America.
It has sharp thorns on its twigs.
Its flowers hang in white, fragrant clusters.
Acacia honey mostly comes from the black locust.
Its fruits are flat pods like beans.
The bark and seeds are poisonous.
Its hard wood is often used for playground equipment.

abschnitte.text: The **black locust** comes from **North America**. It came to Europe about 400 years ago. It gets its German name, “Robinie”, from the French gardener **Jean Robin**, who worked for the king. It is often wrongly called an “acacia” because it looks like true acacias. Its **leaves** are made up of **many small leaflets on one stalk**, which is called pinnate. On the twigs there are sharp **thorns** that can prick.

The black locust flowers in May and June. Its flowers hang from the twigs in **white, fragrant clusters**. Bees collect a lot of nectar from them. The pale, runny **acacia honey** therefore mostly comes from the black locust. After flowering it forms **flat pods** that look like beans. The black locust, in fact, belongs to the **legumes**, like the pea and the bean.

However beautiful the black locust is, some parts are **poisonous**. This applies above all to the **bark** and the **seeds**. Children should therefore not eat seeds from the pods. Horses can also be poisoned if they gnaw at the bark. Anyone who has eaten parts of the plant and feels unwell should get help.

The wood of the black locust is very **hard** and stands up to wind and weather for a long time, even without treatment with chemicals. That is why it is often used for **playground equipment**, for fence posts, garden furniture and vine posts. It is among the most durable woods that grow in Europe.

The black locust grows fast and spreads by root runners. Like other legumes, it has bacteria on its roots that fix nitrogen from the air. As a result it **fertilises** the soil. On poor, dry meadows it thereby pushes out rare plants that need nutrient-poor soil. In Switzerland the black locust is therefore regarded as an **invasive neophyte**, and it is especially widespread in Ticino.

gewusst: What is sold in shops as “acacia honey” almost never comes from true acacias, but from the black locust.
The thorns of the black locust are changed stipules and sit in pairs on the twig.

teile.einleitung: The **Pusteblume**, or dandelion clock, is the dandelion after flowering, with its white, fluffy ball. If you blow on it, many little parachutes fly away. On each hangs a small fruit with a seed from which a new dandelion can grow.
wichtigste: The dandelion clock is the dandelion after flowering.
Before that the dandelion flowers bright yellow.
The dandelion clock has the shape of a ball.
It consists of many little **parachutes**.
At the bottom of each parachute hangs a small fruit with a seed.
In spring there are especially many dandelion clocks in Swiss meadows.

abschnitte.text: The **dandelion** flowers bright **yellow**. After flowering the flower head closes again. A few days later it opens as a white, fluffy **ball**. This is the **dandelion clock**. So the plant is the same, just at another stage of its life.

The ball consists of many **parachutes**. They sit all round on the **flower base**. At the bottom of each parachute hangs a small **fruit** with a **seed**. The parachute is like a little real parachute. In this way the wind can carry the seed far away.

The parachutes are only **loosely attached**. If you blow hard, they come away and fly off. The wind also carries them off. Wherever a seed lands, a new dandelion can grow. When all the parachutes are gone, only a **bare stalk** with a round little head is left.

In Switzerland the dandelion flowers mainly in **April and May**. Then many meadows glow completely yellow. Shortly afterwards **dandelion clocks** stand everywhere. Many children like to pick them and blow the parachutes into the air.

gewusst: A dandelion parachute can be carried a very long way by the wind.
The German name Löwenzahn, meaning “lion’s tooth”, comes from the jagged leaves, which recall teeth.

teile.einleitung: Rubisco is an enzyme with which plants, algae and some bacteria fix carbon dioxide from the air. It is the first step in making sugar from carbon dioxide, and is regarded as the most abundant protein on Earth.
wichtigste: Rubisco stands for ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase.
It is the most abundant protein on Earth.
Rubisco fixes carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle of photosynthesis.
A single molecule manages only a few reactions per second.
In its active site it needs a magnesium ion.
Rubisco activase frees Rubisco from inhibiting sugar phosphates.
Cyanobacteria concentrate Rubisco and carbon dioxide in carboxysomes.

abschnitte.text: In photosynthesis, plants use light to make sugar from carbon dioxide and water. Rubisco is an **enzyme**, that is, a protein that speeds up a chemical reaction. It works in the **Calvin cycle** in the chloroplasts. There Rubisco attaches a carbon dioxide molecule to the sugar **ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate**. This produces two smaller molecules from which the plant later builds sugar.

The long name **ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase** describes two abilities. As a **carboxylase**, the enzyme fixes carbon dioxide. As an **oxygenase**, however, it can also fix oxygen by mistake. This produces a substance that the plant has to break down again, using energy. This process is called **photorespiration**.

A single Rubisco molecule is very **slow**: it manages only **a few reactions per second**. Other enzymes are many thousands of times faster. Plants make up for this by producing huge amounts of it. In leaves, Rubisco can make up as much as about half of the soluble protein. That is why it is regarded as the **most abundant protein on Earth**.

The Rubisco of land plants consists of **8 large and 8 small subunits**. The gene for the large subunit lies in the **genetic material of the chloroplast**, and the one for the small subunit in the cell nucleus. In its active site, Rubisco needs a **magnesium ion**, or it cannot work. Some sugar phosphates can block the enzyme. **Rubisco activase** removes these inhibitors and so keeps Rubisco active.

Some living things help Rubisco by concentrating carbon dioxide. **Cyanobacteria** pack Rubisco together with carbon dioxide into tiny compartments, the **carboxysomes**. There, a lot of carbon dioxide and little oxygen is present. Plants such as maize have a different way: they first collect carbon dioxide in particular cells and then pass it on to Rubisco in a targeted way.

gewusst: Researchers have been trying for decades to make Rubisco faster or more accurate in order to make crop plants more productive.
Almost all the carbon in plants, animals and humans was at some point fixed from the air by Rubisco.

teile.einleitung: Pressed leaves and flowers last a very long time. You can make cards with them or start your own plant collection. All you need is paper, weight and a little patience.
wichtigste: At home you can simply press leaves with heavy books.
You lay the plants between absorbent paper.
After about one to two weeks they are flat and dry.
Wet leaves can go mouldy, so you press only dry ones.
A plant press consists of two boards that you screw firmly together.
Flat, thin flowers and bright autumn leaves are especially suitable.

abschnitte.text: The easiest way to press leaves is with **heavy books**. You lay the leaf between two sheets of **absorbent paper**, for example newspaper or blotting paper. Then the whole thing goes into a thick book, and on top you put more books. The paper takes up the **moisture**, and the weight presses the leaf flat. In this way it becomes flat and dry.

A **plant press** consists of **two boards**. You lay paper and plants between them and pull the boards firmly together with **screws** or **straps**. In this way an even pressure arises. You can even build a simple press yourself. Researchers also take small presses with them on journeys.

The water in the plant needs time to **evaporate**. It usually takes **one to two weeks** until a leaf is completely dry. In the first days the paper becomes damp. So after a few days you **change** it for fresh, dry paper. In this way the plant dries faster and stays beautiful.

Collect the plants on a dry day. **Wet** leaves with raindrops dry slowly and can go **mouldy** and turn brown. Especially suitable are **flat, thin flowers**, because they dry quickly and evenly. Thick parts stay damp for a long time. In **autumn**, bright **maple leaves** are very popular, because they are flat and glow yellow, orange or red. You must not pick protected plants.

From pressed leaves you can make **cards**, **pictures** or bookmarks. You can also start your own plant collection. Such a collection is called a **herbarium**. For each plant you write down the name, the place where it was found and the date. In this way a little nature book is created.

gewusst: In museums and botanical gardens there are herbaria with plants that were pressed several hundred years ago.
The Conservatory and Botanical Garden of Geneva owns one of the largest herbaria in the world.

teile.einleitung: Oxygen is a colourless gas that we need for breathing. Almost all the oxygen in the air comes from plants, algae and cyanobacteria. They release it during photosynthesis.
wichtigste: Dry air consists of about 21 per cent oxygen.
During photosynthesis, plants release oxygen from water.
The oxygen is produced in the light reaction of photosynthesis.
Oxygen is detected with the glowing splint test.
Cyanobacteria were the first to bring a lot of oxygen into the air, over 2 billion years ago.
Joseph Priestley showed around 1771 that plants renew used air.

abschnitte.text: Dry air consists of about 78 per cent **nitrogen** and about 21 per cent **oxygen**. The rest is mainly argon and carbon dioxide. Oxygen is colourless, odourless and tasteless. Its chemical symbol is **O**. People and animals need it to gain energy from food in their cells.

In **photosynthesis**, plants use light to build up sugar. In the **light reaction**, water molecules are split. This frees oxygen, which passes out through the stomata. That the oxygen comes from the **water** and not from the carbon dioxide was proved in 1941 with labelled oxygen atoms.

Oxygen strongly promotes burning. This is used in the **glowing splint test**: a glowing wooden splint flares up brightly in pure oxygen. With a water plant such as **Canadian waterweed**, you can even see oxygen being formed. In the light, small **gas bubbles** rise. The more bubbles you count, the stronger the photosynthesis.

The English researcher **Joseph Priestley** let a candle burn out under a glass bell jar around 1771. After that, no flame would burn there any more. When he put a **sprig of mint** under the jar, the air was usable again after some time. A candle could burn once more. In this way he showed that plants renew used air.

abschnitte.titel: Oxygen in the history of the Earth
abschnitte.text: The young Earth had almost no oxygen in the air. Only **cyanobacteria** carried out photosynthesis and gave off oxygen over a very long time. Over 2 billion years ago the atmosphere slowly built up a supply of it. Only then could animals that breathe oxygen develop later. Today land plants and algae in the sea supply the oxygen.

gewusst: A large part of the oxygen on Earth comes from tiny algae in the sea.
Liquid oxygen is pale blue.

teile.einleitung: When the sun breaks through after a rain shower, a coloured arc sometimes stretches across the sky. A rainbow is not a bridge or an object, but a play of light in water droplets. You can only see it when the sun and the rain are in exactly the right places.
wichtigste: A rainbow forms when the sun shines on raindrops.
A rainbow usually has seven colours that people tell apart.
The light is refracted, reflected and split into colours inside the droplets.
You can only see a rainbow if you have the sun behind you.
In the primary rainbow, red is on the outside and violet on the inside.
Sometimes you can see a fainter secondary rainbow with the colours reversed.
From an aeroplane, a rainbow can be a complete circle.

abschnitte.text: A **rainbow** is an optical effect created by sunlight and water droplets. Sunlight looks white but contains all the colours. In the droplets this light is split into its parts, which is called **dispersion**. The colours are red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet.

A ray of light enters a raindrop and is bent as it does so, which is called **refraction**. At the back of the drop it is reflected and comes out again at the front. Each colour is bent by a slightly different amount, which is why the light fans out. Each drop sends us only one colour, and millions of drops together make the arc.

To see a rainbow, the sun must be behind you and the rain in front of you. The arc always appears at an angle of about 42 degrees around the point opposite the sun. That is why you mainly see it in the morning or in the late afternoon, when the sun is low. Everyone sees their own rainbow, because the droplets are different for each eye.

Outside the main arc, a paler **secondary rainbow** often appears at about 51 degrees. Here the light is reflected twice inside the drop, which is why the colours are reversed. Between the two arcs the sky is noticeably darker. This strip is called **Alexander’s dark band**, after the Greek scholar Alexander of Aphrodisias.

Scholars were already thinking about the rainbow in ancient times. In 1637 the Frenchman René Descartes explained how the arc forms, using experiments with glass balls filled with water. **Isaac Newton** later showed with a prism that white light is made up of colours. He also fixed the number of colours at seven, although the colours actually blend smoothly into one another.

You can make a rainbow yourself by making a fine spray with a garden hose while you have the sun behind you. At large waterfalls such as the **Rhine Falls** or the Staubbach Falls in Lauterbrunnen, you can often see rainbows when the sun is out.
