At night, a pale **moonbow** can form in bright full moonlight. Rainbow colours also appear in soap bubbles and on CDs, though for different reasons.

begriffe.erklaerung: The bending of a ray of light as it passes into another substance.
The splitting of white light into its colours.
A transparent block of glass that splits light into colours.
A paler second arc with the colours in reverse order.

gewusst: You can never reach the end of a rainbow, because it moves along as you get closer.
If you photograph a rainbow through sunglasses with a polarising filter, it can partly disappear.
If the sun is higher than about 42 degrees, you cannot see a rainbow from the ground.

teile.einleitung: Rhynia is one of the oldest known land plants. It lived about 407 million years ago and is so well preserved in the Rhynie chert in Scotland that individual cells can still be seen.
wichtigste: Rhynia is named after the village of Rhynie in Scotland.
The Rhynie chert is about 407 million years old and dates from the Early Devonian.
The plants were turned to silica in hot springs.
Rhynia had no leaves and no true roots.
Its sporangia sat at the ends of the stems.
It grew only a few decimetres tall.

abschnitte.text: Near the village of **Rhynie** in **Scotland** there is a special rock, the **Rhynie chert**. It is about **407 million years** old and dates from the **Early Devonian**. At that time there were **hot springs** in the area. Their water was rich in dissolved silica. Plants that were flooded by it were **silicified**, that is, turned to stone. In this way they were preserved down to **individual cells**. As well as plants, **fungi** and small **arthropods** are found in it.

**Rhynia** was an early **vascular plant**. It already had channels for carrying water, but still **no leaves** and **no true roots**. Its shoots were thin, green and forked again and again. It grew only **a few decimetres** tall. In the ground it was anchored with **horizontal shoots** and fine **rhizoids**, which are root-like hairs. At the **ends of the stems** it formed **sporangia**, small capsules in which the spores developed.

In the past, several plants from the Rhynie chert were assigned to the genus Rhynia. One of them was called **Rhynia major**. Closer study showed that it did not yet have **true tracheids**, that is, no typical water-carrying cells. Today it is called **Aglaophyton**. Finds like these help researchers to understand how plants conquered the land.

gewusst: Even fungi that lived closely with the plants have been preserved in the Rhynie chert, much as many fungi live with plant roots today.
The Rhynie chert is one of the most important fossil sites for the history of land plants.

teile.einleitung: The peony is a popular garden flower with large, lush blooms. It flowers at about the time of Whitsun, which in German gives it the name “Pfingstrose”, meaning “Whitsun rose”. Despite its name, it is not a true rose.
wichtigste: The peony flowers in May and June, at about the time of Whitsun.
It belongs to a family of its own and is not a true rose.
Its flowers are large, often double and round like a ball.
Ants often crawl on the buds because they give off a sweet juice.
A peony can flower in the same place for decades.
It does not like being transplanted at all.

abschnitte.text: With its large flowers the **peony** looks like a rose. But it belongs to a family of its own, the **peony family**. Unlike roses, it also has **no thorns**. It has its German name “Pfingstrose” because it flowers in **May and June**, so at about the time of **Whitsun** (“Pfingsten”). The Latin name is **Paeonia**.

Peonies have **large**, lush flowers. Many garden varieties are **double**, so they have very many petals and look **round like a ball**. They come in many colours from **white** through **pink** to **dark red**, and some varieties even flower yellow. Many smell pleasant. As cut flowers they are very popular.

You often see **ants** crawling on the round **buds**. The buds give off a **sweet juice** that the ants like to lick. They do the plant no harm in doing so. When the flower opens, the ants usually move on.

The most common form is the **herbaceous peony**. In autumn its stems and leaves die back. The plant overwinters in the earth, and in spring it sprouts anew from the **root**. There are also **tree peonies** with woody twigs that stay standing in winter.

A peony can become very old. In the same place it often flowers for **many decades**. In return it does not like being **transplanted** at all. After being moved it often does not flower for a few years. So it is best to find it a sunny spot right at the start where it may stay.

gewusst: The plant is slightly poisonous, so you should not eat any part of it.
The name Paeonia goes back to Paean, a healer from Greek legend.

teile.einleitung: Phytosociology studies which plant species regularly grow together. Such communities are called plant communities. An important method for this comes from a botanist from the Grisons.
wichtigste: Phytosociology arranges plant communities by the species that occur in them.
Josias Braun-Blanquet of Chur founded the Zurich-Montpellier school.
The basic unit of the system is the **association**.
Several similar associations form an **alliance**, above them come order and class.
In a **vegetation relevé**, the cover and abundance of each species are estimated.
**Character species** mark a community, **differential species** separate related communities.

abschnitte.titel: A man from the Grisons as founder
abschnitte.text: Josias Braun-Blanquet was born in 1884 in Chur. From the 1920s he developed a method by which plant communities can be described and arranged precisely. He worked in Zurich and later in Montpellier in southern France. That is why his school is called the **Zurich-Montpellier school**. His method is still used today in many countries.

Researchers mark out a sample plot and note all the plant species on it. For each species they estimate the **abundance-cover value**, that is, how much area it covers and how frequent it is. The Braun-Blanquet scale runs from r and + for very rare species up to 5 for species that cover almost everything. The plot has to be big enough. The smallest area on which you find almost all the species of a community is called the **minimum area**.

A **character species** occurs almost only in a particular community. If you find it, you know which community it is. **Differential species** occur in one community and are missing in a related one. In this way similar communities can be told apart. Species that grow in many communities are called **companions**.

Plant communities carry Latin names. The ending shows the rank. Associations end in **-etum**, for example the woodruff beech wood is called Galio odorati-Fagetum. Alliances end in **-ion**, for instance Fagion sylvaticae for the beech woods. Orders end in -etalia and classes in -etea.

gewusst: The Braun-Blanquet method is also used in nature conservation to describe and compare habitats.
From the name of a community you can often already tell the most important plants, such as Fagus for the beech in the Fagetum.

teile.einleitung: A rosette plant has its leaves spread out in a circle, close to the ground. This growth form is found in well-known meadow plants such as the dandelion and in mountain plants such as the houseleek.
wichtigste: In rosette plants the leaves lie in a circle close to the ground.
The stem between the leaves is very much shortened.
The dandelion is a well-known rosette plant of meadows.
The houseleek forms thick, fleshy rosettes on rocks and walls.
In the mountains it is warmer and less windy at ground level.
In winter the snow covers the flat rosettes and protects them from frost.

abschnitte.text: In a rosette, all the leaves grow from one point close to the ground. The stem there is so shortened that the leaves lie densely on top of one another. From above it looks like a circle or a rose, hence the name. Well-known examples are the **dandelion**, the daisy and the plantain. When the plant flowers, a long flower stem often grows from the middle of the rosette.

In the mountains the weather is harsh. Directly above the ground, though, it is **warmer and less windy** than higher up. Flat rosettes make use of this sheltered layer. In winter a **blanket of snow** settles over the plants. The snow acts like a warm blanket and protects against hard frost and drying winds.

The **houseleek** grows on rocks, walls and stony soils. Its leaves are thick and fleshy, because they store water for dry times. In the **cobweb houseleek**, fine white hairs join the leaf tips, which looks like a spider’s web. A houseleek rosette flowers only once and **dies afterwards**. Before that, though, it has formed small daughter rosettes that live on.

In the past, people liked to plant houseleeks on roofs. According to old **folk belief**, they were supposed to protect the house from lightning. The German name “Hauswurz”, meaning “house plant”, comes from this. There is no scientific evidence for this protection. Today the houseleek is a popular plant for rock gardens and cracks in walls.

gewusst: Because its leaves lie so flat on the ground, the dandelion survives mowing and simply carries on growing afterwards.
The scientific name of the houseleek, Sempervivum, means “always living”.

teile.einleitung: Soils can be acidic, neutral or alkaline. This is measured with the pH value. It helps to decide which plants grow well and how well they can take up nutrients.
wichtigste: The pH value shows how acidic or alkaline a soil is.
A neutral soil has the pH value 7.
Below 7 the soil is acidic, above 7 alkaline.
With lime you can improve a soil that is too acidic.
Under coniferous woods the soil is usually rather acidic.
The bilberry likes to grow on acidic soils.
With indicator test strips you can easily measure the pH.

abschnitte.text: The **pH value** shows how **acidic or alkaline** something is. The scale usually runs from 0 to 14. The value **7 is neutral**, like pure water. Values **below 7** mean **acidic**, values **above 7** mean **alkaline**. Most soils lie roughly between 3 and 9. Many garden plants grow best on slightly acidic to neutral soil.

Under a **coniferous wood** the soil is usually **rather acidic**. The fallen needles decay slowly and make the soil acidic. Moors and soils on granite, for example in parts of the Alps, are also often acidic. Here grow plants that like this, for example the **bilberry**, heather and the rusty-leaved alpenrose.

On **limestone**, for example in the **Jura**, the soil is usually **neutral to alkaline**. Lime can buffer acid. On such soils other plants grow, such as many orchids and the hairy alpenrose. If a garden or field soil is too acidic, you **scatter lime** on it to raise the pH. This is called **liming**.

You can easily measure the pH of a soil yourself. You mix some earth with distilled water, let it settle and dip an **indicator test strip** into the liquid. The strip changes colour, and you read the value off a colour scale. Garden centres sell small test kits for this. For exact measurements there are soil laboratories.

The pH influences how well plants can take up **nutrients**. In very acidic or very alkaline soils, some nutrients are poorly available. **Earthworms** and many other soil organisms also dislike soil that is too acidic. That is why farmers and gardeners watch the pH when they look after the soil.

gewusst: In some hydrangeas the flower colour depends on the soil: on acidic soils they often turn blue, on alkaline soils rather pink.
In Switzerland you can tell from the two species of alpenrose whether the soil is acidic or rich in lime.

teile.einleitung: Plant physiology is the science of how plants live and function. It studies how plants gain energy, transport water and react to their environment. Many of these processes take place invisibly in tiny cells.
wichtigste: Plant physiology studies the life processes in plants.
The light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis take place in the thylakoid membrane of the chloroplasts.
The enzyme rubisco binds carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle.
For one molecule of glucose a plant needs six molecules of CO2.
Transpiration pull is the main driving force for water transport in tall trees.
In the phloem, carbohydrates are transported mainly as sucrose.
Phytohormones such as ethylene and abscisic acid control ripening and stress reactions.

abschnitte.text: **Plant physiology** is a branch of botany and biology. It asks how a plant breathes, grows, makes food and processes signals. It includes photosynthesis, water balance, nutrition and **phytohormones**. Its results help in agriculture, horticulture and climate research.

Photosynthesis takes place in the **chloroplasts** in two parts. In the thylakoid membrane, pigments capture light, split water and produce energy carriers, and oxygen is released. In the **Calvin cycle**, the enzyme rubisco binds carbon dioxide to ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate. Overall, 6 CO2 and 6 water become one molecule of glucose and 6 oxygen.

Water constantly evaporates through the stomata of the leaves, which is called **transpiration**. This creates a pull that draws water in the thin tubes of the xylem from the root up to the crown. The water molecules cling together like the links of a chain. In this way water reaches even redwoods over 100 metres tall.

The sugar made in the leaves is distributed in the **phloem**. It travels mainly as **sucrose**, that is, ordinary household sugar. It flows to roots, fruits and growing tips. In potatoes or grains of cereal it is stored as starch.

Plants control their growth with **phytohormones**. Auxin makes shoots grow towards the light, and gibberellins promote growth in length. The gaseous **ethylene** makes fruits such as apples and bananas ripen. **Abscisic acid** makes sure in drought that the stomata close.

**CAM plants** such as cacti, agaves and the pineapple open their stomata only at night. They store the CO2 as malic acid and process it in the daytime with the pores closed. In this way they hardly lose any water in the heat. Other plants such as maize and sugar cane use a special route that is called **C4 photosynthesis**.

begriffe.erklaerung: An enzyme that binds CO2, probably the most common protein on Earth.
Evaporation of water through the leaves.
Household sugar, the transport form of sugar in plants.
A messenger substance that controls the growth and development of the plant.
A membrane system in the chloroplast where light is captured.

gewusst: If you put an unripe avocado next to a ripe apple, it ripens faster, because the apple gives off ethylene.
Rubisco is a rather slow enzyme, which is why plants make huge amounts of it.
A large birch can evaporate several hundred litres of water on a hot summer day.

teile.einleitung: Living things have very different strategies for reproducing and surviving. In simple terms, ecology distinguishes between r-strategists, which have very many offspring, and K-strategists, which have few, well-cared-for offspring. The terms come from a formula for the growth of populations.
wichtigste: r-strategists have very many small offspring that they hardly look after.
K-strategists have few offspring and look after them intensively.
The aphid is a typical r-strategist, the African elephant a typical K-strategist.
r-strategists have the advantage in unstable habitats that are often disturbed.
The letters r and K come from the logistic growth equation.
In 1970 Eric Pianka set out the features side by side in a well-known overview.
The dandelion also shows features of an r-strategy.

abschnitte.text: The terms come from the **logistic growth equation**, a formula that describes the growth of a population. The letter **r** stands for the **growth rate**, that is, how quickly a population can grow. **K** stands for the **carrying capacity**, the largest number of living things that a habitat can support permanently. The idea of r- and K-selection was developed in the 1960s.

**r-strategists** reproduce quickly and have very **many small offspring**. They hardly look after their young, and many die early. They are usually small and short-lived. A typical example is the **aphid**, which can multiply in huge numbers in a short time. Among plants, the **dandelion** shows these features: it produces very many seeds, which the wind carries far away.

abschnitte.titel: K-strategists: few and well cared for
abschnitte.text: **K-strategists** have only **few offspring**, but they look after them for a long time and **intensively**. This is called **parental care**. They are usually larger, become adult late and live a long time. A typical example is the **African elephant**: a young one stays with its mother and the herd for many years. K-strategists often live in stable habitats where space is short and there is competition.

In **unstable habitats that are often disturbed**, r-strategists have the advantage. These include freshly dug fields, gravel banks after a flood or puddles that will soon dry up. Anything that spreads quickly here can use the opportunity before it is over. In stable habitats such as old forests, K-strategists are more likely to succeed.

In **1970** the ecologist **Eric Pianka** set out the features of both strategies side by side in a well-known overview. Many r-strategists have a **type III survival curve**: almost all the young die early, and only a few grow old. K-strategists tend to show type I, in which most survive into old age. Today we know that most species lie somewhere in between. The model is a useful simplification.

gewusst: Under favourable conditions, a single aphid can give rise to thousands of offspring within a few weeks.
A dandelion often produces well over a hundred fruits with tiny parachutes on each flower head.

teile.einleitung: Some living things live at the expense of others. They are called parasites. They feed on their host and harm it, usually without killing it at once.
wichtigste: In parasitism, one living thing uses another and harms it.
Ectoparasites such as ticks, fleas and lice live on the outside of the host.
Endoparasites such as the tapeworm live inside the host.
Mistletoe is a hemiparasite: it carries out photosynthesis but taps water.
The cuckoo is a brood parasite.
Ticks can transmit diseases such as Lyme disease.

abschnitte.text: A **parasite** lives on or in another living thing, the **host**. It takes food from it, for example blood or nutrients. The host is harmed by this, but usually not killed at once. This is what distinguishes parasitism from **symbiosis**, in which both partners benefit. Another word for parasite is **sponger**.

“Ecto” means outside. **Ectoparasites** live on the surface of the body, for example **ticks**, **fleas** or **lice**. “Endo” means inside. **Endoparasites** live in the body of their host. One example is the **tapeworm** in the gut. It has no mouth but takes up nutrients directly through its body surface from the food pulp.

Plants can also be parasites. The **mistletoe** grows high up on trees. With its green leaves it makes sugar itself, so it carries out photosynthesis. But it taps water and minerals from the tree with suction roots. That is why it is called a **hemiparasite**. Other plants such as the broomrape have no chlorophyll at all and live entirely off the host, so they are **holoparasites**.

abschnitte.titel: The cuckoo as a brood parasite
abschnitte.text: The **cuckoo** builds no nest of its own. The female lays her eggs in the nests of other birds. The cuckoo chick often throws the eggs of the host birds out of the nest. The host parents then feed only the foreign young bird, which is soon much bigger than they are. This is called **brood parasitism**.

Some parasites transmit diseases. **Ticks** can pass on bacteria that cause **Lyme disease**, and viruses that cause **TBE** (tick-borne encephalitis), an inflammation of the brain and its membranes. In large parts of Switzerland, vaccination against TBE is recommended. After being in the woods you should check yourself for ticks. Animals also suffer from parasites: the **varroa mite** sucks on honey bees and their brood, so beekeepers have to treat their colonies regularly.

gewusst: A tapeworm can grow several metres long in the gut.
The seeds of the mistletoe are spread by birds that eat the sticky berries and leave the seeds behind on branches.

teile.einleitung: On every walk you meet many plants. What are they called? With a few simple features you can identify them, that is, find out which species they belong to.
wichtigste: In identifying, you first look at the flower, its colour and shape.
Often you count the petals.
The shape of the leaves is also an important feature.
Conifers have needles, broadleaved trees broad leaves.
Ferns have no flowers; they reproduce by spores.
You never eat unknown berries, they can be poisonous.

abschnitte.text: The **flower** helps especially in identifying, because it is often colourful and has a typical shape. First look at its **colour**. Then **count** the **petals**. Many species have a fixed number, for example four or five. Also watch whether the flowers stand singly or in groups.

As well as the flower, you also look at the **leaves**. Are they round, long, narrow or toothed? Do they sit opposite one another or alternately on the stem? The **maple leaf** usually has five points and looks like an open **hand**. You recognise **grasses** by their long, narrow leaves. They grow densely and form the green meadow.

With trees there are two big groups. **Conifers** such as fir and spruce have narrow **needles**. **Broadleaved trees** such as beech and oak have broad **leaves**. In the forest you also find **ferns** with large fronds. They have **no flowers** at all. They reproduce by tiny **spores** that sit under the fronds.

You do not have to pull up an unknown plant. Just take a **photo**, best of the flower, the leaves and the whole plant. At home you can then identify it in peace with an **identification book** or an app. An identification book often asks questions: does the plant have flowers? What colour? In this way you get step by step to the right species. And the plant stays outdoors.

Some **berries** look tasty but are **poisonous**. So in the woods you do not eat unknown berries. Eat only berries that an adult knows for certain. Some plants in Switzerland are also **protected**, for example the edelweiss. These you must not pick.

gewusst: In Switzerland about 3,000 different species of ferns and flowering plants grow.

Many plant names reveal a feature, for example the German names “Hahnenfuss” (“cockerel’s foot”, the buttercup), “Glockenblume” (“bell flower”, the bellflower) or “Löwenzahn” (“lion’s tooth”, the dandelion).

teile.einleitung: Plants cannot eat as we do, and yet they grow. They make their food themselves and also take important substances from the soil. This interplay is called plant nutrition.
wichtigste: To grow, plants need light, water, air and nutrients from the earth.
With sunlight they make sugar in the leaves, which is photosynthesis.
The most important nutrients from the soil are nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
The roots take up nutrients dissolved in water.
If nutrients are lacking, plants show deficiency symptoms such as yellow leaves.
Fertiliser and compost bring nutrients back into the soil.
Too much fertiliser can burden waters and groundwater.

abschnitte.text: Plants are **autotrophic**, which means that they feed themselves. In the green leaves they make sugar from carbon dioxide and water with the help of light. This process is called **photosynthesis**. They use the sugar as energy and as building material for new cells.

Besides sugar, a plant needs **minerals**, which it takes up through the roots. Most important are **nitrogen** for the growth of the leaves, phosphorus for roots and flowers and potassium for firm cells. In addition it needs magnesium, calcium and sulphur. Trace elements such as iron or zinc are needed only in tiny amounts.

A plant with nitrogen deficiency gets light green to yellow leaves and grows poorly. If magnesium is lacking, the leaves turn yellow between the veins, because magnesium is part of **chlorophyll**. In the 19th century the chemist Justus von Liebig made the **law of the minimum** known. It says that the scarcest nutrient limits growth, like the shortest board in a barrel.

Farmers and gardeners add nutrients with **fertiliser**. There are natural fertilisers such as dung, slurry and compost, and artificially made mineral fertiliser. Compost is made from garden waste and kitchen waste that is broken down by small organisms. In Switzerland, fertilising in agriculture is regulated by law.

Legumes such as peas, beans and clover live together with **nodule bacteria**. These take nitrogen straight from the air and pass it on to the plant. Many trees also work together with fungi that supply them with water and phosphorus. That is why clover is sometimes sown as natural fertilising.

abschnitte.titel: Too much of a good thing
abschnitte.text: If too much fertiliser gets into lakes, algae grow there in masses. When they die, bacteria use up a lot of oxygen in breaking them down, and fish can suffocate. This is called **over-fertilisation**. Some Swiss lakes such as Lake Baldegg were therefore aerated artificially with oxygen for years.

begriffe.erklaerung: Substances that a plant needs to grow.
An agent that supplies nutrients to the soil.
The green pigment with which plants capture light.
Bacteria on roots that fix nitrogen from the air.
Too many nutrients in soil or water.

gewusst: Carnivorous plants such as the sundew live on nutrient-poor moors and get nitrogen from trapped insects.
Air consists of almost 80 per cent nitrogen, yet most plants cannot use it directly.
In Switzerland, phosphates in laundry detergents have been banned since 1986 to protect the lakes.

teile.einleitung: **Radishes** are small, round roots with red skin and a white inside. They taste sharp and grow very quickly. You can harvest them just a few weeks after sowing.
wichtigste: Radishes are usually red on the outside and white on the inside.
They taste **sharp**, a bit like mustard.
From sowing to harvest it takes about four to six weeks.
Typical radishes are small and round.
They are closely related to the **white radish**.
The leaves can also be eaten.

abschnitte.text: Most radishes are **bright red** on the outside. Only the thin skin is red, and inside they are **white**. There are also white varieties. The typical radish is small and **round like a ball**. There are also longer varieties.

Radishes contain **sharp substances** that taste a bit like mustard. That is why they burn a little on the tongue. Radishes and the **white radish** belong to the same species of plant. Both taste sharp. The white radish is much bigger, though.

Radishes grow very quickly. You can harvest them just **four to six weeks** after sowing. That makes them good for children who are sowing something in the garden for the first time. However, they must not be left in the ground too long. Otherwise they become **woody** or spongy inside and no longer taste good.
Radishes are mostly eaten raw, for example on bread or in a salad. The **leaves** can also be eaten. They can be added to salads, soup or pesto. That way nothing gets thrown away.

gewusst: Radishes are among the fastest-growing vegetables in the garden.
Radishes are related to cabbage and mustard, which is why they taste similarly sharp.

teile.einleitung: The giant horsetail is the largest horsetail that grows wild here. With its ivory-white stems and its green, whorled branches, it looks like a plant from prehistoric times.
wichtigste: The giant horsetail is the largest native horsetail.
The stems of its green summer shoots are ivory-white.
It grows on wet, limy spring slopes and stream banks.
Silica makes the stems rough and hard.
Its brownish spring shoots carry the spores and have no chlorophyll.
“Equisetum” means horse’s tail.

abschnitte.text: Horsetails are ancient plants that reproduce by **spores** and have no flowers. The **giant horsetail** is the largest native one and often grows more than a metre tall. Its green **summer shoots** have a striking **ivory-white** stem. On it, many thin green branches sit in rings. The scientific genus name **Equisetum** means **horse’s tail**, because the plant, with its many branches, is reminiscent of one.

The giant horsetail loves **wet, limy** places. It is found on **spring slopes**, on **stream banks** and in damp woods. It often grows there in large stands. Underground it has long runners from which new shoots keep growing.

The stem of a horsetail is divided into sections that fit into one another like boxes. The German name “Schachtelhalm”, meaning “box stem”, comes from this. The **leaves** are tiny: they form **small teeth** that have grown together into a **sheath** around the stem. The green work is done by the stems and branches. A lot of **silica** is stored in the stems. It makes them **rough and hard**. Another horsetail was therefore used in the past for scouring pewter ware, and in German it is still called “Zinnkraut”, meaning pewter herb.

In **spring**, **brownish shoots** grow first. They lack **chlorophyll**, so they cannot carry out photosynthesis. At their tip sits a cone with the **spores**. The spores have **ribbon-like appendages**. In dry weather they stretch out, and in damp weather they curl up. In this way they help the spores to **spread**. Only after that do the green summer shoots appear.

About 300 million years ago, in the **Carboniferous** period, there were relatives of the horsetails that grew as big as trees. Part of the **coal** later formed from the forests of that time. Today’s horsetails are the last survivors of this ancient group of plants.

gewusst: If you rub two horsetail stems against each other, you can clearly feel how rough the silica makes them.
Horsetails have existed for many millions of years, and are much older than the dinosaurs.

teile.einleitung: The Pampas is a huge, flat grassland in South America. It lies mainly in Argentina and Uruguay. Here live gauchos, herds of cattle and the flightless rhea.
wichtigste: The Pampas is a wide, almost treeless grassland in South America.
The word “pampa” comes from the Quechua language and means plain.
The gauchos are mounted cattle herders and a symbol of Argentina and Uruguay.
Cattle breeding is especially important in the Pampas, along with arable farming.
The rhea is the largest bird in South America and cannot fly.
The pampero is a cool, often stormy south-westerly wind.

abschnitte.text: The **Pampas** is a flat plain as far as the eye can see. It lies mainly in **Argentina** and **Uruguay**, and a small part also in southern Brazil. Originally almost only grasses and herbs grew here, and there were hardly any trees. The word comes from the **Quechua** language of the Andean peoples and means **plain**. The soil is very fertile.

On the wide grassland graze large **herds of cattle**. Argentina is therefore known worldwide for its beef. Today much **soya** and **wheat** are also grown in the Pampas. At the edge of the Pampas lies the capital **Buenos Aires**, on the wide mouth of the Río de la Plata. To the west and south of it the flat land begins.

The **gauchos** are mounted cattle herders. For centuries they have herded cattle and horses in the Pampas. Typical are their poncho, their knife and drinking **mate**, a tea from a gourd vessel. They are regarded as a symbol of Argentina and Uruguay, and there are many songs and stories about them.

The best-known bird is the **rhea**. It is the largest bird in South America and, like the African ostrich, cannot fly but can run very fast. In the Pampas there also live the rare **pampas deer** and the **mara**, a rodent with long legs that looks a little like a hare. Many animals live in burrows, because there are hardly any hiding places.

The climate in the Pampas is temperate, with warm summers and mild winters. Often the **pampero** blows, a cold, sometimes stormy wind from the south-west. After hot days it brings sudden cooling and sometimes thunderstorms. Because there are no mountains, the wind can sweep across the land unchecked.

gewusst: The **pampas grass** that grows in many gardens here comes from the grasslands of South America.
The Pampas is so flat that in some places you can hardly see a rise as far as the horizon.

teile.einleitung: Common sage is a culinary and medicinal herb with soft, velvety leaves. It is used for cooking and drunk as a tea, and in Switzerland it is also known from “Müslichüechli”.
wichtigste: The leaves of common sage are soft and velvety.
Sage belongs to the mint family.
Its flowers are mostly blue-violet.
The name comes from the Latin “salvare”, which means “to heal”.
Sage tea is traditionally used for gargling when you have a sore throat.
Müslichüechli are fried sage leaves, whose stalk looks like a mouse’s tail.
Saltimbocca and gnocchi with brown butter are well-known dishes with sage.

abschnitte.text: Common sage is a small **subshrub**: the twigs become woody at the bottom, while the top parts stay soft. Its grey-green leaves feel **soft and velvety** because they are covered with fine hairs. If you rub a leaf, you smell a strong, spicy scent. It comes from **essential oils**. Sage originally comes from the Mediterranean region but also grows well in Swiss gardens.

Sage belongs to the **mint family**, like rosemary, thyme and mint. Its flowers look like an open mouth with an upper and lower lip. In common sage they are mostly **blue-violet**. Bees and bumblebees like to visit them. On Swiss meadows a wild relative also grows, the **meadow sage**.

The name sage comes from the Latin word **“salvare”**, which means **“to heal”**. Sage has been regarded as a medicinal plant for a long time. Sage tea is traditionally used **for gargling when you have a sore throat**. For longer-lasting complaints, though, you should always ask a doctor.

In Switzerland people know **Müslichüechli**: sage leaves are dipped in batter and fried. They are named that because the stalk sticks out like a **mouse’s tail**, “Mäuseschwanz” in German. In Italy there is **saltimbocca**: veal is fried with **raw ham** and a sage leaf. **Gnocchi with brown butter** and crisply fried sage leaves are also very popular.

gewusst: The genus Salvia is very large and includes hundreds of species all over the world.
The name saltimbocca means in Italian roughly “jump into the mouth”.

teile.einleitung: A mushroom closed season is a time when you may not collect mushrooms. In Switzerland the cantons set such rules. They are meant to protect mushrooms and the forest floor.
wichtigste: During a **closed season** collecting mushrooms is forbidden.
The rules on collecting mushrooms are set by the **cantons**.
In nature reserves collecting is often completely forbidden.
In the **Swiss National Park** you may not take any mushrooms.
A long-term study by **WSL** showed: trampling harms more than picking.
Very young and old mushrooms and poisonous mushrooms are left standing.

abschnitte.text: Collecting mushrooms in Switzerland is **regulated by the cantons**. That is why the rules differ from canton to canton. In many places certain **protected days** apply each month, on which collecting is forbidden. Many cantons also allow only a certain amount per person and day. If you go collecting, it is best to find out about the local rules beforehand.

In **nature reserves** nature is meant to stay as undisturbed as possible. That is why collecting is often completely forbidden there. In the **Swiss National Park** in the Engadine you may take neither plants nor mushrooms. Nature is meant to develop there without human interference.

The research institute **WSL** observed mushroom reserves in the canton of Fribourg, such as La Chanéaz, for about 30 years. The result: **picking** did not reduce the number of fruiting bodies. Heavy **trampling** of the forest floor, however, did, even if only temporarily. The actual fungus lives as a fine web, the **mycelium**, in the soil. What we collect is only the fruiting body.

Protection rules are meant to reduce collecting pressure and spare the forest floor. Very **young mushrooms** are hard to identify, **old** ones often spoiled. You leave them standing so that they can spread their spores. You also leave **poisonous mushrooms** undamaged. They are important for the forest, for example as partners of trees and as food for animals.

gewusst: Many fungi live together with trees and supply their roots with water and nutrients.
The mycelium of a single fungus can spread under the forest floor over a large area.

teile.einleitung: We meet paper every day: in the school exercise book, as cardboard or as a tissue. It is made from the fibres of plants, mostly wood. Waste paper can be collected and made into new paper again.
wichtigste: Paper consists of plant fibres, which mostly come from wood.
From fibres and water, a paper pulp is made.
Recycled paper is made from collected waste paper.
Cardboard is thick, strong paper.
In many Swiss municipalities, waste paper is bundled and collected on collection days.
In the Basel Paper Mill you can watch how paper is scooped by hand.

abschnitte.text: Paper was invented almost 2,000 years ago in **China**. Before that people wrote, for example, on **papyrus** made from reed stems or on **parchment** made from animal skin. Via Arabia, the art of papermaking came to Europe in the Middle Ages. For a long time paper was expensive and was made from old scraps of cloth, the rags.

Today paper is mostly made from **wood**. The wood is broken down into fine **fibres**. With a lot of water, a **paper pulp** is made from them. This is spread thinly on a sieve, the water runs off, and the fibres felt together. Then the sheet is pressed and dried. In the factory a huge **paper machine** does this in one long ribbon.

There are very many kinds of paper. **Cardboard** is thick and strong, and boxes are made from it. **Tissues** consist of soft, thin layers. Newsprint is cheap and thin, drawing paper on the other hand thick and smooth. Depending on the purpose, other fibres and additives are used.

From collected waste paper, **recycled paper** is made. This spares the forests and needs less energy and water. In many **Swiss municipalities** you bundle newspapers and paper with string and put them out on the street on **collection days**. School classes or clubs often help with this. Cardboard is usually collected separately.

In **Basel**, in the St Alban valley, there is an old mill by the water. Today it is a **museum** for paper, writing and printing. There paper is still **scooped by hand** as it used to be. Visitors can even scoop a sheet themselves.

gewusst: Paper can be recycled several times, but not endlessly, because the fibres become shorter each time.
If you hold some banknotes up to the light, you see a **watermark**. It is made right at the production of the paper.

teile.einleitung: Regenerative agriculture is a way of farming fields that puts healthy, living soil at the centre. Its main aim is to build up **humus**, the dark, fertile top layer of the soil.
wichtigste: The main aim is to build up humus and keep the soil healthy.
With direct drilling, seeds are sown without ploughing.
The soil should be covered for as much of the year as possible, so that it is protected from erosion and drying out.
Heavy machinery on wet soil leads to soil compaction.
Humus stores carbon that was previously in the air as CO2.
The earthworm is regarded as an indicator of living soil.

abschnitte.text: A handful of good soil contains more living things than there are people on Earth: bacteria, fungi, small animals and **earthworms**. They break down plant remains and turn them into **humus**. Humus holds water and nutrients like a sponge. Regenerative agriculture aims to build up this humus and keep the soil healthy. Lots of **earthworms** are a good sign that this is working.

When land is ploughed, the soil is turned over. This loosens it, but it also disturbs the life in the soil. With **direct drilling**, seeds are sown without ploughing first, and the machine places the seeds straight into the soil. Another problem is **soil compaction**: when heavy machinery drives over a wet field, the soil is pressed together. Then water and roots find it harder to get in.

A bare field is washed away by rain or blown away by the wind, which is called **erosion**. It also dries out faster. That is why the soil should be **covered all year round** as far as possible, for example with **cover crops** after the harvest or with plant remains. Varied **crop rotations** are also part of it. With grazing animals there is **mob grazing**: many animals graze for only a short time on a small area and then move on.

Plants take **CO2** from the air. Part of the carbon reaches the soil through roots and plant remains and is **stored in the humus**. At the climate conference in **Paris in 2015**, the initiative **“4 per 1000”** was launched. It calls for the carbon content of soils to be raised by **0.4 per cent** every year. Experts point out that soils cannot take up humus without limit and that it can be broken down again if the land is farmed badly.

In the Amazon region, people created an especially fertile, dark soil centuries ago: **terra preta**, which is Portuguese for “black earth”. It contains a lot of **charcoal** and remains from kitchens and settlements. Even today it is more fertile than the soil around it. It shows that people can improve soils over a long period.

gewusst: The term “regenerative agriculture” is not defined by law, so not everyone understands exactly the same thing by it.
In terra preta you often find pieces of broken old clay pots, traces of the people who created it.

teile.einleitung: The phosphorus cycle describes how phosphorus travels between rock, soil, water and living things. Unlike carbon, the air plays hardly any part in it. The cycle is very slow.
wichtigste: Under natural conditions phosphorus hardly forms gases, so there is no significant gas phase.
The largest reservoirs are **rocks** and **marine sediments**.
The most important source of phosphorus in rocks is the mineral **apatite**.
Plants take up phosphorus as dissolved **phosphate**.
Phosphorus is part of DNA, ATP and phospholipids.
Phosphorus deposited in the sea only returns to land through the building of mountains.

abschnitte.text: Most of the Earth’s phosphorus is bound in minerals and sediments. The most important mineral is **apatite**, a calcium phosphate. Through **weathering** the phosphorus is slowly released and reaches soils and waters. Because phosphorus forms hardly any gaseous compounds, it does not enter the air. It travels mainly with water and dust.

Plant roots take up phosphorus as dissolved phosphate ions from the soil water. **Mycorrhizal fungi** often help with this. Animals get phosphorus from their food. In all living things it forms the backbone of **DNA**, stores energy in **ATP** and builds cell membranes. Teeth and bones also consist mostly of a form of apatite. When living things die, the phosphorus is released again.

Rivers carry phosphate into the sea. There, part of it sinks to the bottom and is locked into **sediments**. Over millions of years these become rock. Only when they reach land through **tectonic uplift** and the building of mountains, and weather, does the phosphorus become available again. Seabirds also bring phosphorus to land: their droppings, called **guano**, were a sought-after fertiliser in the 19th century.

Too much phosphate in lakes makes algae grow strongly. When they die, their breakdown uses up oxygen in the deep water. That is why Swiss **sewage works** precipitate phosphate out, and phosphate in textile detergents has been banned since 1986. Today a large part of the input comes from **agriculture**, when rain washes fertiliser and slurry into streams. Some lakes, such as Lake Baldegg, have been artificially aerated for decades.

gewusst: Morocco, including Western Sahara, holds by far the largest part of the world’s known phosphate reserves.
A phosphorus atom can lie in the seabed for many millions of years before it returns to land.

teile.einleitung: Oilseed rape is a crop whose fields blossom bright yellow in spring. Its small seeds are pressed to make rapeseed oil, one of the most important cooking oils in Switzerland and in Europe.
wichtigste: Oilseed rape blooms bright yellow in spring, usually in April and May.
After flowering, the seeds grow in long pods.
Rapeseeds are small, round and blackish brown.
Rapeseed oil is pressed from the seeds.
Bees collect a lot of nectar and pollen from rape flowers.
A flowering rape plant is about a metre tall.

abschnitte.text: When oilseed rape blooms in **April and May**, whole fields glow yellow. You can see them from far away. The plant grows to about **a metre tall** or a little more. Rape belongs to the **cabbage family** and is related to cabbage. Most farmers sow **winter rape** as early as late summer, and the young plants survive the winter in the field.

Rape flowers have a lot of **nectar and pollen**. That is why **bees** love to fly to the fields. They make **rape honey** from the nectar. It is pale and quickly turns solid and creamy. For beekeepers the rape blossom in spring is therefore an important time.

After flowering, the rape forms long, thin **pods**. The **seeds** grow inside them. They are tiny, round and **blackish brown**, about the size of a pinhead. In **summer** the pods are ripe and dry, and the rape is harvested with a combine harvester. The seeds contain a great deal of fat.

At the oil mill the seeds are pressed, and **rapeseed oil** flows out. It is used in the kitchen **for frying and for salads**. In the past rapeseed oil tasted bitter. Plant breeders have developed new varieties that taste better and are healthier. What is left after pressing is called **rapeseed cake** and is used as animal feed.

In Switzerland rape is the most important **oil plant** grown in the fields. The yellow fields can be seen mainly on the **Central Plateau**. Fuel can also be made from rape, known as **biodiesel**. Opinions differ on whether farmland should be used more for food or for fuel.

gewusst: In spring you can sometimes smell a rape field before you see it.
Rape honey often sets solid in the jar just a few days after harvesting.

teile.einleitung: We speak of **polyploidy** when a cell has more than two complete sets of chromosomes. In plants this is very common. Many important crop plants such as wheat, potato, rape and bananas are polyploid.
wichtigste: Polyploid cells have three, four or more sets of chromosomes.
**Colchicine** from the meadow saffron can trigger polyploidy artificially.
Bread wheat has six sets of chromosomes and 42 chromosomes.
The cultivated potato is tetraploid with 48 chromosomes.
Cultivated bananas are triploid and form hardly any seeds able to germinate.
Rape arose from cabbage and turnip rape.
Polyploid plants often have larger cells and organs.

abschnitte.text: In the cells the genetic material lies in **chromosomes**. Many living things have two sets of them, which is called **diploid**. In **polyploid** cells there are three, four or more complete sets. Three sets is **triploid**, four **tetraploid** and six **hexaploid**. In plants polyploidy is very common.

There are two kinds. In **autopolyploidy** a species multiplies its own set of chromosomes. In **allopolyploidy** the sets of different species join, for example after a cross followed by doubling. **Rape** arose in this way from **cabbage** and **turnip rape**. Bread wheat also goes back to crosses of three grass species.

Today’s **bread wheat** is hexaploid and has 42 chromosomes. The **cultivated potato** is tetraploid and has 48 chromosomes. Most **cultivated bananas** are triploid. With three sets, the chromosomes cannot pair up cleanly when the sex cells are formed. That is why hardly any seeds able to germinate arise, and the bananas are almost seedless.

Breeders trigger polyploidy deliberately with **colchicine**. This substance comes from the poisonous **meadow saffron**. It inhibits the spindle apparatus, so that the chromosomes are doubled but not shared out between two cells. This is also how **seedless watermelons** arise: a tetraploid plant is crossed with a diploid one. The triploid fruits contain only soft, undeveloped ovules.

abschnitte.titel: Bigger thanks to more genetic material
abschnitte.text: More genetic material in the cell nucleus often leads to **larger cells**. That is why polyploid plants often have larger leaves, flowers or fruits than the diploid original form. This is called **gigantism**. This property is used in plant breeding. Polyploidy has also played an important part in the origin of many new plant species.

gewusst: The small soft grains in seedless watermelons are undeveloped ovules.
Bread wheat carries the genetic material of three different grass species within it.

teile.einleitung: **ProSpecieRara** is a Swiss foundation that saves rare breeds of farm animals and old varieties of crop plants from extinction. It was founded in 1982 and has its head office in Basel. Thanks to it, Stiefelgeiss goats, Rhaetian Grey cattle and Appenzell Spitzhauben hens live again today.
wichtigste: ProSpecieRara preserves rare breeds of farm animals and plant varieties.
The foundation was founded in 1982.
The head office is in Basel on the Brüglingen estate.
It looks after, for example, the **Stiefelgeiss** (booted goat) and the **Rhaetian Grey cattle**.
The **Appenzell Spitzhauben hen** is also preserved.
Old vegetable varieties stay alive through being grown by many gardeners.
Most ProSpecieRara varieties are **open-pollinated**.

abschnitte.text: ProSpecieRara was founded in **1982**. At first it was mainly about endangered **breeds of farm animals**, and later **plant varieties** were added. The foundation preserves breeds and varieties that are valuable in terms of cultural history and genetics. To do this it works with farmers, gardeners and variety keepers. Its office is in **Basel** on the Brüglingen estate, and there are also offices in French-speaking Switzerland and in Ticino.

The **Stiefelgeiss** from the St Gallen Oberland was almost extinct in the 1980s. ProSpecieRara helped to build the numbers up again. The **Rhaetian Grey cattle** from the Grisons were regarded as extinct in Switzerland. With animals from the Tyrol they were resettled from the 1980s. Such breeds are often robust and well adapted to their region.

The **Appenzell Spitzhauben hen** is an old Swiss breed of chicken. Typical is its forward-pointing **feather crest**. Around 1950 the breed was almost extinct. ProSpecieRara started a conservation project in 1983. Today many people keep these hens again.

Old vegetable varieties stay alive when you **grow** them. They grow in gardens and on farms, and their **seed** is saved anew every year. In this way they stay adapted to the environment. This works because most varieties are **open-pollinated**: they pass on their characteristics to their offspring. With modern **F1 hybrids**, the characteristics split up in the next generation.

gewusst: Anyone who grows an old variety in their own garden can help as a variety keeper.
The Stiefelgeiss is so called because its legs are darker in colour, as if it were wearing boots.

teile.einleitung: Pluto is an icy little world far out at the edge of the Solar System. For over 75 years it was regarded as the ninth planet. Since 2006 it has counted as a dwarf planet.
wichtigste: Pluto was discovered in 1930 by the American Clyde Tombaugh.
Since 2006 Pluto has counted as a dwarf planet and no longer as a full planet.
The reason: it has not cleared its orbit of other objects.
At about 2,380 kilometres across, Pluto is smaller than the Moon.
It takes about 248 years to go once round the Sun.
Its largest moon is called Charon and is half as big as Pluto itself.
The space probe New Horizons was the first to fly past Pluto, in 2015.

abschnitte.text: The young astronomer **Clyde Tombaugh** discovered Pluto in February 1930 at the Lowell Observatory in Arizona. To do so he compared photographs of the night sky taken on different days. A tiny point of light had moved, and that was Pluto. The name was suggested by eleven-year-old Venetia Burney from England, after the Roman god of the **underworld**.

From the 1990s astronomers found more and more icy bodies in Pluto’s region, a zone called the **Kuiper Belt**. In 2005 Eris was discovered, an object about as big as Pluto. That is why the **International Astronomical Union** laid down in Prague in 2006 what a planet is. A planet must have cleared its orbit, and Pluto has not.

On average Pluto is almost 40 times as far from the Sun as the Earth is. It is extremely cold there, about minus 230 degrees. Its surface consists of frozen nitrogen, methane and water ice, which is as hard as rock. Pluto has a very thin **atmosphere**, which freezes and falls to the ground when it moves away from the Sun.

Pluto has five known moons, the largest called **Charon**. Charon is about half as big as Pluto, so the two circle each other almost like a double system. They always show each other the same side. The smaller moons are called Nix, Hydra, Kerberos and Styx.

The NASA probe **New Horizons** launched in 2006 and flew past Pluto on 14 July 2015. It was under way for over nine years. Its pictures showed mountains of water ice and a huge bright plain in the shape of a heart. This region is now called **Tombaugh Regio**, in honour of the discoverer.

Pluto is smaller than seven moons in the Solar System, including our Moon. Its orbit is strongly elliptical and tilted relative to the orbits of the planets. At times Pluto is even closer to the Sun than the planet **Neptune**, most recently from 1979 to 1999. Since its discovery it has not yet managed even one full circuit of the Sun.

begriffe.erklaerung: A body that orbits the Sun and is round, but has not cleared its orbit.
A ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune.
The worldwide association of astronomers, which lays down names and terms.
An unmanned spacecraft that explores other bodies in space.

gewusst: Part of the ashes of Clyde Tombaugh travels aboard New Horizons.
Light from the Sun takes on average about five and a half hours to reach Pluto.
After the demotion, the English word “plutoed” was chosen as Word of the Year 2006 by the American Dialect Society.

teile.einleitung: Saprotrophic living things feed on dead organic material such as wood, leaves or dung. Fungi and bacteria in particular belong here. Without them, the forest would be smothered under waste.
wichtigste: Saprotrophs feed on dead plants and animals and on their remains.
They return nutrients to the cycle of nature.
White rot fungi can break down the hard lignin in wood.
Brown rot fungi mainly break down cellulose, and the wood crumbles into brown cubes.
The cultivated button mushroom grows as a saprotroph on compost.
Instead of “saprophyte”, people now say saprotrophic, because fungi are not plants.

abschnitte.text: Every year huge amounts of leaves, branches and dead animals pile up in the forest. **Saprotrophic** living things break down this material. They include above all **fungi** and **bacteria**. They release digestive substances to the outside and absorb the dissolved nutrients. In this way nitrogen, phosphorus and other substances are freed again, and plants can use them anew.

Wood consists mainly of **cellulose** and **lignin**. Lignin is very hard and hardly any living thing can break it down. **White rot fungi** manage it: pale, fibrous cellulose is left behind. **Brown rot fungi**, by contrast, mainly break down the cellulose and leave the brown lignin. The wood shrinks and breaks into cube-like pieces.

Some saprotrophic fungi also attack timber that has been built into houses. Especially feared is the **dry rot fungus**. It causes brown rot in beams and floors and can even grow through masonry. Dampness in buildings favours it. That is why it is important to keep the wood in houses dry.

The **cultivated button mushroom** breaks down compost made of straw and manure. That is why it can be grown well in halls. **Leafcutter ants** also use a fungus: they carry pieces of leaf into the nest, chew them up and use them to start a **fungus garden**. The fungus breaks down the leaf material, and the ants eat parts of the fungus.

When wood and leaves are broken down, fungi respire the carbon compounds. In doing so, **carbon** returns to the air as **carbon dioxide**. Plants take it up again and build new substances from it. In the past, such fungi were called **saprophytes**. But the ending “phyte” means plant, and fungi form a kingdom of their own. Today people therefore speak of saprotrophic organisms or saprobionts.

gewusst: Leafcutter ants have been practising a kind of farming with fungi for millions of years.
Without fungi that break down lignin, dead wood would lie in the forest for much longer.

teile.einleitung: In a revitalisation, a straightened or built-over stream or river is made more natural again. This creates new habitats for fish, insects and plants, and often flood protection is improved at the same time.
wichtigste: In daylighting, a culverted stream is allowed to flow in the open again.
Bankside trees and shrubs shade the water and keep it cooler.
The cantons must designate a water space.
Deadwood such as root stumps gives fish places to shelter.
The Third Rhône Correction combines flood protection and ecology.
The Confederation protects floodplain areas with its own ordinance.
Fish passes make it possible to migrate upstream.

abschnitte.text: In **canalisation**, a river is made straight and uniform, with fixed banks of stone or concrete. A **revitalisation** does the opposite: it creates **variety**. The river gets more room, with deep and shallow places and fast and calm stretches. In **daylighting**, a stream that used to flow in pipes under the ground is brought back into the light. It can then flow in the open again.

Trees and shrubs on the bank, the **bankside vegetation**, **shade the water** and keep it cooler. This is important for many fish, because they need cool, oxygen-rich water. In revitalisations, **deadwood** such as **root stumps** is also deliberately placed in the water. Underneath, fish find **shelter** where they can hide and rest.

Loose **gravel banks** are important for fish such as the **grayling**, because they serve as **spawning grounds**: the fish lay their eggs there. Many fish migrate upstream during their lives. A **fish pass** at a weir makes this **migration** possible. It often consists of many small pools through which the fish swim upwards step by step.

The cantons must designate a **water space** along waters. This strip is reserved for the natural functions of the water and for **flood protection**. Building and fertilising are only allowed there to a limited extent. **Floodplains** are especially valuable: shoreland areas that are flooded regularly. The Confederation protects them with its own **Floodplains Ordinance**.

A particularly large project is the **Third Rhône Correction** in the cantons of Valais and Vaud. The Rhône was already embanked in the 19th and 20th centuries. In the third correction, the river is widened in many places. It combines **flood protection** with **ecological improvement** and is being built over several decades.

gewusst: Just a few years after a revitalisation, animals that had previously vanished from the stream often return.
In Switzerland, a large part of the flowing waters in settled and farmed areas is heavily built up or culverted.

teile.einleitung: Phenology observes recurring events in nature. It records when plants put out leaves, flower or change the colour of their leaves. The arrival of migratory birds also belongs to it.
wichtigste: Phenology studies the development phases of plants and animals that recur every year.
MeteoSwiss has run a nationwide observation network since **1951**.
In Geneva a **horse chestnut** has been observed for over 200 years.
In **Liestal** the cherry blossom has been recorded since the end of the 19th century.
Many plants now put out leaves earlier than in the middle of the 20th century.
Early flowers are endangered by **late frost**.

abschnitte.text: Phenology divides the year not by the calendar but by nature. The **hazel** with its yellow catkins rings in early spring, often as early as February. The **forsythia** marks the first spring. **Apple blossom** counts as a sign of full spring. With the white flower umbels of the **black elder**, early summer begins.

In Geneva there is an official tree, a **horse chestnut** on the Promenade de la Treille. Every year an official of the cantonal parliament, the **Sautier**, notes when the first leaf appears. This observation has been going for over 200 years. It is among the oldest such series in the world.

In **Liestal** in the canton of Basel-Landschaft, the start of flowering of a cherry tree has been recorded since the end of the 19th century. It is one of the longest phenological series of measurements in Switzerland. It shows that cherries now flower clearly earlier on average. Since 1951, **MeteoSwiss** has also been collecting observations from all over the country with volunteers.

The long series show that leaf-out and flowering now begin earlier than a few decades ago. The reason is the **higher temperatures**. This has consequences. If fruit trees flower very early, the blossoms are exposed longer to the danger of frosty nights in April. Frozen blossoms bear no fruit.

gewusst: In Kyoto in Japan, the cherry blossom has been written down for over a thousand years.
The phenological clock distinguishes ten seasons instead of four.

teile.einleitung: A Red List shows how seriously species of animals, plants and fungi are threatened. The worldwide Red List is published by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, the IUCN, which has its headquarters in Switzerland.
wichtigste: A Red List shows how seriously species are threatened.
The worldwide Red List comes from the IUCN.
The IUCN has its headquarters in Gland in the canton of Vaud.
“Critically Endangered” is the highest level of threat for a species that is still alive.
If knowledge about a species is lacking, the category is “Data Deficient”.
Switzerland has its own Red Lists for its territory.
Red Lists are revised regularly, every few years.

abschnitte.text: A **Red List** is a register of species with their **degree of threat**. Experts check, for example, how many animals or plants there still are, whether their numbers are falling and how large their habitat is. Then they assign each species to a **category**. This shows at a glance which species most urgently need protection. Red Lists help the authorities and nature conservation to plan the right measures.

The worldwide Red List is published by the **IUCN**. This is the abbreviation of the English name of the **International Union for Conservation of Nature**. It was founded in 1948. Its headquarters are in **Gland** in the canton of Vaud, on Lake Geneva. Its members are states, authorities and many nature conservation organisations. Thousands of experts from all over the world work on the list.

The list has several levels. The highest level of threat for a species that is still alive is called **“Critically Endangered”**. Below it come “Endangered” and “Vulnerable”. **“Near Threatened”** means: the species is not yet threatened, but soon will be if nothing is done. “Least Concern” means that the species is doing well. If the experts know too little about a species, they give it the category **“Data Deficient”**.

Switzerland has its own Red Lists, which the **Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN)** publishes together with specialist bodies. They exist for many groups, for example for birds, dragonflies, ferns and flowering plants or fungi. Here there is a special category: **“Extinct in Switzerland”**. It means that the species is missing here but still lives elsewhere. To keep the lists up to date, they are revised **regularly, every few years**.

gewusst: The beaver was wiped out in Switzerland in the 19th century. It was later reintroduced and today lives on many rivers.
The colour red stands for alarm: it is meant to show that many species need help.

teile.einleitung: Sainfoin is a fodder plant with pretty pink flowers. It grows on limy, dry soils and is popular with bees and farmers alike.
wichtigste: Sainfoin is a legume.
Its flowers are pink with darker veins.
Nodule bacteria on the roots fix nitrogen from the air.
It prefers limy, rather dry soils.
A deep taproot helps it through dry summers.
It was traditionally grown as a fodder plant.
Its tannins can help sheep and goats against intestinal worms.

abschnitte.text: Sainfoin belongs to the **legume family**, like clover, peas and beans. Its leaves are pinnate, which means they consist of many small leaflets on one stalk. The flowers stand in elongated clusters. They are **pink with darker veins**. The plant can grow half a metre or taller and flowers in early summer.

Sainfoin prefers **limy, rather dry soils**. There it manages with little water because it has a **deep taproot**. This root gets water from a great depth, even when the summer is dry. **Nodule bacteria** also live on the roots. They **fix nitrogen from the air** and supply the plant with it. That is why sainfoin hardly needs any nitrogen fertiliser.

Sainfoin was traditionally grown **as a fodder plant** for animals, fresh or as hay. It contains **tannins**. These substances can help **sheep and goats** to fight **intestinal worms**. They also prevent ruminants from getting bloated after eating, as can happen with a lot of fresh clover. That is why experts, in Switzerland too, are studying sainfoin more closely again.

The flowers of sainfoin supply **plenty of nectar**. That is why it is very popular with **honeybees**, but also with wild bees, bumblebees and butterflies. Where sainfoin blooms, there is often a loud humming. Beekeepers value the pale, mild honey. In species-rich, dry meadows sainfoin also grows wild.

gewusst: The name sainfoin comes from French.
The roots of sainfoin can reach several metres deep into the soil.

teile.einleitung: A seed is a small package that holds a whole new plant. Inside lie a tiny embryo and a store of food, well packed in a protective covering. A huge tree can grow from a seed smaller than a grain of rice.
wichtigste: A seed contains an embryo, nutritive tissue and a protective seed coat.
Seeds form after the pollination and fertilisation of a flower.
To germinate, a seed needs water, warmth and soil, and also air to breathe.
Many seeds can rest for a long time, waiting for good conditions.
Plants spread their seeds by wind, water, animals or by flinging them.
Cereals, nuts, beans and stones are seeds that people eat.

abschnitte.text: A seed is the organ by which **seed plants** spread and survive. Inside lies the **embryo** with a small root, a shoot and one or two seed leaves. Beside it there is nutritive tissue with starch, oil or protein as provisions. On the outside, the hard **seed coat** protects against drying out and injury.

First, pollen has to land on the stigma of a flower. This is called pollination, and bees or the wind often help with it. Then a male cell joins with a female cell, which is **fertilisation**. The fertilised ovule becomes the seed, and a fruit such as an apple or a cherry often grows around it.

To germinate, a seed needs water, warmth and soil, and also oxygen from the air. First it takes up water and swells, which is called **imbibition**. Then the coat bursts, and the root grows downwards. After that the shoot pushes up towards the light, where the first leaves turn green.

Plants cannot walk, so they send their seeds on journeys. The dandelion has little parachutes that the **wind** carries far, and maple seeds spin like propellers. Burrs hook into the fur of animals, and birds eat berries and pass the seeds out again somewhere else. The touch-me-not even flings its seeds several metres away.

Many of our most important foods are seeds. Wheat, rice and maize are the seeds of **cereals**, and bread is baked from wheat. Beans, lentils, peas, nuts and sunflower seeds are seeds too. In Switzerland, nurseries and associations such as ProSpecieRara preserve old varieties so that their seeds are not lost.

Some seeds stay able to germinate for decades if they are kept dry and cool. That is why there are **seed banks** that store the seeds of many plant varieties. The best known is the Svalbard Global Seed Vault on the island of Spitsbergen in the far north. Switzerland also keeps a national gene bank for crop plants at Changins near Nyon.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tiny baby plant inside the seed.
The first leaf of the young plant, often filled with food.
When pollen lands on the stigma of a flower.
The awakening of the seed when it begins to grow.

gewusst: The largest seeds in the world come from the coco de mer palm and can weigh over 20 kilograms.
Orchid seeds are as tiny as dust.
Researchers made a palm grow again from a date seed about 2,000 years old from Israel.

teile.einleitung: The **prairie** is the great grassland in the interior of North America. It stretches from Canada to Texas. In the past huge herds of bison roamed there; today most of it is farmland.
wichtigste: The prairie lies in North America, from Canada to Texas.
In the past millions of **bison** lived there.
**Prairie dogs** dig large underground colonies.
Fire and grazing herds kept the prairie free of trees.
In the wetter east taller grass grows than in the dry west.
Since the 19th century most of it has become farmland.
In the 1930s there was the **Dust Bowl** with severe dust storms.

abschnitte.text: The prairie is a wide, flat to hilly **grassland** in North America. It stretches from **Canada** to **Texas**. The Canadian **Prairie Provinces** include Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. From east to west it gets drier and drier, because the **Rocky Mountains** hold back rain. That is why the **tallgrass prairie** in the east is followed by the **shortgrass prairie** in the west.

In the past millions of **bison** lived on the prairie. In the 19th century they were almost wiped out. Today they live mainly in protected areas. **Prairie dogs** are ground squirrels that live in burrows with many tunnels. Their colonies are called “towns”, because very many animals live there.

By nature, **fire** and **grazing herds** kept the prairie free of trees. Lightning started prairie fires again and again. The big herds ate young woody plants. Grasses survive this because their buds sit **close to the ground**. Trees and shrubs, by contrast, had hardly any chance.

From the 19th century settlers ploughed up the fertile soil. They planted **wheat** and **maize**. Of the original tallgrass prairie only a small remnant survives. Today the region is among the most important grain-growing areas in the world. In the Canadian Prairie Provinces too, a lot of grain is grown.

After the ploughing, no grass protected the soil any more. In the **1930s** a long **drought** came. The wind carried away huge amounts of soil, and there were severe **dust storms**. This period is called the **Dust Bowl**, which in German means roughly “Staubschüssel”, a bowl of dust. Many families had to leave their farms.

gewusst: The roots of prairie grasses often reach much deeper into the ground than the stalks are tall.
Prairie dog colonies can spread over very large areas.

teile.einleitung: With the **quadrat method**, researchers estimate how many plants or slow-moving animals live on an area. To do this they lay frames of known area on the ground and count inside them. From the samples they then calculate up to the whole area.
wichtigste: A **sample quadrat** is a frame of known area, for example 1 m by 1 m.
The method suits organisms that are fixed in place or slow.
The **population density** is the number of individuals per area.
The **frequency** is the share of quadrats in which a species occurs.
You choose the position of the quadrats with random numbers.
Permanent quadrats show changes over many years.

abschnitte.text: A **sample quadrat** is a frame of known area. Often it measures 1 m by 1 m. You lay it on the ground and count all the plants of one species inside it. The method suits organisms that are **fixed in place or slow**, such as plants, lichens or barnacles. Moving animals would flee from the frame or be counted twice.

If you divide the individuals counted by the area studied, you get the **population density**. An example: in 10 quadrats of 1 m² each, you count 45 daisies. The density is 45 ÷ 10 = **4.5 per m²**. For a meadow of 2,000 m² you estimate 4.5 times 2,000 = **9,000** daisies. If a quadrat measures only 50 cm by 50 cm, that is 0.25 m², and contains on average 3 plants, that makes 3 times 4 = **12 per m²**.

Sometimes you only want to know **how widespread** a species is. Then you count in how many quadrats it occurs. This share is called the **frequency**. If a species occurs in 14 of 20 quadrats, 14 divided by 20 gives 0.7. The frequency is therefore **70%**.

For the result to be right, the quadrats must be spread **at random**. It is best to use **random numbers** to fix the x and y coordinates in a grid. Throwing the frame blindly seems random, but is often biased. For plants exactly on the edge a fixed **edge rule** applies: you count them only on two set sides. What matters is that everyone uses the same rule.

For repeat surveys, sample quadrats are often marked **permanently** in the field, for example with metal markers in the ground. Such **permanent quadrats** are surveyed again and again over many years. Because it is always the same area, differences show real changes in the vegetation. In this way you can observe, for example, how a meadow develops after a change in how it is managed.

gewusst: With a few sample quadrats you can estimate the plants of a huge meadow without counting every single one.
The quadrat method is also used on rocky sea coasts, for example to count barnacles.

teile.einleitung: The foxglove is a striking plant with purple-red, bell-shaped flowers. It is very poisonous, but it also supplies substances for important heart medicines.
wichtigste: The flowers fit over a finger like a thimble, hence the German name “Fingerhut”.
They are mostly purple-red and spotted inside.
The flowers hang one below another on one side of the stem.
All parts of the plant are poisonous.
The poison acts especially on the heart.
Heart medicines are made from substances in the foxglove.
A plant usually lives for two years.

abschnitte.text: The flowers of the foxglove are shaped like small **bells** or tubes. They fit like a **hat on a finger**, which is where the German name “Fingerhut”, meaning “thimble”, comes from. The scientific name **Digitalis** recalls this too, because “digitus” is Latin for finger. The flowers are mostly **purple-red**, and inside they have dark spots with a pale edge. They hang **one below another on one side** of the tall stem.

The flowers are visited mainly by **bumblebees**. A bumblebee crawls right into the flower tube to reach the nectar. The spots inside show it the way. As it crawls in and out, it picks up pollen and carries it to the next flower. The lower flowers on the stem open first, and the upper ones later.

The foxglove often grows **at the edge of woods**, in woodland clearings and along paths. It prefers rather acid soils. A plant usually lives for **two years**. In the first year it forms only a rosette of leaves on the ground. In the second year a flower stem grows that can reach over a metre tall. After that the plant produces many tiny seeds and dies.

**All parts** of the foxglove are **poisonous**. Even small amounts can be dangerous, so you must never put it in your mouth, and you should wash your hands after touching it. The poison acts especially on the **heart**. In exactly measured amounts, however, these substances can help: **heart medicines** are made from them, for example for heart failure. Such remedies may only be prescribed by doctors.

gewusst: The healing effect of foxglove on heart conditions was described in detail by an English doctor in the 18th century.
A single foxglove plant can produce tens of thousands of tiny seeds.

teile.einleitung: The **Rafflesia arnoldii** has the largest single flower of any plant. The flower can grow to about a metre across and smells of rotting meat. The plant has neither leaves nor roots and lives as a parasite in the rainforest of South-East Asia.
wichtigste: The rafflesia has the largest single flower in the world.
The flower can grow to about 1 metre across.
It can weigh up to about 11 kilograms.
The plant has no leaves, no stem and no roots.
It lives as a parasite inside a climbing plant.
Flies pollinate the flower, which smells of rotting meat.

abschnitte.text: The **rafflesia** has the largest **single flower** of any plant. Other giants are actually many small flowers grouped together. Its flower can grow to about **a metre** across. It can weigh up to about **11 kilograms**, as much as a child of about one year old. It lies on the forest floor like a big plate.

All you can see of the rafflesia is the flower. It has **no leaves**, no stem and **no roots**. The plant is a **parasite**. It lives inside a **climbing plant** and takes water and food from it there. That is why it does not need photosynthesis either.

abschnitte.titel: The smell of rotting meat attracts flies
abschnitte.text: The flower is **reddish brown** with pale spots. It looks a little like raw meat. It also smells of **rotting meat**. This attracts **carrion flies**. They carry the pollen on to other flowers.

The rafflesia grows in the damp **tropical rainforest** of South-East Asia. The climbing plants it needs grow there too. The flower is open for only a few days. Because the rainforests are getting smaller, the plant has become rare in many places.

gewusst: The Rafflesia arnoldii is one of the national flowers of Indonesia.
It is named after Stamford Raffles and Joseph Arnold, who found it on Sumatra in 1818.

teile.einleitung: How does a plant know that it is spring or autumn? Many plants measure the length of day and night and time their flowering accordingly. This ability is called photoperiodism.
wichtigste: Photoperiodism is the reaction of plants to day length, for example when flowering.
Long-day plants flower when the days get long.
Short-day plants flower when the days get short.
Day-neutral plants flower regardless of day length.
In fact plants mainly measure the length of uninterrupted darkness.
Light is sensed in the leaves with the pigment phytochrome.
Animals also react to day length, for example in bird migration or in changing their coat.

abschnitte.text: The word **photoperiodism** comes from the Greek word for light and from period. It means that living things react to the ratio of day to night. In plants, day length mainly controls the time of **flowering**. Tuber formation, leaf fall and winter dormancy also often depend on it.
