**Long-day plants** flower when the days exceed a certain length, that is, in early summer. They include spinach, radishes, oats and wheat. **Short-day plants** only flower when the days get shorter, for example chrysanthemums and the poinsettia. Day-neutral plants such as tomatoes and cucumbers flower as soon as they are big enough.

In the leaves sits the light sensor **phytochrome**, which senses red light. Together with an inner clock, the plant measures how long it is dark. If the night length is right, the leaves make a messenger substance that travels to the shoot tip and triggers flowering there. Even a short flash of light in the middle of the night can upset this measurement.

The American researchers Wightman Garner and Harry Allard described photoperiodism in 1920. They studied a variety of tobacco that did not flower in summer, but did in a greenhouse in winter. They found out that the short winter days triggered flowering. Later it turned out that it is really the long **night** that matters.

Nurseries cover poinsettias in the evening in autumn so that they bear red bracts in time for Christmas. Chrysanthemums are brought into flower all year round with artificial light or darkening. Spinach, on the other hand, **bolts** in high summer: it forms flowers and goes tough. That is why it is best sown in spring or late summer.

Day length is a very reliable calendar, much more exact than temperature. In this way plants of one species flower at the same time and can pollinate one another. Farmers choose varieties that suit the **day length** of their region. Hens also lay fewer eggs in winter because the days are short.

begriffe.erklaerung: The daily duration of light and darkness.
A plant that flowers when the days are long.
A plant that flowers when the days are short.
A light sensor in plants that senses red light.

gewusst: The tobacco variety with which photoperiodism was discovered was called Maryland Mammoth.
The poinsettia comes from Mexico and flowers there naturally in winter.
Because of day length, trees under street lamps sometimes change colour later in autumn than their neighbours.

teile.einleitung: Saturn is the sixth planet of our solar system and the second largest after Jupiter. It is famous for its magnificent ring system of ice and rock. Even with a small telescope you can see the rings from Earth.
wichtigste: Saturn is the sixth planet counting from the Sun.
It is a gas planet and consists mainly of hydrogen and helium.
Its rings consist of countless chunks of ice and rock.
Saturn has a lower density than water.
It takes almost 30 Earth years to orbit the Sun once.
Saturn has a great many moons, and the largest is called Titan.

abschnitte.text: Saturn is a **gas planet**, so it has no solid surface like the Earth. It consists mainly of **hydrogen** and helium. Its diameter is about nine times that of the Earth. Because it spins fast, it is clearly flattened at the poles.

The **ring system** consists of countless chunks of ice and rock. Some are as small as grains of dust, others as big as houses. The rings are very wide but usually only a few tens of metres to about a kilometre thick. Between them there are gaps, and the largest is called the Cassini Division.

Saturn is on average about 1.4 billion kilometres from the Sun. It takes almost 30 years to go once round the Sun, and this is one **Saturn year**. A day, by contrast, lasts only about ten and a half hours. At around minus 140 degrees Celsius in the upper clouds, it is icy cold on Saturn.

Saturn has over 200 known moons, more than any other planet (as of 2025). The largest is **Titan**, which is bigger than the planet Mercury and has a dense atmosphere. On Titan there are lakes of liquid methane. The small moon **Enceladus** hurls fountains of water vapour and ice into space.

Galileo Galilei was the first to see Saturn through a telescope in 1610, but he did not yet recognise the rings properly. Christiaan Huygens explained in 1655 that it is a ring, and discovered the moon Titan. The space probe **Cassini** orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017 and sent thousands of pictures. Its landing probe Huygens landed on Titan in 2005.

begriffe.erklaerung: A giant planet without a solid surface that consists mainly of gas.
Many chunks of ice and rock that orbit a planet in a flat disc.
A heavenly body that orbits a planet.
An unmanned spacecraft that explores planets.

gewusst: Saturn is so light for its size that it would float in a huge bathtub full of water.
At Saturn’s north pole there is a hurricane in the shape of a hexagon.
Every few years the rings are seen exactly edge on, and then they are almost invisible.

teile.einleitung: Many animals eat only plants. They are called plant-eaters or herbivores. But plants are hard to digest, so these animals have special teeth and stomachs.
wichtigste: Plant-eaters are called herbivores in technical language.
Ruminants such as cow, goat and chamois chew their food a second time.
The largest section of a cow’s stomach is called the rumen.
Micro-organisms in the digestive tract help to break down the tough cellulose.
Plant-eaters have broad molars with grinding surfaces.
The giant panda eats almost only bamboo, the koala almost only eucalyptus leaves.

abschnitte.text: The word **herbivores** comes from the Latin **herba**, which means grass or herb. Herbivores feed on plants: on grass, leaves, buds, bark, fruit or seeds. They include large animals such as cows and elephants, but also many **insects**, such as caterpillars. Plant-eaters are food for **meat-eaters** and so an important part of every food chain.

Plants have to be broken up thoroughly. That is why plant-eaters have **broad molars** with **grinding surfaces**. With these they crush the food as between two millstones. They have no need of the pointed tearing teeth that predators have. So from the teeth of a skull you can often tell what an animal ate.

**Cow**, **goat**, **sheep** and **chamois** are **ruminants**. Their stomach has four sections. The largest is the **rumen**. There countless **micro-organisms** break down the grass. Later the animal brings the food up again and chews it once more thoroughly. That is why you often see cows lying quietly in the pasture chewing.

Plants contain a lot of **cellulose**, a tough substance in the cell walls. Mammals cannot break down cellulose themselves. This work is done by **bacteria** and other tiny organisms in the stomach or gut. In horses and rabbits this happens mainly in the **gut**. Without these helpers, plant-eaters could hardly survive.

Some animals eat almost only one plant. The **giant panda** belongs to the bears but eats almost only **bamboo** and needs large amounts of it daily. The **koala** eats almost only the leaves of certain **eucalyptus trees**. These are low in nutrients, so it sleeps a great deal. In Switzerland the **beaver** is a pure plant-eater. In winter it eats mainly bark and twigs and even fells trees for them. **Roe deer** and red deer like to eat the buds of young trees. You often see this **browsing damage** in the forest.

gewusst: Heavy browsing can make it harder for the forest to grow back. Foresters therefore sometimes protect young trees with fences or guards.
A koala often sleeps or rests for up to 20 hours a day.

teile.einleitung: The **quagga mussel** is a small freshwater mussel from the area around the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea. It has spread to many countries and is regarded as an invasive species. In Switzerland it was discovered in Lake Constance in 2016, and it has caused problems there ever since.
wichtigste: The quagga mussel comes from the Black Sea and Caspian region.
It is named after the **quagga**, an extinct form of zebra.
It filters plankton out of the water.
It also settles on soft lake beds and at depths of more than 100 metres.
Its larvae are called **veliger larvae**.
It clogs the pipes of drinking water intakes.
It was first recorded in Lake Constance in 2016.

abschnitte.text: The quagga mussel’s scientific name is *Dreissena rostriformis bugensis*. It comes from the catchment area of the **Dnieper** and the **Southern Bug** in the Black Sea and Caspian region. It has spread far and wide along waterways and on ships. Its name comes from the **quagga**, an extinct form of zebra with stripes on only part of its coat. The mussel has similar stripes on its shell.

The quagga mussel is related to the **zebra mussel**. However, it can cope with colder temperatures. It can also settle on muddy **soft lake beds** and at depths of more than **100 metres**. As a result it is pushing out the zebra mussel in many lakes. It was discovered in **Lake Constance** in **2016** and has spread in huge numbers since then.

The mussel is a **filter feeder**. It sucks in water and sieves out tiny floating particles and **plankton**. Large populations make the water clearer. At the same time, however, they take the plankton out of the food chain. This can leave other animals in the lake, such as fish, short of food.

The mussels attach themselves to pipes and filters in dense colonies using **byssus threads**. In this way they clog the pipes of **drinking water intakes**. Water suppliers therefore have to carry out costly cleaning or rebuild their systems. This costs a lot of money.

The free-swimming **veliger larvae** drift in the water for a few weeks before they settle. They are barely visible to the naked eye. They can survive in the **leftover water** in boats, and young mussels cling to the hull. This is the most common way for the mussel to travel from one lake to the next. That is why boats should be **cleaned and dried** before they move to another body of water.

gewusst: A single trip with a boat that has not been cleaned can be enough to bring the quagga mussel to a new lake.
The quagga that the mussel is named after used to live in southern Africa.

teile.einleitung: The earthworm lives almost everywhere in the soil, in gardens, on meadows and in forests. It is unremarkable to look at, but enormously important for the earth: it loosens the soil and makes it fertile.
wichtigste: The earthworm belongs to the annelids, or segmented worms.
It has no legs and no bones.
In the garden it is usually reddish brown.
It swallows soil together with plant remains.
Its droppings, in small crumbs, are very fertile.
Its burrows let air and water into the soil.
In the blazing sun it dries out.

abschnitte.text: The earthworm belongs to the **annelids**. Its body is made up of many small sections that lie one behind the other like rings. It has **no legs** and **no bones**. Even so, it can move well: it contracts its muscles and stretches out again. Tiny **bristles** on its underside hold it in place in the soil as it does so. The common earthworm can grow to about 30 centimetres long.

An earthworm has no lungs. It **breathes through its skin**, and this only works when the skin is damp. That is why it likes damp soil. If it lies for a long time in the **blazing sun**, it **dries out** and dies. It has no eyes, but it can sense with its skin whether it is light or dark. After heavy rain, many earthworms come up to the surface.

The earthworm pulls **leaves and plant remains** into its burrows. It eats them together with **soil**. Inside its gut everything is mixed. At the back end, small dark crumbs come out: its **droppings**. These crumbs are very **fertile**, because they contain many nutrients for plants. You often see them as little heaps on the lawn.

Earthworms dig **burrows** through the soil, and some reach deep down. Through these burrows **air and water** get into the earth, and plant roots grow through more easily. In heavy rain the water soaks away faster instead of washing the soil away. Lots of earthworms are therefore a sign of **healthy soil**.

Earthworms are food for many animals. The **blackbird** hops across the lawn, listens and then pulls a worm out of the ground. Hedgehogs, moles, toads and foxes also eat earthworms. Anyone digging in the garden often sees how quickly a worm pulls itself back into the soil.

gewusst: Charles Darwin wrote a whole book about earthworms and their work in the soil.
Under a meadow, more than a hundred earthworms can live in every square metre.

teile.einleitung: Rosemary is a small, evergreen shrub from the Mediterranean region. It has a strong scent and is often used as a herb in cooking.
wichtigste: Rosemary is a small shrub that stays green all year round.
Its leaves are narrow like needles.
It comes from the Mediterranean region.
The flowers are usually pale blue.
The Latin name “ros marinus” means “dew of the sea”.
In Switzerland it often needs protection from hard frost in winter.
In a pot, rosemary needs rather little water.

abschnitte.text: Rosemary is a **small shrub** with woody twigs. Its leaves are narrow like **needles** and slightly leathery. On top they are dark green, and underneath they are paler and slightly felty. The leaves stay green even in winter, which is why it is called **evergreen**. If you rub the leaves between your fingers, you can smell the **essential oils** that give it its scent.

Rosemary comes from the **Mediterranean region**. There it grows wild on dry, sunny slopes, often close to the coast. The Latin name **“ros marinus”** means “dew of the sea”. It belongs to the **mint family**, like sage, thyme and mint. Its small flowers are usually **pale blue**, sometimes also white or pink.

Rosemary is a popular **herb**. Oven-roasted potatoes with rosemary, baked together in the oven, are very well known. It is also used to season meat, vegetables and bread such as Italian focaccia. Because its flavour is strong, a small amount is usually enough. The needles can be used fresh or dried.

Rosemary likes a **sunny and warm spot**. In a pot it needs **rather little water**. Too much wetness or standing water in the pot harms its roots. In Switzerland, winter is often colder than on the Mediterranean. That is why rosemary here often needs **protection from hard frost**, for example against a sheltered house wall or in a bright, cool place indoors.

gewusst: Bees like to visit rosemary flowers because they offer nectar early in the year.
In botany, rosemary is now counted as part of the genus Salvia, the sages.

teile.einleitung: **Pro Natura** is the oldest nature conservation organisation in Switzerland. It was founded in 1909 to raise money for the Swiss National Park. Today it looks after several hundred protected areas and makes children familiar with nature.
wichtigste: Pro Natura was founded in 1909.
It used to be called the **Swiss League for Nature Protection**.
Its first purpose was to finance the National Park.
It looks after several hundred protected areas in Switzerland.
Every year Pro Natura chooses an **Animal of the Year**.
In youth groups children discover nature outdoors.
The Pro Natura Centre Aletsch is near Riederalp.

abschnitte.text: Pro Natura was founded in **1909**. At that time it was called the **Swiss League for Nature Protection**. Its first purpose was to raise money for the planned **National Park** in the Engadine. With this money the area could be leased. The organisation has carried its present name since 1997. It is the oldest nature conservation organisation in Switzerland.

Pro Natura looks after **several hundred protected areas** in Switzerland. They include meadows, ponds, moors and forests. Many of these areas have to be looked after so that rare plants and animals can live there. Volunteers help, for example, with mowing or clearing scrub. Pro Natura also campaigns in politics for nature conservation.

Every year Pro Natura chooses an **Animal of the Year**. It stands for a habitat that needs protection. In this way many people get to know the animal and its surroundings better. For the Animal of the Year there is information, brochures and events. The choice is meant to show what everyone can do for nature.

In the **youth groups** of Pro Natura children go outdoors. They watch animals, build nest boxes and learn a lot about nature. Pro Natura also runs visitor centres. The **Pro Natura Centre Aletsch** is near Riederalp in the Valais. From there you can see the **Aletsch Forest** and the Great Aletsch Glacier.

gewusst: Without Pro Natura the Swiss National Park would probably not have come into being so early.
The Aletsch Forest is among the best-known Swiss stone pine forests.

teile.einleitung: Renaturation means bringing a habitat that people have changed back to a near-natural state. In Switzerland this often concerns streams and rivers that used to be straightened or put into pipes.
wichtigste: The aim is to restore a near-natural state.
For waters, the term often used in Switzerland is revitalisation.
Around 4,000 kilometres of flowing waters are to be improved over about 80 years.
In the Jura Water Correction, the Aare was diverted into Lake Biel from 1868.
A fish ladder helps fish to get past a weir.
A culverted stream flows in pipes under the ground.

abschnitte.text: In the past, people **straightened** many streams and rivers and forced them into fixed banks. They wanted to gain land, drain marshes and protect themselves from floods. Many small streams were **culverted**, which means they flow in pipes under the ground. In the process, habitats for fish, birds and plants were lost. In a **renaturation**, people try to restore a **near-natural state**. For waters, the usual term in Switzerland is **revitalisation**.

A particularly large water engineering project was the **Jura Water Correction**. From **1868** the **Aare** was diverted into **Lake Biel**. The aim was to stop the frequent flooding in the Seeland region and to drain the marshy area. This worked, and today the Seeland is an important vegetable-growing area. At the same time, large wetlands disappeared. This shows that such interventions have advantages and disadvantages.

The **Water Protection Act** requires the cantons to improve their waters. Over **about 80 years**, around **4,000 kilometres** of flowing waters are to be given a near-natural form. Streams and rivers are given more room, and the banks become shallower and more varied. Revitalised waters often also protect better against floods, because the water can spread out.

Many fish travel up and down the river. The **weir** of a river power station is a wall to them. A **fish ladder** with many small pools helps them to get past the obstacle. Loose **gravel banks** are also important: many fish lay their **eggs** there. Below storage power stations there is often **hydropeaking**: the water changes rapidly between high and low levels. This too is to be reduced.

gewusst: Because of the Jura Water Correction, the water level of the three lakes at the foot of the Jura fell by about two and a half metres.
It is not only waters that are renaturated, but also, for example, moors, gravel pits or quarries.

teile.einleitung: The Confederation’s **Parks Ordinance** (“Pärkeverordnung”) regulates the **parks of national importance** in Switzerland. These include regional nature parks, nature discovery parks and new national parks. It sets out how a park comes into being and what applies in its zones.
wichtigste: The Parks Ordinance regulates the parks of national importance.
The label is awarded by the Confederation, more precisely by the **FOEN**.
The municipalities involved must agree to a park.
Every park sets its goals in a **charter**.
The Wildnispark Zürich Sihlwald was the first nature discovery park.
The planned Parc Adula failed in 2016 in votes in the municipalities.
The Swiss National Park has its own law.

abschnitte.text: The Parks Ordinance knows three categories. **Regional nature parks** are partly populated rural areas. They are meant to preserve and enhance nature and landscape and at the same time strengthen a **sustainable economy** in the region. **Nature discovery parks** lie close to cities. In addition there are **national parks** with large protected core zones.

A nature discovery park has a **core zone**. There use is given up so that nature can develop freely. Visitors stay on marked paths. In the **transition zone**, experiencing nature and environmental education are possible. The **Wildnispark Zürich Sihlwald** was the first park to receive this label. In its core zone the forest may develop freely.

Parks arise on the initiative of the **region**. The **municipalities** involved must agree, often at the municipal assembly or at the ballot box. Every park needs a **charter**. It is a contract between the park municipalities and the park management body and sets goals and measures for ten years. On the canton’s application, the **Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN)** awards the label if the requirements are met. The park then also receives money from the Confederation.

abschnitte.titel: Parc Adula and the National Park
abschnitte.text: In the area of the Grisons and Ticino, the **Parc Adula** was planned around the Rheinwaldhorn as a second national park. In **2016** several of the municipalities concerned rejected it, so it did not come about. The **Swiss National Park** in the Engadine was founded as early as **1914**. With the National Park Act of 1980 it has its own legal basis. The Parks Ordinance regulates the newer parks.

gewusst: After the no to the Parc Adula, the park in the Engadine remained the only national park in Switzerland.
Whether a park comes into being is decided in Switzerland partly by the voters of the municipalities.

teile.einleitung: Peppermint smells fresh and tastes cool. You drink it as tea and find its taste in toothpaste and sweets. The plant grows fast and likes to spread in the garden.
wichtigste: Tea is made from the leaves of peppermint.
The substance menthol gives the cool feeling in the mouth.
Peppermint is a cross between water mint and spearmint.
It spreads by long runners in the soil.
Its stem is four-sided, typical of mints.
Peppermint likes to grow on damp ground.

abschnitte.text: **Peppermint** is a **cross** between two other mints: **water mint** and **spearmint**. It probably arose in **England**. It got its name because it tastes strong and a little **hot**, like pepper. But it is not related to real pepper.

If you turn the **stem** between your fingers, you feel **four edges**. This is typical of mints and many other plants of the **mint family**, which also includes sage and thyme. The leaves sit opposite one another and smell strongly when you rub them. In summer small, pale violet flowers appear in spikes.

In the leaves is an **essential oil** with a lot of **menthol**. Menthol creates a cool, fresh feeling in the mouth, although nothing is actually cold. That is why many **toothpastes**, chewing gums and sweets taste of mint. This makes for fresh breath.

For **tea** you use the fresh or dried **leaves**. You pour hot water over them and let them steep for a few minutes. Peppermint tea tastes good warm and cold. Many people also drink it for tummy ache, because it can calm digestion.

Peppermint forms long **runners** under the ground. In this way it grows quickly in all directions and can push out other plants. Many gardeners therefore plant it in a pot or a ring without a bottom. Mints like **damp soil**, so you have to water them regularly.

gewusst: Because peppermint is a cross, it hardly forms seeds that can germinate. It is propagated by runners and cuttings.
Menthol irritates in the mouth and skin the same nerve cells that otherwise report cold.

teile.einleitung: Roots hold a plant in the ground and fetch water and nutrients. In some plants a thick main root grows straight down into the depths like a stake. It is called a taproot (“Pfahlwurzel” in German).
wichtigste: In a taproot, a strong main root grows vertically deep into the ground.
It arises from the radicle of the seed.
Oaks and dandelions form typical taproots.
Trees with a taproot are especially stable in storms.
In drought the taproot reaches water in deep layers of soil.
Grasses, on the other hand, form many equally thick fibrous roots.

abschnitte.text: When a seed germinates, the **radicle** comes out first. It grows down into the earth. In many plants this radicle grows on directly into the **main root**. It becomes thick and strong and grows like a **stake** straight down. From it thinner **lateral roots** branch off.

A taproot is formed mainly by **dicotyledons**. In them the radicle remains as the main root. In the **grasses**, on the other hand, the radicle dies early. Instead many equally thick roots grow from the base of the stem. This is called a **fibrous root system**. It forms a dense net near the surface.

The **oak** drives a long taproot deep into the ground even as a young plant. The **silver fir** also has a taproot. Such trees are held as if with an **anchor** and are less often uprooted in a **storm**. The spruce, on the other hand, is a **shallow-rooted tree**. In Storm **Lothar** in December 1999, very many trees fell in Switzerland, especially many spruces.

Plants whose roots reach especially far down are called **deep-rooted plants**. When in long **drought** the upper layers of soil dry out, there is often still water at depth. Taproots reach this water. That is why such plants often survive dry summers better.

Anyone who has ever tried to pull a **dandelion** out of the garden knows its long, fleshy taproot. It breaks off easily. If a piece stays in the ground, the dandelion often sprouts again. The **carrot** also has a taproot. In it the main root is strongly thickened and stores nutrients. This is exactly the part we eat.

gewusst: Parsnips and salsify are also thickened main roots that are eaten as vegetables.
In some trees the taproot becomes weaker with age, and strong lateral roots take over the holding.

teile.einleitung: In breeding for resistance, experts breed plant varieties that can defend themselves better against diseases and pests. This means fewer plant protection products are needed, and the harvest is more secure.
wichtigste: Horizontal resistance is based on many genes and is regarded as especially lasting.
Harold Flor put forward the gene-for-gene hypothesis.
Resistance genes often come from wild relatives of the crop plant.
When a pathogen overcomes a resistance, this is called a resistance breakdown.
PIWI means resistant to fungal diseases.
Divico is a red wine grape variety resistant to fungal diseases, bred by Agroscope.

abschnitte.text: A **resistance** is the ability of a plant to defend itself against a pathogen. Sometimes it is based on **a single gene**. It then often works very strongly, but only against certain races of a pathogen. This is called **vertical** resistance. **Horizontal** or **quantitative resistance** is based on **many genes**, each of which helps a little. It usually does not protect completely, but is regarded as **especially lasting**.

The American researcher **Harold Flor** studied the rust fungus on flax. He put forward the **gene-for-gene hypothesis**: each **resistance gene** of the plant has a matching **avirulence gene** in the pathogen. If the plant recognises the pathogen by it, it fights it off. If the pathogen changes, it is no longer recognised. Then a **resistance breakdown** occurs, and the variety falls ill again.

Many resistance genes come from **wild relatives** of the crop plants, for example from wild potatoes or wild wheat. Breeders cross them in, which can take many years. To make a resistance last longer, several resistance genes against the same pathogen are combined in one variety. This is called **pyramiding**. In **marker-assisted selection**, DNA features are used to tell, already at the **seedling** stage, whether it carries the desired genes.

Vines are often attacked by fungal diseases such as mildew and are therefore sprayed frequently. **PIWI** varieties are **resistant to fungal diseases** and need far fewer sprayings. The Swiss research institute **Agroscope** bred the red PIWI variety **Divico**. It is now grown in several wine regions of Switzerland.

Besides classical breeding there are genetic engineering methods. In **cisgenesis**, genes are transferred that come from the same species or from one that can be crossed with it. Supporters say this gets you to robust varieties more quickly. Critics fear unknown risks and want genetic engineering to be strictly regulated. In Switzerland, a moratorium on growing genetically modified plants has applied since 2005 and has been extended several times.

gewusst: A pathogen can sometimes overcome a new resistance after just a few years, which is why breeders are constantly working on new varieties.
The name Divico recalls a leader of the Helvetii from the time of the Romans.

teile.einleitung: Plasmolysis is a process in plant cells. If a cell lies in a strongly concentrated solution, it loses water. Its living contents shrink and come away from the cell wall.
wichtigste: In **plasmolysis** the protoplast comes away from the cell wall.
It occurs in a **hypertonic** solution.
The reverse process is called **deplasmolysis**.
The space between cell wall and protoplast is filled by the **outer solution**.
The red kitchen onion is good for observing it.
**Incipient plasmolysis** shows the osmotic value of the cell.

abschnitte.text: A plant cell consists of the firm **cell wall** and the living contents, the **protoplast**. Inside lies a large vacuole with cell sap. If the cell lies in a **hypertonic** solution, one that is more concentrated than the cell sap, water flows out by **osmosis**. The vacuole shrinks and the protoplast comes away from the wall. The cell wall is permeable, so the outer solution fills the space that is freed.

Plasmolysis can be observed well in the skin of the **red kitchen onion**. Its cell sap is coloured red, so you can see the vacuole clearly. If you add salt or sugar solution, the red area shrinks. In some places the membrane stays stuck to the wall. This produces thin strands, the **Hechtian strands**.

If you put plasmolysed cells back into pure water, the vacuole takes up water again. The protoplast expands and lies against the cell wall once more. This is called **deplasmolysis**. In **incipient plasmolysis** the protoplast is only just beginning to come away. Then the outer solution is about as concentrated as the cell sap. In this way you can determine the osmotic value of the cell.

Normally the cell sap presses firmly against the wall. This pressure is called **turgor** and keeps leaves firm. If you put lettuce leaves into a strongly salted dressing, the cells lose water by osmosis. They plasmolyse, and the leaves go **limp**. That is why it is best to add salad dressing only shortly before eating.

gewusst: Road salt in winter can harm plants at the roadside, because it draws water out of them.
Salt and sugar make food keep longer, because they also draw water out of bacteria and fungi.

teile.einleitung: Seed plants are all the plants that produce seeds. They include conifers, broadleaved trees, grasses and flowers, so most of the plants that we see every day.
wichtigste: Seed plants are called Spermatophyta in scientific terms.
A seed contains an embryo, nutritive tissue and a seed coat.
The seed coat develops from the integument, the covering of the ovule.
The nucellus of the ovule corresponds to the megasporangium.
A pollen grain is a greatly reduced male gametophyte.
The oldest known seeds date from the Late Devonian.
The coco de mer palm produces the heaviest seeds in the world.

abschnitte.text: A seed is like a small package for a new plant. It contains an **embryo**, a tiny young plant. In addition there is **nutritive tissue** as a store for the first period. On the outside it is protected by the **seed coat**. This lets a seed survive dry or cold periods and germinate only when conditions are good. Seed plants are called **Spermatophyta** in scientific terms.

A seed develops from an **ovule**. Its inner part is called the **nucellus**. It corresponds to the **megasporangium**, the container in which the large spores form in plants. The nucellus is surrounded by the **integument**. This covering later becomes the **seed coat**. Gymnosperms such as conifers carry the ovules openly on scales, while angiosperms carry them in an ovary.

Plants have an **alternation of generations**: two different generations take turns. In mosses, the green plant is the **gametophyte**. In seed plants, by contrast, the gametophyte is tiny. A **pollen grain** is a **greatly reduced male gametophyte** that consists of only a few cells. Pollen is carried by the wind or by animals. For this reason, unlike ferns and mosses, seed plants do not depend on water for it.

The **oldest known seeds** date from the **Late Devonian**, a geological period about 365 million years ago. An early group were the **seed ferns**. They had fern-like fronds but already bore seeds. Today they are extinct. Later the conifers and their relatives appeared, and finally the flowering plants, which are today the largest group of seed plants.

gewusst: The coco de mer palm produces the heaviest seeds in the world, which can weigh many kilograms.
The smallest seeds are produced by some orchids: they are as fine as dust.

teile.einleitung: A rainforest is a dense, evergreen forest in which it rains a great deal. The tropical rainforests around the equator are the richest habitats on land in terms of species. But they are also under serious threat.
wichtigste: A rainforest is a dense, evergreen forest with a great deal of rain.
Most rainforests lie in the tropics near the equator.
The largest rainforest on Earth is the Amazon rainforest in South America.
In tropical rainforest, more than 2,000 millimetres of rain usually falls each year.
Rainforests cover only a small part of the land area, but are home to more than half of all animal and plant species.
Clearing for pasture, soya and palm oil is making the rainforests shrink.
Besides tropical rainforests there are also temperate rainforests, for example on the west coast of North America.

abschnitte.text: The large **tropical rainforests** lie in South America, in Central Africa around the Congo and in South-East Asia. The **Amazon rainforest** is the largest and stretches across several countries, mainly Brazil. It is warm there all year round, usually about 25 degrees. There are no seasons as we have them.

In many rainforests it rains almost every day, often in the afternoon as a heavy thunderstorm downpour. The air is very damp, because the trees themselves give off a lot of water. A large part of the rain in the Amazon region comes from this **evaporation** from the forest. So the rainforest partly makes its own rain.

The rainforest is divided into **layers**. At the very top, a few giant trees tower more than 50 metres high. Below them the dense **canopy** forms a green roof in which most of the animals live. On the ground, by contrast, it is so dark that only a few plants grow there.

Jaguars, gorillas, orang-utans, sloths, parrots and countless insects live in the rainforest. Many plants, such as **epiphytes**, for example orchids and bromeliads, grow high up on branches to reach the light. Hundreds of species of beetle can live on a single tree. Many species have not even been discovered yet.

Cocoa, bananas, rubber and many spices originally come from rainforest regions. Numerous medicines are based on substances from rainforest plants. The rainforest stores huge amounts of carbon and influences the climate of the whole Earth. It is also home to many **indigenous peoples**.

Every year a great deal of rainforest is cleared, for cattle pastures, soya fields, **palm oil** plantations, timber and mining. Without trees, the thin soil is quickly washed away and becomes infertile. The Basel man **Bruno Manser** lived for years among the Penan on Borneo and fought for their rainforest until he vanished without trace in 2000. Anyone who looks out for labels for sustainable timber and palm oil when shopping can help.

begriffe.erklaerung: Evergreen forest with a great deal of precipitation.
A dense layer of treetops high above the ground.
A plant that grows on other plants without harming them.
Cutting down forest so that the land can be used in another way.
Native inhabitants who have lived in an area for a very long time.

gewusst: The soil in tropical rainforest is usually poor in nutrients; the nutrients are mostly held in the plants themselves.
In the dense rainforest, raindrops sometimes take several minutes to reach the ground.
The Amazon carries more water than any other river on Earth.

teile.einleitung: The **quince** is a golden-yellow fruit that looks like an apple or a pear. Raw, it is hard and tart, but cooked it becomes soft and delicate. In Switzerland it is often made into jelly and quince sweets called “Quittenpästli”.
wichtigste: Ripe quinces are **golden yellow**.
Raw quinces are very hard, so they are mostly eaten cooked.
Their skin is covered in a fine **down**.
Ripe quinces have a strong scent.
There are **apple quinces** and **pear quinces**.
Quinces are ripe in autumn.

abschnitte.text: Ripe quinces glow **golden yellow**, while unripe ones are still green. Some are round like an apple, others long like a pear. They are then called **apple quinces** and **pear quinces**. The skin is covered in a soft **down**. It is rubbed off with a cloth before cooking.

Raw quinces are **hard** and tart. That is why they are almost never eaten raw. Only when cooked do they become soft and delicate. Ripe quinces have a **strong scent**. Just a few quinces can fill a whole room with their fragrance.

Quinces contain a lot of **pectin**. That is why their juice sets nicely when boiled, making **jelly**. In Switzerland **Quittenpästli** are popular. To make them, quince purée is boiled down with sugar until thick. It is then cut into cubes, which are rolled in sugar.

Quinces ripen late in the year, usually in **October**. They are picked before the first **frost**. In spring the quince tree blossoms with large, pale pink flowers. It is related to the apple and the pear.

gewusst: The word marmalade comes from the Portuguese word for quince, “marmelo”.
The quince tree originally comes from western Asia, from around the Caucasus.

teile.einleitung: Reindeer lichen looks like a small, grey-white bush and is often called “reindeer moss”. But it is not a moss. It is a lichen, and in the far north it is the most important winter food for reindeer.
wichtigste: Reindeer lichen belongs to the lichens, not to the mosses.
True reindeer lichen is shrub-shaped and heavily branched.
It is grey-white to silvery.
It grows only a few millimetres a year.
A grazed carpet of lichen takes several decades to recover.
It belongs to the genus Cladonia.

abschnitte.text: A **lichen** is a partnership between a **fungus** and an **alga** or a cyanobacterium. The fungus forms the framework and gives protection, while the alga makes food using sunlight. Together they can live in places where neither could survive alone. **True reindeer lichen** belongs to the genus **Cladonia**. Although it is called “reindeer moss”, it is not related to mosses.

True reindeer lichen is **shrub-shaped** and **heavily branched**, like a tiny little tree. Its colour is **grey-white to silvery**. It has no roots and takes water and nutrients from rain, fog and air. In dry weather it becomes hard and brittle, and in damp weather it turns soft again. It grows very slowly, only **a few millimetres a year**. It is found in the tundra, in northern forests and also in the Alps and in moors.

In winter, **reindeer** scrape the snow away with their hooves and eat the lichen underneath. Because the lichen grows so slowly, a heavily grazed carpet takes **several decades** to recover. That is why reindeer herds move on and only return to the same place after years.

Lichens take substances straight from the air and store them for a long time. After the **Chernobyl reactor accident in 1986**, radioactive **caesium** spread as far as Scandinavia. The reindeer lichens stored it, the reindeer ate them, and so the **reindeer meat in Lapland** was contaminated. Because lichens react so sensitively to air pollutants, they are also used as indicators of air quality.

gewusst: In model-making, dried and dyed reindeer lichens are used as bushes and little trees in model landscapes.
Reindeer lichens can dry out completely and simply carry on living after the next rain.

teile.einleitung: A reed bed is the belt of tall plants such as common reed and bulrush at the edge of lakes, ponds and slow rivers. It is a habitat for many animals and protects the shore.
wichtigste: On Swiss lakes, reed beds are usually formed by the common reed.
Common reed can grow up to about 4 metres tall.
It spreads mainly by underground rootstocks.
The bulrush has brown, club-shaped flower spikes.
Reed beds slow waves and hold the ground in place.
They take up nutrients and filter the water.
In spring and summer many birds breed there, such as the reed warbler.

abschnitte.text: The most important plant in the reed beds on Swiss lakes is the **common reed**. It is a grass and can grow **up to about 4 metres** tall. Alongside it often grow the **bulrush** with its brown, **club-shaped** flower spikes and the lakeshore bulrush. These plants stand with their feet in the water or in the wet shore soil. Together they form a dense green belt.

Common reed does produce seeds, but it spreads mainly in another way. In the ground grow long **rootstocks**, also called **rhizomes**. New stalks keep shooting up from them. In this way a single plant can cover a large area over time. The rootstocks store nutrients so that the reed can quickly sprout again in spring.

abschnitte.titel: Protection for the shore and the water
abschnitte.text: The reed bed is like a natural defensive wall. The many stalks **slow the waves**, and the roots **hold the soil in place**. In this way the shore is worn away less. In addition, the **reed bed takes up nutrients** and **filters the water**. Suspended particles settle between the stalks. That is why reed is also used in constructed wetlands for treating wastewater.

Many animals live in the reeds: insects, fish, frogs and above all **birds**. The **reed warbler** is even named after its habitat. It builds its nest between the reed stalks. Great crested grebes and coots also breed in the reed bed. Because so many birds breed there in spring and summer, **entering reed areas** is then often **forbidden**. Disturbance could drive the birds away from their nests.

gewusst: In Switzerland, shore vegetation such as the reed bed is protected by the Federal Act on the Protection of Nature and Cultural Heritage.
In the past, houses in some parts of Europe had roofs thatched with reed.

teile.einleitung: Palms are among the best-known plants of the warm countries. They supply dates, coconuts and palm oil. You can also see them in Switzerland, mainly in Ticino.
wichtigste: Most palms have a trunk without branches and a tuft of large leaves at the top.
Palms grow mainly in the tropics and subtropics.
The date palm grows in the oases of the desert.
Palm oil is obtained from the fruits of the oil palm.
Rattan comes from climbing palms in Asia.
The Quindío wax palm can grow about 60 metres tall.

abschnitte.text: Most palms have a slender trunk **without branches**. At the very top sits a tuft of large leaves. These are either fan-shaped or feathered like a feather. Botanically, palms are not true trees like oak or beech. Their trunk does not grow thicker every year and so has **no annual rings**.

Worldwide there are about 2,600 species of palm. Most grow in the **tropics** and **subtropics**, where it is warm all year round. Only a few species can stand frost. The tallest palm is the **Quindío wax palm** in the Andes. It can grow about 60 metres tall and is the national tree of Colombia.

Palms are very important for many people. The **date palm** grows in oases and supplies sweet dates. The **coconut palm** grows on tropical coasts and bears coconuts. From the fruits of the **oil palm**, **palm oil** is pressed, which is in many foods and soaps. For new oil palm plantations, large areas of rainforest were cleared in South-East Asia, which is why there is much debate about palm oil.

Not all palms stand upright. The **climbing palms** from Asia grow up other trees with long, thin stems. They hold on with hooks. Their flexible stems are called **rattan**. From it people weave chairs, baskets and other furniture.

In **Ticino** the climate is mild, and many gardens have palms. Especially common is the **windmill palm** from Asia. It can also stand some frost. In Ticino it even spreads wild in the woods and pushes out native plants there. Experts therefore take a critical view.

gewusst: The coco de mer has the largest seed of all plants. It can weigh over 15 kilograms.
Palms belong to the monocotyledons, like grasses and lilies.

teile.einleitung: The Parc Ela is a regional nature park in the canton of the Grisons. It is the largest of its kind in Switzerland. Here high mountains, old passes, three languages and a famous railway line meet.
wichtigste: The Parc Ela lies in the Grisons around the Albula valley and the Surses.
It is named after the mountain Piz Ela.
At about 550 square kilometres it is the largest regional nature park in Switzerland.
In the park people speak Romansh, German and, in Bivio, also Italian.
The Landwasser Viaduct of the Rhaetian Railway stands near Filisur.
The Albula Pass and the Julier Pass lie in the park.

abschnitte.text: The **Parc Ela** lies in the canton of the **Grisons**, in the region around the **Albula valley** and the **Surses**. It is named after the **Piz Ela**, a striking peak in the Albula Alps. At about **550 square kilometres** it is the largest regional nature park in Switzerland by area. In a regional nature park people live. Nature, landscape and villages are meant to be protected and at the same time used sustainably.

The Parc Ela is a **trilingual** park. In many villages **Romansh** is spoken, in others **German**. In **Bivio** on the Julier Pass, **Italian** is also spoken. You hardly find this variety in so small a space anywhere else in Switzerland.

Through the park runs the **Albula line** of the **Rhaetian Railway**. It winds up the narrow valley with spiral tunnels and bridges. Its most famous structure is the **Landwasser Viaduct** near **Filisur**. Together with the Bernina line, the Albula line has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** since **2008**.

In the area of the park lie two important Alpine passes. The **Albula Pass** links the Albula valley with the Engadine. The **Julier Pass** leads from the Surses into the Upper Engadine. The Romans already used the route over the Julier. Today in summer many cars, motorbikes and bikes travel over the passes.

In winter the Albula Pass is closed to cars. Then the pass road between **Preda** and **Bergün** becomes a popular **toboggan run**. The railway then takes people back up. In summer, hiking trails, mountain lakes and alps with many animals and flowers attract visitors.

gewusst: The Landwasser Viaduct is about 65 metres high and leads straight into a tunnel in a vertical rock wall.
The Piz Ela is over 3,300 metres high.

teile.einleitung: Plastids are small organelles in plant cells. The best known are the green chloroplasts, in which photosynthesis takes place. But there are other forms with other jobs.
wichtigste: New plastids arise by **division** of existing plastids.
In tissues that form new cells lie small precursors, the **proplastids**.
The plastids of land plants are surrounded by **two membranes**.
The genetic information of a plastid is called the **plastome**.
Plastids have their own **70S ribosomes**, like bacteria.
In the dark **etioplasts** form, in the light **chloroplasts**.

abschnitte.text: Plastids cannot be made from scratch. They multiply by **division** and are shared out to the daughter cells when a cell divides. Their envelope consists of two membranes. They have their own DNA, the **plastome**, and their own **70S ribosomes** like bacteria. In the cytoplasm of the plant cell, by contrast, there are 80S ribosomes. All this suggests that plastids descend from **cyanobacteria** that once lived freely.

In the tissues that form new cells, the meristems, lie small, little-structured **proplastids**. Depending on the tissue and the light, they develop into different types. If seedlings grow in the dark, **etioplasts** form with a crystalline prolamellar body. When lit, these quickly become chloroplasts.

**Chloroplasts** have an inner membrane system, the **thylakoids**. In their membranes lie the chlorophyll and the light reactions of photosynthesis. The fluid around the thylakoids is called the **stroma**. In it lie small lipid droplets, the **plastoglobuli**. In ageing chloroplasts they grow larger.

**Chromoplasts** contain yellow, orange or red pigments, the carotenoids. They colour, for example, carrots, petals and ripe fruit. Their plastoglobuli can store these pigments. **Leucoplasts** are colourless. Some of them store starch, for example in the potato tuber.

gewusst: When a tomato ripens, its green chloroplasts turn into red chromoplasts.
The genome of the mitochondria is called the chondriome, by comparison with the plastome.

teile.einleitung: A whole plant in miniature is hidden inside a tiny seed. When it gets water and warmth, it wakes up and begins to germinate. This is how a small acorn can become a huge oak.
wichtigste: A seed contains a plant embryo, nutritive tissue and a protective coat.
A plant grows from a seed when it gets water and warmth.
When a seed starts to grow, this is called germination.
Putting seeds in the soil is called sowing.
Seeds are spread by wind, water or animals.
Squirrels hide nuts and seeds as a winter store and so help to spread them.
Some seeds stay able to germinate for many years.

abschnitte.text: On the outside, the hard **seed coat** protects against drying out and injury. Inside lies the **embryo**, a tiny plant with a root, a shoot and seed leaves. Beside it there is a food store of starch, protein or oil. In beans this store is in the thick seed leaves.

For a seed to germinate, it needs **water**, warmth and oxygen. First it swells and bursts the seed coat. Then the root grows downwards and the shoot grows upwards towards the light. Until the first green leaves carry out photosynthesis, the **seedling** lives off its store.

Plants cannot walk, so they send their seeds on journeys. The dandelion has little parachutes, and maple seeds spin through the air like propellers. The **coconut** floats across the sea to new islands. The touch-me-not flings its seeds out of exploding capsules.

Many animals eat fruits and pass the seeds out again in a different place. Burrs cling with tiny hooks to the fur of passing animals. **Squirrels** and jays hide nuts and acorns in autumn as a winter store. What they forget can germinate in spring and grow into a new tree.

Anyone who puts seeds in the soil is **sowing**. Farmers sow cereals, maize or oilseed rape in their fields, and gardeners sow vegetables and flowers. Good **seed** is the basis of our food. The Swiss foundation ProSpecieRara has been preserving old vegetable and cereal varieties since 1982 so that they are not lost.

On the Norwegian island group of Spitsbergen lies the **Svalbard Global Seed Vault**, a vault in the permafrost. Since 2008, seed samples from almost every country in the world have been stored there as a back-up copy for emergencies. The seeds of conifers lie openly on the scales of cones, and these plants are called gymnosperms. In flowering plants, by contrast, the seeds are enclosed in a fruit.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of a plant from which a new plant can grow.
The beginning of a seed’s growth.
The tiny plant inside the seed.
Seeds that are meant for sowing.
A young plant shortly after germination.

gewusst: From a date stone about 2,000 years old found in Israel, a new date palm grew in 2005.
The coco de mer produces the heaviest seeds in the plant kingdom, weighing more than ten kilograms.
Orchid seeds are so tiny that they are blown away like dust by the wind.

teile.einleitung: **Poikilohydry** means that a living thing can hardly control its water content. It dries out together with its surroundings and soaks itself full again when it is damp. Many mosses and lichens live this way and so even survive complete drought.
wichtigste: In poikilohydric organisms the water content adapts to the surroundings.
Most vascular plants, by contrast, are **homoiohydric**.
Mosses and lichens are typical examples of poikilohydry.
When dried out they fall into a resting state, **anhydrobiosis**.
Sugars such as trehalose protect the cells as they dry out.
Photosynthesis is only possible when they are moist, so many lichens grow slowly.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from Greek and means roughly “of changing moisture”. **Poikilohydric** organisms have hardly any means of holding on to water. If the air is dry, they dry out. If it becomes damp, they quickly take up water again. They include above all **mosses**, **lichens** and some algae.

Most **vascular plants** keep their water content largely constant. This is called **homoiohydry**. They have a waxy protective layer, the **cuticle**, adjustable **stomata** and large water stores in the cells. Moss leaflets, by contrast, are mostly only one cell layer thick. Without a thick cuticle and adjustable stomata, they lose water quickly to the air.

Dried-out mosses fall into a state with an almost resting metabolism. This is called **anhydrobiosis**. The tiny **tardigrades** can survive in this way too. So that the cells do not break, many of these living things form **sugars** such as sucrose or trehalose. These replace the water on membranes and proteins and form a glass-like mass that stabilises everything.

Thanks to this ability, lichens and mosses can settle **bare rock** that at times dries out completely. Most vascular plants would wither there. After being moistened, many mosses take up photosynthesis again after **minutes to a few hours**. However, they can only grow when moist. That is why many lichens grow only very slowly.

Some vascular plants are poikilohydric too. A well-known example is **Selaginella lepidophylla**, a spikemoss from dry regions of America. As it dries out, it rolls up into a brown ball. If you put it in water, it unfolds within hours and turns green again. That is why it is also called the **false rose of Jericho**.

gewusst: The false rose of Jericho is sometimes sold as a curiosity, because it opens in water as if by magic.
Dried-out tardigrades can survive for a very long time and wake up again when there is water.

teile.einleitung: Permaculture is a way of planning gardens and farming so that they work like a natural ecosystem. Natural cycles are imitated and waste is avoided. The idea comes from Australia and is now spread worldwide.
wichtigste: “Permaculture” comes from the English “permanent agriculture”.
Bill Mollison and David Holmgren developed the idea in the 1970s in Australia.
The garden is divided into zones, depending on how often an area is looked after.
Mulch protects the soil from drying out and feeds soil organisms.
A herb spiral offers dry and damp spots in a small space.
A forest garden is laid out like a forest in several storeys.

abschnitte.text: The term **permaculture** is made up of the English words **permanent** and **agriculture**, that is, lasting farming. The two Australians **Bill Mollison** and **David Holmgren** developed the idea in the 1970s. In 1978 they published a first book on it. Since then permaculture has spread all over the world, and in Switzerland too there are many permaculture gardens.

At the centre is the idea of **imitating natural cycles** and **avoiding waste**. The model is ecosystems such as the forest, where nothing is lost. Plant remains become **compost** or **mulch**. Different plants grow mixed side by side and help one another. Rainwater is collected and used.

A permaculture garden is divided into **zones**. What matters is how often you have to visit and look after an area. The **herb bed**, which you need every day, lies near the house. Fruit trees stand further away. At the very edge lies a piece of **wilderness** that you hardly look after and leave to the animals. In this way you save paths and work.

A **herb spiral** is a spiral-shaped mound of stones and earth. At the top it is sunny and dry, good for thyme or rosemary. At the bottom it is damp and cool, good for mint or parsley. You cover the soil with **mulch** of leaves, straw or grass cuttings. It keeps the moisture in the soil and, as it rots, serves as food for **soil organisms**.

A **forest garden** is laid out like a forest in several **storeys**. At the top grow fruit trees, below them berry bushes, then herbs and ground cover. After it is laid out, it needs little care. The Austrian mountain farmer **Sepp Holzer** became well known. In the **Lungau** he farmed a farm at high altitude following permaculture ideas and laid out ponds and terraces.

gewusst: One principle of permaculture is: every element in the garden should fulfil several tasks. A pond, for example, supplies water, habitat for animals and cooler air.
You can also garden on a balcony following permaculture ideas.

teile.einleitung: The Spatial Planning Act, **RPG** for short, sets out in Switzerland where building is allowed and where it is not. It is meant to protect scarce land and make sure that settlements, farming and nature all have room side by side.
wichtigste: The Spatial Planning Act dates from 1979.
Its most important principle is the separation of building land from non-building land.
The cantonal structure plan must be approved by the Federal Council.
The land-use plan is binding on landowners.
In 2013 voters accepted the first revision (RPG 1).
Building zones may cover no more than the needs of 15 years.
When land is newly rezoned for building, there is a value-gain levy of at least 20 per cent.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland is small and mountainous, and good land is scarce. The **Spatial Planning Act of 1979** is meant to make sure that it is used sparingly. Its most important principle is the **separation of building land from non-building land**. Houses, roads and factories should stand in the building zones, while farmland and nature outside them should stay free. According to the Federal Constitution, the Confederation sets the principles, and the actual planning is done by the **cantons and municipalities**.

Each canton draws up a **structure plan**. It shows how the canton is to develop and applies to the authorities. The **Federal Council** must approve it. The municipalities issue the **land-use plan**, often called the zoning plan. For every plot it sets out whether homes, businesses or farming belong there. The land-use plan is **binding on landowners**.

Because more and more land was being built on, voters accepted a revision in **2013**, known as **RPG 1**. Since then, building zones may cover no more than the expected needs of **15 years**. Building zones that are too large have to be made smaller. When land is newly rezoned for building, its value rises sharply. The owner has to hand over a **value-gain levy** of at least **20 per cent** of this. In addition, more building is to be done inwards, that is, more densely within existing settlements.

With the **Sectoral Plan for Crop Rotation Areas**, the Confederation protects the **best farmland**, so that Switzerland can feed itself even in times of crisis. In **2012** voters accepted the **second homes initiative**. Since then, the share of second homes in a municipality may be no more than **20 per cent**. This mainly affects holiday resorts in the mountains.

On **10 February 2019** the people voted on the **urban sprawl initiative**. It wanted to freeze building zones overall. Supporters wanted to protect the landscape in this way, while opponents found the rule too rigid. Voters **rejected it**. After that, Parliament worked on a second stage of the revision, which mainly concerns **building outside the building zones**.

gewusst: A plot of land can rise greatly in value simply because it is rezoned from farmland to a building zone.
Spatial planning in Switzerland is divided between three levels: the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities.

teile.einleitung: In **primary succession**, plants and animals settle step by step a place where there was no soil at all before. Examples are fresh lava or the ground that a melting glacier releases. In the Alps you can observe this in glacier forelands such as at the Morteratsch Glacier.
wichtigste: Primary succession begins on **bare ground** with no soil formation.
Secondary succession, by contrast, begins on existing soil after a disturbance.
Glacier forelands are a classic example in the Alps.
Pioneers such as mountain avens, green alder and larch come first.
With age the pH of the topsoil falls on limestone moraine.
The island of Surtsey off Iceland has been studied since 1963.

abschnitte.text: In **primary succession** there is no soil at all at the start. This is the case, for example, on fresh **moraines** or cooled **lava**. In **secondary succession**, by contrast, soil is already there, for example after a forest fire or storm. In the Alps the **glacier foreland** is a classic example. When glaciers retreat, bare moraine material is left behind.

On the bare ground **pioneer plants** come first. On limestone scree **mountain avens** (Dryas octopetala) forms carpets with white flowers. The **green alder** is especially competitive, because it lives together with **Frankia bacteria** in root nodules. These fix nitrogen from the air, which is scarce in bare ground. Among trees, the light-loving **larch** is a typical pioneer; fir and beech follow only later.

With time soil slowly forms from scree. Plants die and form humus. On lime-rich moraine, rainwater dissolves the lime and washes it out of the topsoil. In decomposition acids also form. That is why the **pH falls**, and older areas are often more acidic than young ones.

A succession takes centuries, which no one can observe for that long. Researchers therefore use the **chronosequence**. In a glacier foreland the soil is the older, the further it lies from the end of the glacier. If you compare areas next to one another, you see the development as in a film. On the **Morteratsch Glacier Trail** in the Upper Engadine, signs show where the ice used to lie.

A famous object of research is **Surtsey**, a volcanic island off Iceland. It formed in **1963** in an eruption in the sea. Since then it has been precisely documented how plants and animals settle the island. So that the observations are not disturbed, people have hardly any access. The island shows how life begins on completely new land.

gewusst: Mountain avens gave its name to a cold period at the end of the last ice age: the Younger Dryas.
In a glacier foreland you can walk through decades of plant development in a few minutes on foot.

teile.einleitung: Plants need light to make food. But what happens at night or in a dark cellar? The plant goes on living, breathes and even changes its growth.
wichtigste: In the dark no photosynthesis takes place, but cell respiration goes on.
In doing so the plant gives off carbon dioxide.
Seedlings grow long, thin and pale in the dark, which is called etiolation.
Without light hardly any chlorophyll forms, so potato sprouts in the cellar are whitish.
Long darkness makes plants die, because they use up their stores.
Fungi need no light, because they do not carry out photosynthesis.

abschnitte.titel: What happens in the leaf at night
abschnitte.text: For **photosynthesis** a plant needs **light** as a source of energy. In the first step, the **light reaction**, light energy is captured. Without light it comes to a standstill, and soon the building of sugar stops too. But **cell respiration** goes on day and night. In doing so the plant uses up sugar and oxygen and gives off **carbon dioxide**.

Some people wonder whether house plants do harm in the bedroom at night. Plants do breathe, but only weakly. A sleeping person gives off **much more** carbon dioxide in breathing than a few house plants in the same room. So they are harmless in the bedroom.

Seedlings that grow in the dark look quite different. They become **long**, **thin** and **pale**. This is called **etiolation**. The plant puts its energy into fast growth in length, to reach the light as quickly as possible. For the green pigment **chlorophyll**, most plants need light. That is why the sprouts of **potatoes** in a dark cellar are whitish. If they get light, they turn green after a while.

In the light, leaves store part of the sugar as **starch**. With **iodine solution** you can detect starch, which then turns blue-black. Before such an experiment you usually put the plant **in the dark** for one or two days. In this time it breaks down the starch in the leaves and transports it away. In this way the test later shows only the starch that was newly made in the light during the experiment.

If a plant stands for weeks in a dark cupboard, it goes on breathing and uses up its **stored nutrients**. It cannot make new ones without light, so it finally dies. **Fungi**, on the other hand, have no chlorophyll and do not carry out photosynthesis. They break down organic matter such as compost and straw. That is why **button mushrooms** can grow in dark halls.

gewusst: Chicory is grown in the dark on purpose. In this way it stays pale and tastes less bitter.
White asparagus is also pale, because it grows under a mound of earth without light.

teile.einleitung: Rye is a cereal from which dark, strongly flavoured bread is baked. It is especially hardy and grows even where it is too cold for wheat or the soil is too poor.
wichtigste: Dark bread is made from rye.
Valais rye bread is a well-known Swiss bread.
Rye withstands cold especially well.
Its stalks are longer than those of wheat.
A ripe rye field is yellow-brown.
Ergot is a poisonous fungus that forms dark grains in ears of rye.
Rye bread tastes stronger and a little sour.

abschnitte.text: Like wheat, barley and oats, **rye** is a **cereal**. It is very **hardy** and withstands **cold** especially well. It still grows even on poor, sandy soils where wheat hardly thrives. That is why it used to be grown mainly in the mountains and in northern Europe. The **stalks** of rye are **longer** than those of wheat. A field of ripe rye is **yellow-brown**.

**Dark bread** is baked from rye flour. For the dough to rise well, **sourdough** is usually needed. Rye bread therefore tastes **stronger and a little sour** compared with white bread. It stays fresh for a long time and contains a lot of fibre. The flat, crunchy **crispbread** is also often made from rye. It originally comes from Scandinavia.

A well-known Swiss rye bread is **Valais rye bread**. In the Valais, rye used to be grown high up in the mountains because it tolerates the cold well. The bread is dark and round and has a cracked crust. It carries the protected designation of origin **AOP**. This means that it must be made in the Valais from Valais rye according to fixed rules.

A fungus called **ergot** can grow on rye. Instead of a grain, a **dark**, elongated body then forms in the ear. Ergot is **poisonous**. In the Middle Ages, many people fell ill because they ate bread made from contaminated flour. Today the grain is cleaned and checked, so that this danger hardly exists any more.

gewusst: Rye can be sown in autumn even in harsh locations and survive the winter in the field.
Rye straw is especially long and was often used in the past for thatching roofs.

teile.einleitung: Sand is made up of many small grains of rock. You can find it on the beach, in rivers, in the desert and in the sandpit at the playground.
wichtigste: Sand is made up of many small grains of rock.
It forms when rock slowly crumbles.
Sand feels rough and gritty.
Water drains away quickly through sand.
Sandy soil holds water badly and dries out quickly in summer.
Damp sand is best for building sandcastles.
If sand is heated very strongly, glass is formed.

abschnitte.text: Sand is made up of **many small grains of rock**. Each grain is smaller than two millimetres but coarser than dust. Most of the grains consist of the hard mineral **quartz**. Between your fingers, sand feels **rough and gritty**. Under a magnifying glass you can see that the grains have different colours and shapes.

Sand forms when **rock slowly crumbles**. This takes a very long time. Water, frost, wind and heat attack the rocks. Rivers carry the little stones along and rub them against each other until they become smaller and rounder. In Switzerland, glaciers also broke up a great deal of rock. Sand and gravel are extracted from rivers and old glacial deposits, for example for concrete.

If you pour water on sand, it **drains away quickly**. There are many gaps between the grains through which the water flows downwards. That is why **sandy soil dries out quickly** in summer: it holds water badly. This is difficult for some plants, while others such as pines or beach grasses cope well with it.

The best time to build a sandcastle is **when the sand is damp**. The water forms tiny bridges between the grains that hold them together. Dry sand, by contrast, trickles apart. But too much water is not good either: then the sand turns to mud and the castle collapses. The right amount of water is the secret.

**Glass** is made from sand. For this, quartz sand is **heated very strongly** together with other substances, to well over a thousand degrees Celsius. The sand melts, and glass forms as it cools. In an **hourglass**, **fine sand** trickles through a narrow opening from top to bottom. Because this always takes the same length of time, you can use it to measure time.

gewusst: Windows, bottles and mobile phone screens are also made of glass that was originally made from sand.
Some sandy beaches are black because their sand came from volcanic rock.

teile.einleitung: The Parc du Doubs is a regional nature park in the Jura. It lies on the river Doubs, which here forms the border with France. Deep gorges, old little towns and Freiberger horses shape the landscape.
wichtigste: Over a long stretch in the park, the Doubs forms the border with France.
The park spreads over the cantons of Jura, Neuchâtel and Bern.
The municipalities in the park are French-speaking.
The medieval little town of Saint-Ursanne lies directly on the Doubs.
The Freiberger is the only native horse breed of Switzerland.
The Rhone streber now lives in Switzerland only in the Doubs.

abschnitte.text: The **Doubs** rises in France and then flows for many kilometres exactly on the **national border** between Switzerland and France. It has dug itself a deep, wooded valley into the Jura. Then it makes a big loop through Switzerland and returns to France. There it finally flows into the **Saône**, which flows into the Rhône and so into the Mediterranean.

The **Parc du Doubs** covers municipalities in the cantons of **Jura**, **Neuchâtel** and **Bern**. It lies in French-speaking Switzerland, so **French** is spoken here. As in every regional nature park, people live here who farm, do crafts and run tourism. The park is meant to protect nature and culture and strengthen the region.

abschnitte.titel: Saint-Ursanne and the Saut du Doubs
abschnitte.text: The little town of **Saint-Ursanne** in the canton of Jura lies directly on the river. With its old stone bridge, its town gates and its collegiate church, it is a popular destination for outings. Further west, at **Les Brenets**, the Doubs dams up into the Lac des Brenets. At its end it plunges about **27 metres** as the **Saut du Doubs**.

The park also includes parts of the **Freiberge**, in French Franches-Montagnes. Typical are pastures with single large firs, which are called wooded pastures (“Wytweiden”). From here comes the **Freiberger**, the only native **horse breed of Switzerland**. It is strong, calm and is used for riding and as a draught horse.

In the Doubs lives a very special fish: the **Rhone streber**, in French “Roi du Doubs”, that is, King of the Doubs. In Switzerland it now occurs only here. It is **threatened with extinction** and strictly protected. It needs clean, flowing water with a gravelly bed.

gewusst: The Doubs first flows north-east and later south-west again, so its source and mouth are not far apart at all.
On the Lac des Brenets you can go by boat almost as far as the waterfall.

teile.einleitung: In nature, predators eat other animals, their prey. The numbers of predators and prey are closely linked and often rise and fall in a regular pattern.
wichtigste: When there are many prey animals, the number of predators also rises a little later.
Predators follow with a delay because they need time to reproduce.
The lynx and the snowshoe hare in Canada are a well-known example.
Lotka and Volterra described such relationships with mathematical equations.
Predators usually do not wipe out their prey, because when prey is scarce their own numbers fall too.
In Switzerland the lynx hunts mainly roe deer and chamois.
Prey animals protect themselves with camouflage or mimicry.

abschnitte.text: When there are very many **prey animals**, the **predators** find plenty of food. They can raise more young, and their numbers also **rise a little later**. Then many predators eat many prey animals, and the prey becomes scarcer. Now the predators find less food, and their numbers fall too. After that the prey can recover. This creates a cycle in which the predators follow the prey **with a delay**.

abschnitte.titel: The lynx and the snowshoe hare
abschnitte.text: A well-known example comes from **Canada**. Old records of traded furs showed there that the numbers of **lynx and snowshoe hares** swing widely about every ten years. Many hares were followed by many lynx. Today we know that the hares’ own food also plays an important part. In nature, several causes always work together.

In the 1920s the researchers **Lotka and Volterra**, working independently, described predator-prey relationships with **mathematical equations**. Their model shows how the numbers of predators and prey rise and fall regularly. It also explains why predators normally **do not wipe out** their prey: when prey becomes scarce, the number of predators falls before the last prey animals have disappeared.

The **lynx** was wiped out in Switzerland and was reintroduced from 1971. Here it hunts mainly **roe deer and chamois**. It often catches **sick and weak animals**, because they are easier to catch. This has an advantage for the prey population: it stays **healthier**. Predators also prevent prey animals from multiplying too much and eating too much of the food supply.

Prey animals have many tricks. **Roe deer fawns** lie still in the long grass during the first weeks of life and are **well camouflaged** thanks to their spotted coats. Other animals fool their enemies. The harmless **hoverfly**, with its yellow and black stripes, looks like a wasp that can sting. This copying is called **mimicry**. Many birds therefore leave such flies alone.

gewusst: Plants and plant-eaters can also show similar ups and downs to predators and prey.
The data about the lynx and the snowshoe hare come from many decades of the fur trade.

teile.einleitung: Penicillin was the first antibiotic to be used on a large scale. It is made by a mould and helps against bacteria. Its discovery has saved millions of lives.
wichtigste: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928.
The name comes from the mould Penicillium, Latin penicillus means brush.
Penicillin works against bacteria, not against viruses.
It disturbs the building of the bacterial cell wall.
In the Second World War it was made in large amounts for the first time.
Fleming, Florey and Chain received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1945.

abschnitte.text: The Scottish bacteriologist **Alexander Fleming** was growing bacteria on small dishes in London in 1928. On one dish a **mould** had grown. Fleming noticed that around the fungus no bacteria lived any more. The fungus was evidently giving off a substance that killed them. Fleming called it **penicillin**.

The fungus belongs to the genus **Penicillium**. The Latin word **penicillus** means **brush**. Under the microscope, the parts of the fungus that form spores look like small brushes. The name of the drug is derived from the name of the fungus.

Fleming could not yet obtain penicillin in larger amounts. Around 1940, **Howard Florey** and **Ernst Chain** in Oxford managed to purify the active substance and to try it out on people. During the **Second World War**, from about 1943, penicillin was made in large amounts in the USA and in Britain. It saved the lives of many wounded soldiers. In 1945 Fleming, Florey and Chain together received the **Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine**.

Penicillin belongs to the **antibiotics**. These are substances that kill bacteria or hold back their growth. Penicillin disturbs the building of the **cell wall** in growing bacteria. Without a stable wall, the bacteria burst. Against **viruses**, for example in flu or a cold, penicillin does not work, because viruses have no such cell wall.

If antibiotics are taken too often or wrongly, insensitive bacteria can prevail. These are then said to be **resistant**: the drug no longer works against them. That is why in Switzerland antibiotics are available only on **prescription**. You should take them for exactly as long as the doctor says. The Confederation has its own **strategy against antibiotic resistance**, which covers humans, animals and farming.

gewusst: Some people are allergic to penicillin and then get a different antibiotic.
Today penicillin is no longer obtained from Fleming’s original fungus but from especially productive strains of fungus.

teile.einleitung: A phenological observation network collects data in many places about when plants put out leaves, flower or lose their leaves. In Switzerland, MeteoSwiss runs such a network. Most of the observations come from volunteers.
wichtigste: MeteoSwiss built up the nationwide network in **1951**.
Most observations are supplied by **volunteers**.
Every year the same plants are observed at the same site.
The spring phases now occur earlier on average.
Leaf-out is determined mainly by the **temperature** of the weeks before.
Phenological data help with information about **pollen**.

abschnitte.text: The time of flowering also depends on a plant’s position, soil and genes. That is why, if possible, **the same plants at the same site** are observed every year. If these things stay the same, the differences between years mainly reflect weather and climate. In this way the data become comparable over many years.

The MeteoSwiss network includes stations all over Switzerland, from the lowlands to the mountains. Many **volunteers** report over years when certain plants at their site flower or put out leaves. Their long commitment makes the data series valuable. A particularly old series is the official **horse chestnut** in Geneva, whose first leaf has been noted for over 200 years.
