Many trees put out leaves when enough **warmth** has built up in spring. A warm March therefore moves leaf-out forward. With rising temperatures, leaf-out and flowering now begin on average earlier than a few decades ago. This is a visible sign of **climate change**.

abschnitte.titel: When the timing is no longer right
abschnitte.text: Species react with different strength to warming. If, for example, caterpillars hatch earlier while tits go on breeding at the usual time, the young birds later lack food. This is called **phenological mismatch**. The data are also useful for people: the start of flowering of plants such as **birch** or hazel shows when the pollen season starts. People with pollen allergies can then prepare in good time.

gewusst: Observation needs no expensive equipment, but above all careful looking and staying power.
Some phenological series in Switzerland go back much further than measurements with modern weather stations.

teile.einleitung: The Rothenthurm Initiative was a federal popular initiative to protect moors. It grew out of resistance to an army training ground in the raised bog of Rothenthurm in the canton of Schwyz.
wichtigste: The initiative was directed against a planned army training ground.
The raised bog of Rothenthurm lies in the canton of Schwyz.
The people and the cantons accepted the initiative in December 1987.
Since then the protection of moors and moorland has been in the Federal Constitution.
It was unusual in applying retroactively to 1983.
Peat extraction in protected moors has been forbidden since then.

abschnitte.titel: The dispute over the training ground
abschnitte.text: Near Rothenthurm in the **canton of Schwyz** there is a large area of moorland with a valuable **raised bog**. In the 1970s and 1980s the Confederation planned an **army training ground** there, that is, an exercise area for soldiers. Many people from the region and nature conservation organisations resisted. They wanted to keep the moor. This resistance grew into a **popular initiative**.

With a **popular initiative**, eligible voters can demand a change to the Federal Constitution. This requires enough signatures. For a popular initiative to be accepted, the **people and the cantons** must agree. That means: the majority of those voting and the majority of the cantons. The Rothenthurm Initiative was accepted on **6 December 1987**.

Since then the **protection of moors and moorland** has been in the Federal Constitution. Today it is found in the **article on the protection of nature and cultural heritage**. Especially beautiful moors of national importance may not be altered. It was unusual that the provision applied **retroactively**: installations that had been built in such moors after 1 June **1983** had to be removed again.

After the vote, the Confederation drew up **inventories**, that is, registers of the most important raised bogs, fens and moorland areas. **Peat extraction** in protected moors has been **forbidden** since then. Peat used to be dug as fuel and for garden soil. Moors are important because rare plants and animals live there and because they store a lot of water and carbon.

gewusst: The Rothenthurm Initiative is one of the few popular initiatives that have been accepted in Switzerland.
Swiss moors are very old: many have been growing slowly since the end of the last ice age.

teile.einleitung: Photorespiration is a metabolic pathway in plants that takes place in the light. It arises because the enzyme Rubisco sometimes binds oxygen instead of carbon dioxide. In the process the plant loses carbon it has already fixed.
wichtigste: Photorespiration begins when **Rubisco** binds O2 instead of CO2.
This produces **2-phosphoglycolate**, which is worthless to the plant.
The recovery pathway runs in the **chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondrion**.
In the mitochondrion **CO2** is released and **serine** is made from two glycines.
In heat and drought, photorespiration is especially strong in C3 plants.
In the peroxisome, **glycolate oxidase** forms hydrogen peroxide.

abschnitte.text: In the Calvin cycle the enzyme **Rubisco** binds carbon dioxide to ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate. But Rubisco can also bind oxygen, which is the **oxygenase reaction**. This produces one 3-phosphoglycerate and one **2-phosphoglycolate**. The 2-phosphoglycolate is worthless to the Calvin cycle and even inhibits it. The plant has to recycle it at great effort.

In the **chloroplast** the 2-phosphoglycolate becomes glycolate. It travels to the **peroxisome**. There **glycolate oxidase** converts it into glyoxylate, producing hydrogen peroxide. **Catalase** breaks this down again straight away. As glycine the substance reaches the **mitochondrion** and later returns to the chloroplast by way of the peroxisome.

In the mitochondrion two glycines are converted into one **serine**. In the process CO2 and ammonia are released. So part of the carbon the plant had already fixed is lost again. The plant also uses up energy to recover everything. Serine is then built further into glycerate.

In drought, plants close their **stomata** to save water. The CO2 content in the leaf then falls and oxygen builds up. As the temperature rises, CO2 dissolves less well than O2, and Rubisco prefers CO2 less clearly. That is why photorespiration is especially strong in **C3 plants** such as wheat in the heat. **C4 plants** such as maize concentrate CO2 and so avoid a lot of photorespiration.

gewusst: Rubisco is considered the most common protein on Earth.
Researchers are trying to make crop plants more productive with a shortened photorespiration pathway.

teile.einleitung: A saw is a tool with many small teeth. It is used to cut wood, plastic or metal. There are simple hand saws and large machines with motors.
wichtigste: Saws cut with many sharp teeth.
The “Fuchsschwanz”, or hand saw, is a simple saw with a wide blade.
With the fretsaw you saw fine shapes out of thin wood.
The circular saw has a round blade that spins fast.
The chainsaw has a chain with teeth and a motor.
When sawing with power saws you need ear protection, a helmet and protective clothing.

abschnitte.text: A saw has a blade with many small, sharp **teeth**. With each stroke, every tooth tears out a little material. This creates **sawdust**. The teeth are often bent slightly alternately to the left and right. This makes the cut a little wider than the blade, so the saw does not jam.

The **“Fuchsschwanz”**, or hand saw, is a saw with a wide blade and a handle at one end. It is used to saw boards and battens. The **fretsaw** has a very thin blade in a frame. In craft lessons, children use it to saw shapes and curves out of thin wood. For metal there is the **hacksaw** with very fine teeth.

The **circular saw** has a round saw blade that a motor spins very fast. The **jigsaw** moves a short blade quickly up and down and can cut curves. The **chainsaw** has a revolving chain with teeth. Foresters use it to fell trees and cut up trunks. Such machines are very powerful and may only be operated by adults.

When sawing, the **workpiece** must be held firmly, for example in a clamp or a vice. That way it does not slip away. Power saws are very loud, so you wear **ear protection**. You also need a helmet, safety goggles, gloves and cut-resistant clothing. You always keep your hands well away from the saw blade.

gewusst: Japanese saws cut on the pull stroke and not on the push stroke, which is why their blades can be very thin.
The “Fuchsschwanz” is called that because its wide blade, which narrows towards the front, recalls the tail of a fox, “Fuchs” in German.

teile.einleitung: An aggregate fruit develops from a single flower that has many free carpels. Each carpel becomes a small fruitlet, and all together they form one fruit, as in the raspberry or the strawberry.
wichtigste: An aggregate fruit develops from a flower with many free carpels.
A single little ball of the raspberry is a small drupe.
Raspberry and blackberry are aggregate drupes.
The raspberry is hollow inside when picked, the blackberry is not.
The strawberry is an aggregate of achenes, as is the fruit of the buttercup.
The peony forms an aggregate of follicles.
The pineapple is not an aggregate fruit but a multiple fruit made from many flowers.

abschnitte.text: In the middle of a flower sit the **carpels**. In many plants they have grown together into a single ovary. In some flowers, however, **many free carpels** stand side by side. From each one a small fruitlet of its own develops. If these stay together and come away from the plant as a whole, this is called an **aggregate fruit**. Depending on the kind of fruitlets, different types are distinguished.

In the **raspberry**, each red little ball is a **small drupe** with a tiny hard stone. Together they form an **aggregate drupe**. The **blackberry** belongs here too. When picking, you can see the difference: the raspberry comes away from the core in the middle and is therefore **hollow inside**. In the blackberry the core stays in the fruit and is eaten too.

The **strawberry** is an **aggregate of achenes**. The red, juicy flesh is actually the swollen base of the flower. The real fruits are the small yellow **nutlets** on the surface. The **buttercup** also forms an aggregate of achenes: many small nutlets sit there in a round little head. The rose hip of roses is also counted here.

A **follicle** is a fruitlet that opens along **only one seam** to release its seeds. The **peony** forms several such follicles from one flower. This is called an **aggregate of follicles**. The marsh marigold, which grows in damp places in Switzerland, also has this type of fruit.

abschnitte.titel: Not to be confused with: the multiple fruit
abschnitte.text: The **pineapple** looks like a single large fruit. But it develops from **many flowers** of a whole flower cluster that grow together. Such a fruit is called a **multiple fruit**. So the difference is this: an aggregate fruit comes from a single flower, and a multiple fruit from many. The mulberry is also a multiple fruit, although it looks similar to a blackberry.

gewusst: A strawberry often carries well over a hundred small nutlets on its surface.
Raspberries and blackberries both belong to the same plant genus.

teile.einleitung: Pricking out is a gardening term. Young seedlings that are standing close together are set out one by one at wider spacing. This gives the little plants enough room to grow.
wichtigste: Pricking out means moving **seedlings** that stand close together one by one.
You prick out when the first **true leaves** appear after the seed leaves.
An important tool is the **dibber**.
The word comes from the French “piquer”, meaning to prick.
You hold the seedling by a **seed leaf**, not by the stem.
Freshly pricked-out plants stand in a bright place, but not in full sun.

abschnitte.text: If you sow seeds in a tray, many often come up close together. The little plants then take **light, water and nutrients** from one another. So you carefully take them out and set them singly in small pots or at wider spacing. Once separated, they develop more strongly. The word comes from the French verb “piquer”, which means “to prick”.

First the **seed leaves** appear. They often look different from the later leaves. Once the first **true foliage leaves** show, the little plants are strong enough to be pricked out. If you wait too long, the roots become tangled and tear more easily when you take them out.

With the **dibber** you lift the seedlings out of the soil and poke planting holes. A pencil or a chopstick will do too. You hold the seedling by a **seed leaf**. The thin stem bends easily and cannot grow back, while a seed leaf can cope better with a little injury. Then you put the seedling in the hole, press the soil down lightly and water carefully.

**Seed compost** is well suited: fine, loose and low in nutrients. Few nutrients encourage the roots to grow strongly and search. After being moved, the roots first have to take hold again. That is why you put the plants **in a bright place, but not in full sun**, or they dry out.

gewusst: With tomatoes you may set them a little deeper when pricking out, because they form new roots on the stem.
If you sow very thinly, you have to prick out less later.

teile.einleitung: In a sawmill, tree trunks are sawn into boards, beams and battens. The wood comes from the forest and is later used for building, for furniture or as fuel. Almost nothing of the trunk is lost in the process.
wichtigste: In the sawmill, tree trunks are sawn into boards, beams and battens.
Lorries bring the trunks from the forest.
First a machine removes the bark.
In the past a water wheel often drove the saw.
Fresh boards dry stacked with air between them.
Wood waste becomes pellets, chipboard or fuel.

abschnitte.titel: From the forest to the sawmill
abschnitte.text: In the forest, trees are felled and the trunks cut into pieces. **Lorries** bring them to the sawmill. There they are stored on a large yard and sorted by type of wood and thickness. In Switzerland, the **spruce** is the most important wood for sawmills. Before a trunk is sawn, a machine peels off the bark. This step is called **debarking**.

Large saws cut the trunk lengthways. A **board** is flat and much wider than it is thick. A **beam** is a thick, square-edged piece of wood used, for example, to build roof frames. **Battens** are narrow, thin strips of wood. All of this together is called **sawn timber**. Today computers measure the trunk and calculate how best to saw it.

Freshly sawn wood contains a lot of water. To stop it warping later, it has to dry. The boards are stacked with small pieces of wood between them so that **air** can pass through. In the open air this often takes many months. It is quicker in a **drying kiln** with warm air.

Sawing produces **sawdust**, shavings and offcuts. From these, **pellets** and wood chips for heating are made. Chipboard and paper can also be made from such leftovers. The bark is often used as fuel or as bark mulch in the garden. In this way almost the whole trunk is used.

In the past, many sawmills stood on streams. A **water wheel** drove the saw, which moved up and down. A saw like this, with blades clamped in a frame, is called a **frame saw**. In Switzerland you can still visit some old, water-powered sawmills today.

gewusst: The frame saw gets its name in German, “Gattersäge”, because its saw blades are clamped in a frame, the “Gatter”.
When a round trunk is sawn, side pieces with bark always remain, which are called slabs.

teile.einleitung: Salicylic acid is a substance found in plants such as the willow. Acetylsalicylic acid, one of the best-known active ingredients against pain and fever, is derived from it.
wichtigste: The name comes from “Salix”, the Latin name for the willow.
Willow bark contains salicin, which becomes salicylic acid in the body.
Acetylsalicylic acid is one of the non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
It inhibits cyclooxygenase and thereby the formation of prostaglandins.
In low doses it inhibits the clumping of blood platelets.
It is usually not given to children with viral infections because of Reye’s syndrome.
In plants, salicylic acid is a signalling substance for defence.

abschnitte.titel: From the willow to the active ingredient
abschnitte.text: A long time ago, people used **willow bark** against fever and pain. The active substance in it is called **salicin**. In the body it is converted into **salicylic acid**. The name is derived from **“Salix”**, the Latin word for willow. Meadowsweet also contains such compounds. In the 19th century, chemists learned to make salicylic acid artificially.

Today salicylic acid is produced industrially. The most important process is the **Kolbe-Schmitt reaction**. In it, **sodium phenolate** reacts with **carbon dioxide** under pressure and heat. The process is named after the German chemists Hermann Kolbe and Rudolf Schmitt. From salicylic acid, **acetylsalicylic acid** is then made, which came onto the market in 1899 under the name Aspirin.

Acetylsalicylic acid is one of the **non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs**. It inhibits an enzyme called **cyclooxygenase**. As a result, the body makes fewer **prostaglandins**, which are messenger substances that promote pain, fever and inflammation. In low doses it also inhibits the **clumping of blood platelets**. That is why it is prescribed to some people to help prevent heart attacks.

Children and teenagers with **viral infections** such as flu or chickenpox are usually **not given acetylsalicylic acid**. The reason is the rare but dangerous **Reye’s syndrome**, which can damage the liver and brain. The drug can also irritate the stomach. Medicines should therefore only ever be taken on the advice of experts such as doctors or pharmacists.

Salicylic acid itself is used in **skin remedies**, for example in **wart plasters**. It **dissolves hardened skin**, so that it comes off more easily. Salicylic acid is also important for plants. There it is a **signalling substance for defence**: when a plant is attacked by pathogens, salicylic acid helps to switch on the defence in other parts of the plant too.

gewusst: The name Aspirin recalls meadowsweet, which used to be called Spiraea in scientific terms.
Acetylsalicylic acid is one of the most widely used medicines in the world.

teile.einleitung: Rhizobia are bacteria in the soil that work together with legumes such as peas, beans and clover. They live in small nodules on the roots and take nitrogen from the air, which the plant uses as fertiliser.
wichtigste: Rhizobia live in root nodules of their host plant.
From the plant they receive carbohydrates from photosynthesis.
They trigger the formation of nodules with Nod factors.
In the nodule they become bacteroids.
An active nodule is pink inside.
In Switzerland, soya seed is often inoculated with bacteria.
Clover-grass or peas leave nitrogen behind for the following crop.

abschnitte.text: Plants need **nitrogen** to grow. The air is made up of almost four fifths nitrogen, but plants cannot use it in that form. **Rhizobia** can. They live in **symbiosis** with legumes, that is, in a partnership from which both benefit. The bacteria convert nitrogen from the air into a form that the plant can take up. In return they receive **carbohydrates** from the plant, made by **photosynthesis**.

The roots release substances into the soil that attract suitable rhizobia. The bacteria reply with signal substances, the **Nod factors**. These trigger the plant to form **root nodules**. The bacteria move into the nodules and change there into the form that fixes nitrogen. They are then called **bacteroids**. On peas, field beans and clover, the species **Rhizobium leguminosarum** forms such nodules.

If you cut open a root nodule, you can see whether it is working. An active nodule is **pink** inside. The colour comes from a substance similar to the red pigment in blood: **leghaemoglobin**. It keeps the oxygen level in the nodule low, because the bacteria’s tool for fixing nitrogen cannot tolerate oxygen. A grey or greenish nodule fixes hardly any nitrogen.

Farmers make deliberate use of rhizobia. In **crop rotation**, **clover-grass** or **peas** are often grown before **wheat**. They leave **nitrogen** in the soil that the following crop can use, and less fertiliser is needed. **Soya** comes from Asia, and the matching nodule bacteria are usually missing from Swiss soils. That is why **soya seed** is often **inoculated** with the bacteria before sowing.

gewusst: Each group of legumes needs its own matching rhizobia.
The fact that legumes use nitrogen from the air with the help of bacteria was discovered at the end of the 19th century.

teile.einleitung: Many seeds do not germinate at once, even when it is damp and warm. They are in a state of seed dormancy and wait for the right moment.
wichtigste: The technical term for seed dormancy is dormancy.
It prevents seeds from germinating shortly before winter.
Stratification is the deliberate chilling of seeds so that they germinate.
Scarification is scratching a hard seed coat.
Light germinators only germinate with light.
The store of dormant seeds in the soil is called the seed bank.
A seed from a date palm about 2,000 years old germinated in 2005.

abschnitte.text: **Seed dormancy** is a kind of sleep state of the seed. For plants in Switzerland this has a big advantage: many seeds ripen in late summer or autumn. If they germinated at once, the young seedlings would freeze in **winter**. Seed dormancy makes sure that they only germinate in **spring**. Often not all seeds germinate in the same year either, so the plant spreads its risk.

Some seeds first have to lie cold for a while before they germinate. This deliberate chilling is called **stratification**. Gardeners, for example, put such seeds in the fridge for a few weeks. Other seeds have a **very hard coat** that hardly lets water through. They are carefully nicked or rubbed, which is called **scarification**. In nature, frost, soil animals or the gut of birds often do this.

Some seeds only germinate when they receive **light**. They are called **light germinators**. They often lie in the soil for a long time and only germinate when they come to the surface, for example after digging. A large store of dormant seeds that can germinate lies in the soil in this way. This store is called the **seed bank**. That is why many plants often spring up quickly on freshly dug soil.

Some seeds stay able to germinate for a very long time. In Israel, seeds of a **date palm** about **2,000 years** old were found during excavations. In **2005** one of them was made to germinate. For the future, seeds from all over the world are stored in a large vault on **Spitsbergen**, at about **minus 18 degrees Celsius**. Cold and dryness extend seed dormancy there by many years.

gewusst: The date palm that grew from the ancient seed was nicknamed “Methuselah”.
Some seeds of wild herbs stay able to germinate in the soil for decades.

teile.einleitung: Rice is a cereal plant and, for a great many people in the world, the most important staple food, especially in Asia. It often grows in fields that are under water.
wichtigste: Rice is a cereal, like wheat and maize.
It very often grows in flooded fields.
The best-known rice field in Switzerland is in Ticino.
Risotto and rice pudding are cooked from rice.
Brown rice still has its brown husk.
In many Asian countries rice is eaten with chopsticks.

abschnitte.text: Like wheat, barley and maize, rice is a **cereal**, that is, a type of grass. The plant has long, narrow leaves and often grows to about a metre tall. At the top it forms a **panicle** with many grains. Each grain of rice is surrounded by a hard husk, which is removed before eating. Rice has been grown for thousands of years, especially in **China and India**.

Rice very often grows in **flooded fields**, which is called **paddy rice**. The farmers plant the young plants in the shallow water. The water keeps away many weeds, which cannot grow there. In hilly areas, terraces that look like giant staircases are built for this. There are also varieties of rice that grow in dry fields.

Rice grows in Switzerland too. The best-known rice field is in **Ticino**, near Ascona on Lake Maggiore. It is regarded as one of the northernmost rice fields in Europe. **Risotto rice** is grown there. For some years now, farmers in other cantons have also been trying to grow rice in wet fields.

With **brown rice**, the brown husk around the grain is still there. It contains more fibre and vitamins and takes longer to cook. With **white rice**, this husk has been polished off. There are many varieties: long-grain rice such as basmati, round short-grain rice or sticky rice, which is used to make sushi in Japan.

Many dishes are cooked from rice. **Risotto** comes from Italy and is very popular in Ticino. For **rice pudding**, rice is cooked with **milk and sugar**. In many Asian countries rice is served with almost every meal, and it is eaten with **chopsticks**. Rice is also made into rice noodles, rice cakes and rice flour.

gewusst: For more people, rice is a staple food than almost any other plant.
On some rice terraces in Asia, rice has been grown for centuries.

teile.einleitung: The common beech is one of the most important broadleaved trees in Switzerland. It has smooth, grey bark and forms dense, shady woods.
wichtigste: The common beech is a broadleaved tree.
In German it is called the “red beech” because its wood is slightly reddish.
Its bark is smooth and silvery grey.
The edge of the leaf is slightly wavy.
In winter it can be recognised by its long, pointed buds.
Squirrels like to eat beechnuts in autumn.
The copper beech is a variety with dark red leaves.

abschnitte.text: The common beech is a large **broadleaved tree** that can grow to over 30 metres tall. Its bark feels **smooth** and is silvery grey. The leaves are egg-shaped, and the edge is **slightly wavy**. In winter the beech can be recognised by its **long, pointed buds**, which recall small cigars. In autumn the leaves turn golden yellow to brown.

The leaves of the common beech are green. It gets its German name, “Rotbuche”, from its **wood**, which is **slightly reddish**. This is how it is told apart from the hornbeam, which has paler wood and belongs to a different family. There is also a variety with **dark red leaves**: the **copper beech**. It is often planted in parks and gardens.

The fruits of the beech are called **beechnuts**. They are three-sided and sit two at a time in a spiky husk. In autumn they fall to the ground. **Squirrels**, mice, birds and wild boar like to eat them. Squirrels also hide stores in the ground. Forgotten beechnuts can then grow into new trees.

In summer it is often quite dark in a beech wood, because the **canopy is very dense**. Only a little light reaches the ground. That is why many plants such as the wood anemone flower as early as spring, before the beeches get their leaves. The beech itself tolerates a lot of shade, so young beeches can grow up beneath old trees.

Beech wood is hard and strong. It is often used **for furniture and toys**, for example for chairs, building blocks and wooden spoons. It is also popular as firewood because it burns well and for a long time. In Switzerland the beech is the most common broadleaved tree in the forest.

gewusst: The German word “Buchstabe”, meaning “letter”, is probably connected with the beech, “Buche”: in the past, signs were carved into wooden sticks.
A beech can live to be several hundred years old.

teile.einleitung: The common dogwood, called “Roter Hartriegel” in German, is a native shrub that grows at woodland edges and in hedges. Its twigs often glow red in winter, and its wood is especially hard.
wichtigste: The twigs of the common dogwood are often red in winter.
It blooms white in flat flower clusters.
Its fruits are blue-black and bitter, and should not be eaten raw.
The leaf veins curve towards the tip of the leaf.
If you gently pull a leaf apart, you can see fine white threads.
The German name “Hartriegel” points to the hard wood.

abschnitte.text: The common dogwood usually grows a few metres tall and likes to grow **at woodland edges and in hedges**. In winter its twigs are often **red**, especially on the side that faces the sun. In autumn the leaves also turn dark red. That is why the shrub stands out all year round. It is often planted in hedges and parks.

The leaves are egg-shaped and have a smooth edge. Their veins run **in curves towards the tip of the leaf**, which is a good way of recognising it. If you gently pull a leaf apart crosswise, you can see **fine white threads** between the two halves. They are parts of the vessels in the leaf, which stretch like tiny spirals. This also works with other kinds of dogwood.

In late spring many small **white flowers** appear in flat, umbrella-shaped clusters. They attract beetles, flies and bees. From them grow small, round fruits that are **blue-black**. To people they are **bitter** and should not be eaten raw. Many birds, however, like to eat them and so spread the seeds.

The German name **“Hartriegel”** points to the **hard wood**. In the past it was used for objects that had to take a lot of wear, for example tool handles, sticks or small turned items. A close relative is the **Cornelian cherry**, which flowers yellow in early spring. Unlike the common dogwood, it has edible red fruits.

gewusst: The scientific name “sanguinea” means “blood-red” and refers to the red colour of the twigs and autumn leaves.
The white flowers of the common dogwood smell rather unpleasant to people.

teile.einleitung: In some regions of the Earth the ground never thaws completely, not even in summer. This permanently frozen ground is called permafrost. It exists in the Arctic, but also high up in the Swiss Alps.
wichtigste: Permafrost is ground that stays frozen all year round.
Ground counts as permafrost if it is at most zero degrees for at least two years without a break.
About a quarter of the land area of the northern hemisphere lies on permafrost.
In Siberia the frozen ground in places reaches down over a thousand metres.
In Switzerland there is permafrost on about five per cent of the area, mostly above about 2,500 metres.
When permafrost thaws, rockfalls, debris flows and damage to buildings can arise.
A lot of carbon is stored in permafrost, which can be released as a greenhouse gas when it thaws.

abschnitte.text: **Permafrost** means “permanently frozen ground”. It means ground or rock that stays frozen for at least two years in a row. Often it is much older and has been frozen since the last ice age. In summer only a thin upper layer thaws, the **active layer**.

The biggest permafrost regions lie in Siberia, Alaska, Canada and Greenland. There the ground is frozen in places several hundred metres deep. In high mountains such as the Alps, the Himalayas and the Andes there is also **mountain permafrost**. Even under the sea floor of the Arctic lies frozen ground.

In the Swiss Alps you find permafrost mainly on shady north slopes and in scree slopes above about 2,500 metres. It holds loose rock together like a cement. Typical are **rock glaciers**, masses of rubble with ice in them that creep slowly down the valley. The **PERMOS** measuring network has been watching how Swiss permafrost changes since the year 2000.

Through climate change, permafrost is warming. When the ice in the rock melts, rockfalls and debris flows can be set off. Mountain railway stations, pylons and mountain huts that stand on frozen ground can develop cracks. In the Arctic, roads and houses subside, and lakes and hollows form that are called **thermokarst**.

In permafrost are huge amounts of dead plants that have never rotted. When the ground thaws, bacteria break this material down. In doing so **carbon dioxide** and methane form, two greenhouse gases. This can strengthen global warming further.

Because the ground acts like a deep freezer, remains are preserved in it for a long time. In Siberia **mammoths** have been found in which even skin and fur were preserved. Researchers also take drill cores from permafrost to study the climate of earlier times. In this way the frozen ground tells stories from the ice age.

begriffe.erklaerung: Ground that stays frozen for at least two years without a break.
The upper layer of ground that thaws in summer.
A mass of rubble with ice that creeps slowly down the slope.
A strong greenhouse gas that forms in rotting without oxygen.

gewusst: At Pontresina in the Engadine a protective dam was built to protect the village from avalanches and debris flows from thawing slopes.
Researchers have found tiny worms in Siberian permafrost that came back to life after tens of thousands of years.
Houses in Siberia are often built on piles so that their warmth does not thaw the frozen ground.

teile.einleitung: Tendrils are thin, bendy parts of a plant that climbing plants use to hold on. This lets plants with weak stems reach up towards the light without having to build a thick trunk.
wichtigste: Tendrils are used for holding on and climbing.
When a tendril touches a support, it wraps around it.
Many tendrils curl up into a spiral.
Peas, cucumbers, pumpkins and grapevines climb with tendrils.
In the pea, the tendrils have developed from leaves.
In the garden, plants with tendrils need a support such as a trellis or a net.

abschnitte.text: Plants need light to grow. A tall tree builds a strong trunk of wood for this. Climbing plants save themselves the trouble: they hold on to other plants, fences or walls. Many of them have **tendrils** for this. These are thread-like parts that grow out into the air, searching, until they find something to hold on to.

Tendrils can **feel touch**. When a tendril bumps into a stick, it grows faster on one side than on the other. This makes it curve and wrap around the support. After that, the free part often curls into a **spiral** that looks like a little spring. This spring pulls the plant closer to the support and cushions it in the wind.

Tendrils are changed parts of the plant. In the **pea**, parts of the leaves have become tendrils, which are called **leaf tendrils**. In the **grapevine**, the tendrils have developed from parts of the shoot, which are called **shoot tendrils**. From the outside they look similar, but experts can tell from their structure what they grew from.

abschnitte.titel: Plants with tendrils in the garden
abschnitte.text: In the vegetable garden, **peas**, **cucumbers** and **pumpkins** climb with tendrils. On the **vine**, tendrils hold the shoots to the wires on which the grapes grow. To thrive, plants with tendrils need a **support**: a trellis, a net, sticks or a fence. If they lie on the ground, the fruit rots more easily and the plant gets less light.

Not all climbing plants have tendrils. **Ivy** holds on to walls with small clinging roots. The **bean** winds its whole stem around a pole. **Clematis** clings on with its leaf stalks. Tendrils are therefore only one of several solutions for getting upwards.

gewusst: The naturalist Charles Darwin wrote a whole book about climbing plants and their movements.
A cucumber tendril often suddenly turns in the opposite direction in the middle, so that it does not get twisted as it curls up.

teile.einleitung: Pioneer plants are the first plants to settle new, barren ground. They grow on rubble, sand, gravel or rock. In Switzerland you find them, for example, in front of glaciers and on riverbanks.
wichtigste: A **pioneer plant** is the first to settle new, barren ground.
Many have light seeds that fly on the **wind**.
Pioneer plants need a lot of **light** and few nutrients.
Their roots hold the loose **scree** in place.
They form **humus** and so make room for other species.
Examples are Fleischer’s willowherb, alpine toadflax and coltsfoot.

abschnitte.titel: New land in front of the glacier
abschnitte.text: When glaciers retreat, bare rubble is left behind, the **glacier foreland**. There is hardly any soil there yet. Many pioneer plants have tiny seeds with **fluffy hairs**. The wind carries them far over scree and moraines. **Fleischer’s willowherb** with its pink flowers is a typical pioneer plant on glacier rubble and river gravel.

On open scree there is a lot of **light**, but hardly any nutrients and often little water. Pioneer plants are adapted to exactly this. The **alpine toadflax** with violet and orange flowers grows on moving limestone scree. Its long shoots creep through the scree and survive the stones slipping. The roots of many pioneers run through gravel and sand and hold the soil in place.

The **green alder** is a shrub of the mountains. It lives together with bacteria in nodules on its roots. These fix **nitrogen** from the air and so also fertilise the barren soil. **Coltsfoot** quickly settles bare soil, rubble and building sites. Its yellow flowers appear in spring before the big leaves.

When pioneer plants die, **humus** slowly forms. In this soil other plants can now grow. They get bigger and shade the ground. The light-loving pioneers are often pushed out as a result. This sequence of plant communities is called **succession**. In the end, after a long time, a forest can even stand in such places.

gewusst: On building sites and gravel yards in towns, the same pioneers often grow as in the mountains.
In front of many Swiss glaciers you can see on a walk how the plants become denser with distance from the ice.

teile.einleitung: A flowering plant looks very different at first sight, whether a daisy or an oak. Yet almost all are built to the same plan. If you know it, you understand how a plant takes up water, makes food and reproduces.
wichtigste: A typical flowering plant has three basic organs: root, shoot axis and leaf.
The root hairs take up water and minerals from the soil.
In the xylem, water is transported upwards from the root.
In the phloem, sugar and other nutrients are distributed.
In broad leaves, most stomata lie on the underside of the leaf.
From the annual rings of a felled tree you can read its approximate age.
The stamen is the male organ of the flower and makes the pollen.

abschnitte.text: The **root** anchors the plant firmly in the ground. With the fine **root hairs** it takes up water and minerals. Root hairs enlarge the surface enormously, like the fibres of a terry towel. Some plants such as the carrot also store nutrients in the root.

The **shoot axis** is the stem or, in trees, the trunk. It carries leaves and flowers and holds them in the light. In it run conducting tissues: in the **xylem** water rises upwards, in the **phloem** sugar solution flows to all parts of the plant. In trees the shoot axis becomes thicker every year and turns woody.

The **leaf** is the food factory of the plant, and photosynthesis takes place here. It consists of leaf stalk and leaf blade, crossed by leaf veins. On the underside there are usually most of the **stomata**, tiny pores for gas exchange. There it is shadier, so less water evaporates.

The **flower** serves reproduction. On the outside lie green sepals and coloured petals that attract insects. The **stamens** are the male organs and make the pollen. In the middle sits the pistil with the ovary, from which fruit and seeds develop after pollination.

In trees, a thin growth layer under the bark forms new wood every year. In spring light, loose wood forms, in late summer darker, dense wood. In this way one **annual ring** forms per year. If you count the rings on a tree stump, you know roughly the age of the tree.

If you know the structure of a plant, you understand why it has to be watered and needs light. Gardeners and farmers use this knowledge in growing, fertilising and pruning. Features such as leaf shape and flower structure also help in identifying plants. Root, shoot axis and leaf can also be modified, for example into **thorns**, tendrils or tubers.

begriffe.erklaerung: The stem or trunk of a plant.
Conducting tissue that transports water upwards.
Conducting tissue that distributes sugar solution in the plant.
A tiny pore in the leaf for gas exchange.
The male part of the flower that makes pollen.

gewusst: The potato tuber is not a root but a thickened underground part of the shoot axis.
The prickles of the rose are not true thorns but outgrowths of the bark.
From the width of the annual rings you can read whether a year was wet or dry.

teile.einleitung: The bulrush is a plant at the edge of ponds and lakes. It is easy to recognise by its brown, velvety spike, which looks like a sausage on a stick.
wichtigste: The flower spike looks like a brown club.
The bulrush grows in shallow water at the edge.
Its leaves are long and narrow.
The spike feels as soft as velvet.
In winter the spike breaks up into white, fluffy flakes.
The seeds are spread by the wind.
The broadleaf bulrush grows taller than an adult.

abschnitte.titel: A plant at the water’s edge
abschnitte.text: The **bulrush** grows in **shallow water** at the edge of ponds, lakes, ditches and slow streams. Its roots are in the muddy bottom. The **leaves** are **long and narrow** like ribbons. The **broadleaf bulrush** can grow to over two metres tall, so **taller than an adult**. It often forms dense stands in which birds such as the reed warbler find shelter.

Most striking is the **flower spike**. It looks like a **brown club** at the end of a long stem. The spike is made up of thousands of tiny flowers sitting close together. It feels **as soft as velvet**. Above the spike there is a thinner part with flowers that release pollen. It soon withers and leaves only a bare tip.

In autumn and **winter** the spike changes. It bursts open and **breaks up into white, fluffy flakes**. These are countless small seeds, each with fine hairs. With these hairs the seeds are carried far away **by the wind**. If they land on damp ground, a new plant can grow.

People used to use the bulrush in many ways. The fluffy **seed hairs** served **as filling for pillows** and blankets. Mats, baskets and seats for chairs were woven from the leaves. Today the bulrush is also used in constructed wetlands, because it helps to clean water.

gewusst: A single bulrush can produce hundreds of thousands of tiny seeds.
The bulrush is often confused with reed, but reed has no brown spikes.

teile.einleitung: A **population** is all the living things of one species that live in the same area at the same time, for example all the brown trout in a stream. Biologists study how large a population is and how it grows or shrinks. Simple maths often helps with this.
wichtigste: A population includes all the individuals of one species in an area.
The **population density** is the number of animals per area.
Births, deaths, immigration and emigration change the size.
Without limits a population grows **exponentially**.
Near the carrying capacity an **S-shaped** curve appears.
Lynx and snowshoe hare show a famous predator and prey pattern.

abschnitte.text: A population consists of the **individuals of the same species** in a particular area. All the brown trout in a stream, for example, form a population. So do all the roe deer in a forest. The animals of a population live together, compete for food and have young. How many animals live per area is called the **population density**.

You work out the density like this: number of animals divided by the area. If 300 roe deer live in 60 km² of forest, that is 300 ÷ 60 = **5 roe deer per km²**. The size of a population changes through **births** and **deaths**. If a population has 200 animals, 50 young are born and 30 die, there are afterwards 200 + 50 minus 30 = **220**. To this come **immigration** and **emigration**.

If a population has enough food and space, it can grow very fast. A bacterium that divides every 20 minutes becomes 2 in the first 20 minutes, then 4, then **8** bacteria within an hour. The number doubles again and again. This is called **exponential growth**. In nature, however, this cannot go on for ever.

Every habitat has a **carrying capacity**: only so many animals find enough food and space. At first a population grows slowly, then fast and finally more slowly again. The growth curve therefore becomes **S-shaped**. This is called **logistic growth**. In the end the number fluctuates around the limit.

Populations also influence one another. Famous are the figures of the **Hudson’s Bay Company** in Canada. Over many decades it recorded how many pelts it bought. The numbers of **Canada lynx** and **snowshoe hare** fluctuate in cycles of about ten years. When there are many hares, the lynx later increase too.

gewusst: The pelt figures of the Hudson’s Bay Company are among the best-known data series in ecology.
Under good conditions bacteria can divide in less than half an hour.

teile.einleitung: How clean is a stream? The saprobic system answers this question with the help of animals and other living things that live in the water. It shows how heavily a body of water is polluted with degradable organic substances.
wichtigste: Saprobity describes how much a body of water is polluted with easily degradable organic substances.
The system was founded at the start of the 20th century by Richard Kolkwitz and Maximilian Marsson.
A distinction is made between levels from oligosaprobic (clean) to polysaprobic (very heavily polluted).
Indicator organisms such as stonefly larvae or tubifex worms reveal the condition of the water.
The saprobic index according to Pantle and Buck ranges from about 1 to 4.
Saprobity refers to the breakdown, and trophy to the build-up, of organic substances.

abschnitte.text: When sewage, leaves or manure get into a stream, a lot of **organic matter** enters the water. Bacteria break down these substances and use up **oxygen** in doing so. The more degradable substances there are in the water, the less oxygen is left for fish and small animals. **Saprobity** states how heavy this pollution is. The word comes from the Greek “sapros”, which means “rotten”.

The researchers **Richard Kolkwitz** and **Maximilian Marsson** drew up lists of **indicator organisms** around 1908. These are living things that only occur under certain water conditions. Anyone who finds them can draw conclusions about the water quality. The lists were later added to and are still the basis of the system today.

**Oligosaprobic** water is clean and rich in oxygen. Sensitive animals such as **stonefly larvae** live there. **Beta-mesosaprobic** water is moderately polluted, and typical here is the freshwater shrimp *Gammarus*. Alpha-mesosaprobic water is already heavily polluted. In **polysaprobic** water there is hardly any oxygen left, and red **tubifex worms** live in huge numbers in the putrid sludge.

Each indicator species is assigned a **saprobic value** between about 1 and 4. In the method of **Pantle and Buck**, you also count how common each species is. Then you work out a **weighted average**: you multiply each saprobic value by the abundance, add everything up and divide by the sum of the abundances. The smaller the index, the cleaner the water.

The two terms are often confused. **Trophy** describes how much plants and algae build up new material thanks to nutrients such as phosphorus. **Saprobity**, by contrast, describes the **breakdown** of organic substances by bacteria and other decomposers. A body of water can contain many nutrients and still be only slightly polluted with organic matter. In Switzerland, too, streams are assessed by the small animals that live in them.

gewusst: Tubifex worms can be so numerous that the bed of a polluted body of water looks red.
With a magnifying glass and an identification chart, school classes can also assess the water quality of a stream themselves.

teile.einleitung: The spindle tree, in German “Pfaffenhütchen”, is a shrub that stands out especially in autumn. Its pink fruits with orange seeds glow from afar. But take care: the whole plant is poisonous.
wichtigste: The fruits of the spindle tree are pink to purple-red.
The seeds are enclosed in an orange coat.
All parts of the plant are poisonous, especially the seeds.
The shape of the fruit recalls an old headgear of priests.
The shrub is also called the spindle shrub (“Spindelstrauch”) and robin bread (“Rotkehlchenbrot”).
The green twigs often have narrow cork ridges.

abschnitte.text: The fruit of the spindle tree has four lobes. It looks like an old headgear of Catholic priests. In the past priests were also called **“Pfaffen”**, hence the German name **“Pfaffenhütchen”**, meaning “little priest’s hat”. The shrub grows wild in Switzerland at **woodland edges**, in **hedges** and in riverside woods. It usually grows two to three metres tall.

In autumn the spindle tree is very striking. Its **fruits** glow **pink to purple-red**. When they split open, you see the seeds. They sit in a bright **orange coat**. At the same time many **leaves** turn bright **red**. Together this makes one of the most colourful shrubs in the wood.

All parts of the spindle tree are **poisonous**, especially the **seeds**. The colourful fruits look tempting, but you must **never eat them**. Even a few fruits can harm a person. Anyone who has eaten some should inform an adult at once. In Switzerland, the emergency number **145** of Tox Info Suisse helps with poisonings.

For many birds, on the other hand, the seeds are good **winter food**. The **robin** especially likes to eat them. That is why the shrub is also called **robin bread** (“Rotkehlchenbrot”). The birds spread the seeds when they pass them out again. In this way young spindle trees grow in new places.

On the green **twigs** there are often two to four narrow **cork ridges**. That is why the twigs feel angular. The wood is hard and fine. In the past it was used to make **spindles** for spinning wool and flax. That is why the shrub is also called the **spindle shrub** (“Spindelstrauch”).

gewusst: In the past, drawing charcoal for artists was also made from the wood of the spindle tree.
Sometimes a whole shrub is covered by a fine white web. In it live the caterpillars of a small moth, the spindle ermine.
